title: On Reconstructing a Convex Polygon from Partial Information
summary: The reconstruction problem asks to construct a (convex) polygon that has a specified set of features, such as an ordered set of edge-lengths or an ordered set of polygon-angles. In this paper, we do a systematic exploration of the reconstruction problem in all scenarios where one or two sets of features have been specified. Some of these scenarios were well-studied already, for some we develop testing-algorithms and/or hardness results, and many give rise to interesting open problems for future study.

AI.tldr: Systematic survey of convex-polygon reconstruction from one or two feature sets (ordered edge-lengths and/or angles), summarizing known results, introducing testing algorithms and hardness results, and outlining open problems.
AI.motivation: To map the algorithmic landscape of reconstructing convex polygons from partial specifications, clarifying which cases are tractable, which are hard, and what remains as open questions.
AI.method: Comprehensive taxonomy across all one- or two-feature scenarios; review of prior work; development of testing algorithms and hardness proofs for selected cases; synthesis into a unified framework with open questions.
AI.result: A complete taxonomy of reconstruction problems under one- or two-feature specifications; results include new testing algorithms and hardness proofs for certain cases; compilation of existing results and identification of open problems.
AI.conclusion: Provides a roadmap for future research by consolidating results and highlighting gaps, enabling targeted algorithmic and complexity investigations in polygon reconstruction from feature sets.

title: From Ham-Sandwich to Centerpoints: Semialgebraic Algorithms for Cutting Polytopal Measures
summary: We design exact algorithms for the ham-sandwich and centerpoint theorems for polytopal measures. Our key observation is that the cap-volume function of such a measure, i.e., the volume cut off by a halfspace, is piecewise rational on a natural decomposition of the space of oriented hyperplanes. This lets us recast prescribed-proportion cutting problems as semialgebraic feasibility problems. For fixed ambient dimension, this yields polynomial-time algorithms to decide the existence of cuts, describe the full solution set, and sample or enumerate solutions. We extend this framework to the center transversal theorem, showing that spaces of deep affine flats are semialgebraic, which holds for centerpoints. We further show that the set of centerpoints of a convex polytope coincides with its floating body at level $1/(d+1)$, a useful semialgebraic description.

AI.tldr: Cap-volume for polytopal measures is piecewise rational on a natural hyperplane decomposition, enabling semialgebraic feasibility formulations that yield exact, polynomial-time algorithms in fixed dimension for ham-sandwich/centerpoint-type problems; extended to center transversal and to deep affine flats; floating body at level 1/(d+1) semialgebraically describes centerpoints.
AI.motivation: Provide exact, algorithmic solutions for cutting problems (ham-sandwich, centerpoint, center transversal) and to describe associated geometric spaces using semialgebraic methods; bridge discrete geometry with real algebraic geometry.
AI.method: Show cap-volume is piecewise rational over a natural decomposition of oriented hyperplanes; recast prescribed-proportion cuts as semialgebraic feasibility problems; in fixed dimension, obtain polynomial-time decision, full solution descriptions, and sampling/enumeration; extend framework to center transversal and to spaces of deep affine flats; relate centerpoints to the floating body at level 1/(d+1).
AI.result: Polynomial-time algorithms (fixed dimension) for existence of cuts, complete solution sets, and sampling/enumeration; semialgebraic descriptions for spaces of centerpoints and deep flats; equivalence of centerpoints with the floating body at level 1/(d+1).
AI.conclusion: Integrates computational geometry with real algebraic geometry via a semialgebraic framework, enabling exact, efficient solutions for major ham-sandwich/centerpoint-type problems and providing new geometric characterizations (e.g., centerpoints = floating body at δ=1/(d+1)).

title: WaveLander: A Generalizable Hierarchical Control Framework for UAV Landing on Wave-Disturbed Platforms via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on wave-disturbed marine platforms remains challenging due to stochastic platform motion, time-varying platform attitude, and uncertain touchdown conditions. Existing model-based methods often require accurate motion prediction and online optimization, while end-to-end learning approaches may suffer from high training complexity and limited interpretability. This paper presents WaveLander, a hierarchical control framework via reinforcement learning (RL) that decouples vertical landing decision-making from low-level flight stabilization. The RL policy maps a compact platform-relative observation to a scalar vertical velocity reference, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains attitude stability and lateral tracking. This formulation reduces dynamic platform landing to a low-dimensional, timing-aware control problem and enables smooth landing behavior without explicit switching rules. Simulation results under randomized wave-induced platform motions show that WaveLander achieves robust landing performance and generalizes to unseen disturbance conditions, demonstrating the potential of hierarchical learning-based control for marine UAV recovery.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical RL framework WaveLander enables autonomous vertical landing of UAVs on wave-disturbed platforms by decoupling vertical landing from stabilization; demonstrates robust simulation performance and generalization.
AI.motivation: Tackle challenges of stochastic platform motion, time-varying platform attitude, and uncertain touchdown conditions; overcome limitations of model-based and end-to-end learning approaches.
AI.method: RL policy outputs a platform-relative vertical velocity reference from a compact observation; a conventional low-level flight controller handles attitude stabilization and lateral tracking; hierarchical design reduces the problem to a low-dimensional, timing-aware control task and avoids explicit switching rules.
AI.result: Simulation results show robust landing under randomized wave-induced disturbances and generalization to unseen conditions.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical learning-based control is a promising approach for robust marine UAV recovery, offering interpretability and adaptability with reduced complexity.

title: Multilayer Q-Matrix-Embedded Neural Network for Cognitive Diagnosis (M-QCDNet): Structure-Aware Deep Learning Architecture for Psychometric Interpretability
summary: The research proposes a multilayer Q-matrix-embedded neural network for cognitive diagnosis (M-QCDNet), which integrates the structural interpretability of cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs) with the deep learning neural network (NN). M-QCDNet structures the item-skill relationship using the Q-matrix as a structural prior, ensuring latent mastery profiles remain interpretable and consistent with cognitive theory, followed by the proposed loss function with an L2 penalty to penalize skills not aligned with the Q-matrix and to balance predictive performance and structural alignment. Corresponding evaluation matrices, the interpretable alignment-based metrics that quantify the degree to which predicted skill activations correspond to item-level skills, were further developed. M-QCDNet offers practical benefits for classroom practice, enabling early detection of learning difficulties and supporting mastery-based interventions. By embedding diagnostic validity into model design, M-QCDNet bridges psychometric transparency and neural flexibility, advancing interpretable, fair, and actionable AI for cognitive diagnostics.

AI.tldr: A multilayer Q-matrix-embedded neural network (M-QCDNet) integrates cognitive diagnosis models with neural nets using a Q-matrix prior and L2 penalties to ensure interpretable skill mastery predictions and introduces alignment metrics for evaluation, aiming for interpretable, fair, actionable AI in cognitive diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Address the need for interpretable, valid cognitive diagnostics that combine psychometric structure with data-driven learning, enabling early detection of difficulties and mastery-based interventions.
AI.method: Embed Q-matrix as structural prior in a multilayer NN; enforce L2 penalty to align predicted skill activations with the Q-matrix; develop evaluation metrics for interpretability based on skill-item alignment; discuss practical deployment in classroom settings.
AI.result: Conceptual/modeling contribution with proposed loss, metrics, and discussion of practical benefits; no reported empirical results in abstract.
AI.conclusion: M-QCDNet bridges psychometric transparency and neural flexibility, advancing interpretable, fair, and actionable AI for cognitive diagnostics.

title: AnchorSplat: Fast and Structure Consistent Detail Synthesis for Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful representation for high-fidelity rendering. However, existing assets often suffer from quality bottlenecks such as missing details and texture noise. Prior attempts to enhance these assets via 2D image processing introduce multi-view inconsistencies and high computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel 3D-native refinement paradigm named AnchorSplat. AnchorSplat is an end-to-end deep network operating directly on 3D structures, avoiding the expensive optimization overhead of traditional 3D-2D-3D pipelines. Crucially, AnchorSplat is a strictly source-free solution requiring no original multi-view images. Central to the proposed method is the Point Anchor Mechanism, which enforces geometric consistency via local offset constraints, mitigating ill-posed mapping and gradient confounding. Furthermore, AnchorSplat replaces iterative densification with a single-pass multiplication mechanism. To facilitate research, we construct 3DGS-SR, the first large-scale benchmark for this task. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the 3DGS-SR dataset, with throughput up to $10^5$ times faster than optimization methods. Notably, AnchorSplat exhibits robust zero-shot generalization across diverse data distributions, including generative model outputs and real-world scans.

AI.tldr: AnchorSplat is a 3D-native, source-free refinement network for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a Point Anchor Mechanism to enforce local geometric consistency, replaces iterative densification with a single-pass multiplication, and achieves state-of-the-art results with large speedups; introduces the 3DGS-SR benchmark and shows strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: To overcome quality bottlenecks in 3DGS assets (missing details, texture noise) and the inefficiencies of 2D image-based refinements that rely on multi-view optimization, by proposing a 3D-native, source-free refinement framework.
AI.method: An end-to-end 3D network operating directly on 3D structures; introduces Point Anchor Mechanism for local offset constraints to ensure geometric consistency; replaces iterative densification with a single-pass multiplication; strictly source-free (no original multi-view images); accompanied by the 3DGS-SR benchmark.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on the 3DGS-SR dataset; throughput up to 10^5x faster than optimization-based methods; demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization across diverse data distributions, including generative-model outputs and real-world scans.
AI.conclusion: AnchorSplat provides a fast, robust 3D-native refinement framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that surpasses prior 2D-then-3D pipelines, while enabling scalable evaluation via the 3DGS-SR benchmark and exhibiting strong zero-shot generalization.

title: PACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Plausible and Actionable Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Counterfactual explanations explain machine learning predictions by identifying minimal input changes that would alter a model's decision. Although many existing methods successfully generate prediction-changing alternatives, they often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations due to a lack of explicit mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge and intervention constraints. Neuro-symbolic AI offers a promising direction by combining data-driven predictive models with symbolic reasoning capable of representing human-understandable rules and feasible actions. This paper presents PACE, a modular neuro-symbolic framework for generating feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations. The framework separates prediction and reasoning into two components: a neural predictive model for classification and a symbolic reasoning layer that enforces domain-specific constraints during counterfactual generation. By explicitly modeling feasible interventions, the framework produces explanations consistent with domain knowledge while remaining interpretable and actionable. The approach is model-agnostic and adaptable to domains requiring realistic decision support. A case study is conducted on the Adult Income dataset, combining a multilayer perceptron classifier with Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules encoding feasible modifications to education, occupation, and working hours while preserving immutable attributes. Results highlight the trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility and show that symbolic constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements, illustrating the potential of neuro-symbolic methods for transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanation in explainable AI.

AI.tldr: PACE combines a neural predictor with a symbolic ASP-based reasoning layer to generate feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations; it enforces domain constraints to yield realistic, actionable changes, demonstrated on Adults dataset with MLP+ASP rules; shows a trade-off between validity and plausibility and advantages of neuro-symbolic approach.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanations often produce unrealistic or infeasible actions due to lacking domain knowledge and intervention constraints; integrating symbolic reasoning with data-driven models can encode human-understandable rules and feasible interventions, improving interpretability and actionability.
AI.method: A modular two-component architecture: (1) a neural predictive model (e.g., multilayer perceptron) for classification; (2) a symbolic reasoning layer (Answer Set Programming) encoding domain-specific feasible interventions and immutable attributes to constrain counterfactual generation; the framework is model-agnostic and applies domain constraints during counterfactual search.
AI.result: Applied to the Adult Income dataset using MLP + ASP rules governing feasible education, occupation, and working hours changes while preserving immutable attributes; results reveal a trade-off between counterfactual validity (changing the prediction) and plausibility (feasibility of actions); symbolic constraints produce explanations that better satisfy domain feasibility requirements.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic integration yields feasible, interpretable, and actionable counterfactual explanations; the approach is adaptable across domains needing realistic decision support and can be extended to optimize the balance between validity and plausibility.

title: Adaptive Companionship for Group-Following Robots: Handling Dynamically Changing Group Formations
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Accompanying a group of humans is an essential aspect of developing human-like social cognition in robots. However, human groups typically do not follow fixed formations, which poses significant challenges for robots in maintaining natural companionship behaviors. In this paper, we propose an adaptive group-accompaniment method for social robots based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), leveraging their semantic reasoning capabilities to infer companion positions, maintain social distances, and understand group dynamics. The members of the group are first detected, and a perceptual module generates visual representations of the interaction group space as input to the VLM, which is then combined with a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller to ensure stability and safety. Experimental evaluations across five scenarios show that the proposed method enables robots to accompany the group effectively, demonstrating a 15\% improvement in success rate and a 25\% reduction in collision rate compared to baseline approaches. Additionally, a user study indicates that the generated companionship behaviors are perceived as natural and socially appropriate.

AI.tldr: An adaptive, Vision-Language Model–based method enables social robots to accompany human groups with non-fixed formations by inferring companion positions and group dynamics, using perceptual representations and MPPI control for safe, natural interactions.
AI.motivation: To enable robots to maintain natural companionship with human groups whose formations are fluid, addressing challenges in social cognition and safe navigation.
AI.method: Detect group members; generate perceptual visual representations of the interaction space; use a Vision-Language Model for semantic reasoning to infer companion positions and group dynamics; integrate with a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller for stability and safety in motion planning.
AI.result: Evaluated in five scenarios, achieving a 15% higher success rate and a 25% lower collision rate versus baselines; user study reports companionship behaviors as natural and socially appropriate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed VLM-based adaptive group-accompaniment framework improves perceived naturalness and safety of robot companionship with fluid human group formations, highlighting effective integration of semantic reasoning with motion planning.

title: I\textsuperscript{2}RiMA: Spectral Riemannian Representation with Temporal Attention for Mental Stress Detection based on EEG Signals
summary: Cross-subject EEG stress detection remains challenging because discriminative stress-related patterns are both subject-dependent and frequency-specific. Conventional Riemannian methods model spatial covariance mainly in the time domain, overlooking neural oscillations that are critical for high-level cognitive state decoding, while standard temporal tokenization often fragments inter-slice temporal coherence. To address these limitations, we propose \method{}, an Intra-Inter Riemannian Manifold Attention Network for EEG-based stress detection. \method{} constructs spatial covariance matrices independently at each frequency point and maps them to the SPD tangent space, preserving channel-wise geometry together with frequency-specific discriminative cues. It further introduces frequency cluster aggregation to select informative spectral components and reduce redundancy by forming compact, data-driven frequency clusters aligned with EEG rhythms. Finally, an intra-inter slice attention module adaptively integrates local slice-level spectral dynamics and global temporal context across EEG sequences. Experiments on three datasets show that \method{} consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 82.78\% balanced accuracy while remaining efficient with only 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.

AI.tldr: Proposes Intra-Inter Riemannian Manifold Attention Network (INRIANet) for EEG-based stress detection that preserves frequency-wise spatial geometry and enhances temporal dynamics via attention, achieving strong accuracy with efficiency.
AI.motivation: Conventional Riemannian approaches model spatial covariance in the time domain and treat temporal slices independently, ignoring neural oscillations and inter-slice temporal coherence critical for stress decoding. There is a need to preserve channel-wise geometry, capture frequency-specific cues, and integrate local and global temporal information efficiently.
AI.method: Constructs spatial covariance matrices independently at each frequency, maps them to the SPD tangent space to preserve channel geometry and frequency-specific cues; introduces frequency cluster aggregation to form informative, data-driven spectral clusters; employs an intra-inter slice attention module to fuse local spectral dynamics with global temporal context across EEG sequences.
AI.result: On three datasets, the method outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 82.78% balanced accuracy with 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively preserves frequency-aware spatial information and leverages hierarchical attention to capture both local spectral transitions and global temporal structure, delivering superior performance with a compact, efficient model.

title: CPG-PAD: Concept-Informed Prompts Guided Presentation Attack Detection
comment: Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics & Security (TIFS)
summary: Presentation Attack Detection (PAD) serves as a crucial safeguard for face recognition systems against presentation attacks such as printed photos, replayed videos, and 3D masks. Despite significant progress, existing PAD models still struggle to generalize across unseen domains due to variations in sensors, lighting, and attack materials. Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong generalization ability, yet their applications in PAD remain limited because learned prompts, typically optimized under class-label supervision, fail to explicitly align with fine-grained attack-relevant visual semantics. As a result, the learned representations often overfit domain-specific artifacts instead of capturing transferable attack cues. To address this, we propose Concept-Informed Prompts Guided Presentation Attack Detection (CPG-PAD), a framework that introduces model-level concept guidance into the prompt learning process. Specifically, we design a Visual Concept-driven Enhancement (VCE) module that employs eXplainable AI (XAI) techniques to automatically discover PAD-relevant visual concepts and generate concept-associated heatmaps providing localized fine-grained guidance. Guided by these heatmaps, a Prompt-based Concept Injection (PCI) mechanism integrates these concepts into the prompt space through a Visual-Prompt Decoder (VPD) and a concept-mapping loss, enabling prompts to align with the model's internal concept space. This design enables CPG-PAD to capture generalizable and domain-invariant attack cues while effectively suppressing dataset-specific biases. Extensive experiments across nine benchmark datasets demonstrate that CPG-PAD consistently achieves state-of-the-art cross-domain performance under multi-source, limited-source, and single-source settings.

AI.tldr: Concept-Informed Prompts Guided Presentation Attack Detection (CPG-PAD) improves cross-domain PAD by aligning prompts with automatically discovered PAD concepts via XAI heatmaps; uses Visual Concept-driven Enhancement and Visual-Prompt Decoder with a concept-mapping loss; achieves SOTA across nine datasets in multi-source, limited-source, and single-source settings.
AI.motivation: Current PAD models struggle to generalize across unseen domains due to domain shifts in sensors, lighting, and attack materials. Vision-Language Model (VLM) prompts optimized under class-label supervision tend to overfit domain-specific artifacts rather than capturing transferable attack cues. There is a need to explicitly align prompts with fine-grained, attack-relevant visual semantics.
AI.method: VCE (Visual Concept-driven Enhancement) uses XAI to automatically discover PAD-relevant concepts and generate concept-associated heatmaps indicating localized guidance. PCI (Prompt-based Concept Injection) leverages a Visual-Prompt Decoder (VPD) to inject these concepts into the prompt space, guided by the heatmaps, and a concept-mapping loss to align prompts with the model's internal concept space.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across nine benchmark datasets shows consistent state-of-the-art cross-domain performance under multi-source, limited-source, and single-source settings.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating concept-guided prompts via VCE and PCI enables VLM-based PAD to capture generalizable, domain-invariant attack cues while suppressing dataset-specific biases, yielding robust cross-domain PAD.

title: Auto-FL-Research: Agentic Search for Federated Learning Algorithms
summary: Federated learning (FL) research often depends on many small but consequential algorithmic choices: optimizer variants, server aggregation rules, local training schedules, normalization, regularization, and model architecture. These choices are expensive to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly when candidate changes can also alter the FL training or evaluation path. In this work, we present Auto-FL-Research (AFR), a constrained coding-agent workflow for FL algorithmic recipe search. Agents may propose and implement candidate training algorithms, including server aggregation rules, client update schedules, local objectives, and registered model variants, while task profiles fix the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and final model evaluation. Each campaign records candidate scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status. We evaluate AFR on five healthcare cross-silo FLamby tasks and on grouped-client profiles for the five fixed LEAF datasets plus the LEAF synthetic task. Five-seed repeat evaluations support gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles, while also exposing seed-sensitive and search-selected failure cases. Same-budget controls show that several gains correspond to FL-recipe changes, whereas other improvements are recovered by fixed-surface scalar controls or fail under repeat or held-out evaluation. These mixed outcomes are part of the contribution: they show how agent-generated candidates can be separated into repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts.

AI.tldr: Auto-FL-Research (AFR) automates FL algorithmic recipe search using a constrained coding-agent workflow that mutates components like aggregation, client schedules, and objectives under fixed task profiles; evaluation across FLamby and LEAF reveals mixed gains, some due to actual recipe changes and others due to surface or single-run artifacts.
AI.motivation: Automate and fairly compare diverse FL algorithmic choices to reduce manual experimentation, improve reproducibility, and isolate true gains from artifacts.
AI.method: AFR deploys agents that propose and implement candidate FL training algorithms (server aggregation, client update schedules, local objectives, and model variants) within fixed mutation surfaces, budgets, communication contracts, and evaluation protocols; campaigns log candidate scores, runtimes, edited files, artifacts, and failure status; datasets include five healthcare FLamby tasks and grouped LEAF profiles with multiple seeds.
AI.result: Gains are observed on some tasks, but several improvements arise from fixed-surface tuning or single-run artifacts; seed sensitivity and failure cases are exposed; results demonstrate the need to separate repeated FL mechanisms from surface-level or artifact-driven improvements.
AI.conclusion: AFR provides a disciplined framework for FL recipe search that can disentangle repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and single-run artifacts, while highlighting seed-driven variability and evaluation robustness across datasets.

title: The Three Dimensions of ROS 2 Middleware
summary: ROS 2 (Robot Operating System 2) has emerged as the de facto standard for modern robot software development, with middleware implementations such as the Data Distribution Service (DDS) and Zenoh forming the core infrastructure for distributed robotic communication. Despite their architectural flexibility, these middleware systems exhibit structural limitations, particularly under dynamic and resource-constrained wireless environments. This paper presents a systematic survey of ROS 2 middleware and introduces a conceptual framework to examine its architectural limits through three structural dimensions required by distributed robotic systems, namely Space, Time, and State. We first provide a structured analysis of middleware architecture and operational dynamics, including discovery, data exchange, and state management mechanisms. Building on this foundation, we formalize Time as temporal predictability for control loops, Space as spatial abstraction from physical topology to enable modular deployment, and State as contextual continuity despite dynamic node participation and intermittent connectivity. Through a comprehensive review of existing implementations and prior studies, we organize middleware research according to the structural trade-offs that arise among these dimensions. Under constrained wireless conditions, spatial abstraction can obscure network variability and weaken temporal guarantees, while mechanisms that preserve state continuity introduce computational and network overhead that competes with time-critical communication. These interactions reveal structural trade-offs that characterize the practical limits of contemporary robot middleware. By synthesizing architectural patterns and identifying gaps in current modeling and analysis approaches, this survey outlines a principled research roadmap for robust and scalable robotic middleware architectures.

AI.tldr: Survey of ROS 2 middleware (DDS/Zenoh) using a Space-Time-State framework to analyze architectural limits; reveals trade-offs among spatial abstraction, temporal predictability, and state continuity under wireless constraints; provides a roadmap for robust, scalable middleware design.
AI.motivation: Understand how middleware architecture and dynamic, resource-constrained wireless environments impact core guarantees (time, space, and state) in distributed robotic systems.
AI.method: Systematic literature survey of ROS 2 middleware; formalization of Time (temporal predictability), Space (spatial/topology abstraction), and State (contextual continuity); analysis of discovery, data exchange, and state management mechanisms; synthesis of architectural patterns and gaps.
AI.result: Identification of structural trade-offs: Space abstraction can mask network variability and weaken temporal guarantees; State continuity mechanisms add computational and networking overhead; categorization of middleware research along Space/Time/State dimensions; gaps in modeling and analysis approaches; roadmap for future middleware research.
AI.conclusion: A principled framework across Space, Time, and State is needed to build robust and scalable robotic middleware; the paper outlines a research roadmap to address identified gaps and balance competing requirements in real-world wireless scenarios.

title: Fixed-Set Robustness in Programming by Example: Example Corruption and Semantic Partition Recovery
summary: Programming-by-example systems infer programs from a small set of input-output examples. Robust PBE work usually models wrong examples as samples from a stochastic noise process and then minimizes an expected or empirical loss. This paper studies a different failure mode: an adversary who sees the synthesizer and chooses the examples whose corruption most damages the returned program. We formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption for finite PBE version spaces, implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption searches for a string-transformation DSL, and introduce version-space partition aggregation (VPA), a defense that synthesizes on disjoint example groups and votes by semantic signatures. The central claim is deliberately bounded and partly negative: low-margin PBE tasks have an adversarial robustness dimension that random-typo and noisy-PBE evaluations miss, while semantic partition aggregation helps only when the clean semantics keep a partition vote margin, which often fails on realistic tasks. Evidence from curated/generated DSL tasks, accepted public SyGuS PBE_SLIA slices, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and noisy-PBE objective baselines supports that boundary. One curated edit flips all 8 spike tasks while 200-trial typo, DSL-pool, and distance-matched random controls succeed on 10.3%, 11.0%, and 16.7%; generated margin-1 rows flip under budget 1 yet VPA recovers them; on public SyGuS the vote margin is near one, so an adaptive attacker drives VPA accuracy to zero; accepted public SyGuS slices move across exact-within-pool budget boundaries; and Playgol shows positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typo and same-pool random controls on the 141 accepted rows. A small exact-output prompt harness over 20 controlled margin-1 tasks shows the same qualitative clean-to-attacked pattern across local and API models, while it is treated as a scope check, not a broad LLM benchmark.

AI.tldr: This work studies fixed-set worst-case corruption in finite PBE version spaces, introducing a defense (Version-Space Partition Aggregation, VPA) that aggregates over disjoint example groups via semantic voting. It provides exact and heuristic corruption searches and evaluates across multiple datasets. The results show limited adversarial robustness for low-margin PBE tasks: random/typographical baselines miss the adversarial dimension; VPA helps only when clean semantic partitions yield clear margins, which is often not the case in realistic tasks.
AI.motivation: Robust PBE has typically been analyzed under stochastic noise; this work foregrounds a stronger threat model where an adversary observes the synthesizer and selects corrupted examples to maximally damage the produced program. The aim is to formalize this fixed-set worst-case corruption, quantify robustness gaps, and assess defenses under realistic task settings.
AI.method: - Formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption for finite PBE version spaces. - Implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption searches for a string-transformation DSL. - Propose Version-Space Partition Aggregation (VPA): synthesize on disjoint example groups and vote by semantic signatures. - Evaluate on curated/generated DSL tasks, accepted SyGuS PBE_SLIA slices, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and noisy-PBE baselines, comparing against typo/noise baselines and budgeted corruption.
AI.result: Across datasets, results show a boundary case: a curated edit can flip all 8 spike tasks under adversarial corruption, while baseline controls succeed in other settings (12-17%). Margin-1 tasks may flip under a small budget, yet VPA can recover some cases; on public SyGuS slices, vote margins near 1 enable adaptive attackers to drive VPA accuracy to zero; Playgol reveals positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typos and random controls on 141 accepted rows. A small controlled prompt harness confirms the same qualitative pattern across local and API models.
AI.conclusion: The authors’ central claim is intentionally bounded and partly negative: low-margin PBE tasks possess an adversarial robustness dimension that common stochastic-loss evaluations miss. Semantic partition aggregation helps only when the clean semantics preserve a partition margin, which is often false in realistic tasks. Thus, while VPA offers some defense under favorable margins, robust PBE under adversarial corruption remains challenging, calling for broader defenses and more robust evaluation.

title: KathaTrace: Diagnosing Semantic Trajectory Collapse in Generated Visual Narratives
summary: Visual narratives are central to storyboards, comics, children's media, and film previsualization, where viewers understand stories from images alone. Recent generators such as StoryDiffusion produce coherent sequences, but visual coherence does not guarantee that source-story transition meaning remains recoverable. Existing benchmarks assess visual quality, content faithfulness, and scene coherence, but miss a critical failure mode: storyboards where scenes appear visually coherent while the semantic link between scenes disappears. We introduce KathaTrace, a generator-agnostic protocol for diagnosing semantic trajectory collapse, defined as the loss of transition meaning needed to understand how one scene follows another. KathaTrace evaluates transitions under three evidence conditions: text-only, image-only, and text-plus-image, and filters ambiguous items. We contribute KathaBench-25K, with 5,000 narratives from classical collections including Aesop, Panchatantra, and Kathasaritasagara, 20,000 transitions, and 28,712 recoverability questions. We define Semantic Trajectory Gap, or STG, as text-only minus image-only recoverability, measuring transition meaning lost during visualization. Human validation yields Fleiss' kappa = 0.845. Experiments across state-of-the-art generators show substantial STG of 23.5 +/- 1.3. Semantic Compass, an actionability probe, uses KathaTrace signals for post-generation repair and improves storyboard selection.

AI.tldr: Introduces KathaTrace, a generator-agnostic protocol to diagnose semantic trajectory collapse in visual storyboards, via text-only, image-only, and text-plus-image evidence. Builds KathaBench-25K dataset and STG metric (text-only minus image-only recoverability). Demonstrates substantial semantic trajectory gap in current generators and offers Semantic Compass for post-generation repair.
AI.motivation: Current visual coherence in generated storyboards can mask loss of semantic transition meaning between scenes. There is a need to explicitly measure and diagnose semantic trajectory collapse to improve explainability and usefulness of visual narratives.
AI.method: KathaTrace evaluates scene transitions under three evidence conditions (text-only, image-only, text-plus-image), filters ambiguous items, and aggregates recoverability as a recoverability score. Constructed KathaBench-25K with 5,000 narratives from classical sources, 20,000 transitions, and 28,712 recoverability questions for human validation (Fleiss' kappa = 0.845). STG = text-only recoverability minus image-only recoverability. Evaluates state-of-the-art generators and uses Semantic Compass as an actionability probe for post-generation repair.
AI.result: Demonstrates substantial STG (~23.5 ± 1.3) across leading generators, indicating semantic trajectory collapse can occur even when visuals are coherent. Semantic Compass improves storyboard selection by leveraging KathaTrace signals for post-generation repairs.
AI.conclusion: KathaTrace provides a robust, generator-agnostic diagnostic to detect semantic drift in visual narratives and enables actionable repairs via Semantic Compass, representing a meaningful step toward preserving semantic continuity in storyboard-generation systems.

title: The Wiola Architecture for Efficient Small Language Models
summary: We present Wiola, a fully original Small Language Model (SLM) architecture built from first principles, sharing no structural lineage with any existing model family including GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, or Falcon. Wiola introduces five independently novel components: (i) Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (SRPE), which embeds token positions on a three-dimensional helical manifold combining absolute, relative, and hierarchical positional signals; (ii) Gated Cross-Layer Attention (GCLA), providing each decoder layer with soft cross-attention access to compressed summaries of two preceding layers for inter-layer coherence; (iii) Adaptive Token Merging (ATM), which dynamically merges se mantically redundant adjacent tokens in middle network layers to reduce attention complexity without information loss; (iv) Dual Stream Feed-Forward (DSFF), replacing the conventional MLP with two parallel streams fused by a learned per-dimension gate; and (v) WiolaRMSNorm, a modified normalisation introducing a per-dimension learned offset vector that prevents representation collapse. We provide complete mathematical derivations, architectural block diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral. Wiola is released in four sizes (120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters) and is fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem, with all 22 architectural unit tests passing.

AI.tldr: Wiola presents a fully original SLM with five novel components (SRPE, GCLA, ATM, DSFF, WiolaRMSNorm), four sizes (120M–1.5B), and HF compatibility. It provides mathematical derivations, diagrams, complexity analyses, and comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral; 22 unit tests pass.
AI.motivation: Address efficiency and expressivity gaps in existing LMs by introducing novel architectural primitives that purposefully diverge from known model families, enabling improved positional encoding, inter-layer coherence, dynamic token management, alternate FFN structure, and stabilized normalization.
AI.method: Introduce five components with formal derivations and diagrams: SRPE (3D helical positional encoding), GCLA (soft cross-layer attention to compressed summaries of two prior layers), ATM (dynamic token merging to reduce attention cost), DSFF (dual parallel FFN streams with per-dimension gate), and WiolaRMSNorm (learned per-dimension offset to prevent collapse); provide architectural diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons; release four sizes and ensure HuggingFace compatibility with 22 unit tests.
AI.result: Claimed outcomes include improved efficiency and coherence via ATM and GCLA, richer positional signaling via SRPE, enhanced expressivity via DSFF, and stabilized representations via WiolaRMSNorm; comprehensive math, diagrams, complexity analyses, and comparisons to GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral; 22 unit tests pass.
AI.conclusion: Wiola proposes a cohesive, self-contained SLM architecture with multiple novel components and HF compatibility. The claims are substantial but require independent replication and thorough benchmarking to validate novelty, efficiency gains, and real-world performance.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Safety Guidance for Vision-Language-Action Models via Constrained Flow Matching
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising generalization capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks, yet their real-world deployment remains limited by the lack of effective safety measures. Specifically, existing safety measures only prevent collisions caused by the robot's next action. In this paper, we propose a neuro-symbolic safety guidance mechanism for flow matching based VLAs that enables predictive collision avoidance. Flow matching based VLAs determine the next actions by predicting a trajectory (a sequence of actions) through an iterative neural flow matching process. Our method formulates safety enforcement as a minimum-norm constrained optimization problem that corrects safety violations during the denoising process of noisy intermediate trajectory predictions. By analyzing predicted trajectories and applying corrections during iterative denoising, our approach anticipates collisions before they become unavoidable. This interleaving of symbolic constraint satisfaction with neural trajectory generation enables predictive collision avoidance rather than reactive intervention. On the SafeLIBERO benchmark, our method achieves 82.8% collision avoidance and 81.6% task success, a 6.3% and 19.8% improvement respectively over single-step methods, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks where compounding distribution shift is most pronounced. Video demonstrations of our approach are included on our project page at https://willenglish.tech/SafetyGuidedFlowMatching/.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic safety guidance mechanism for flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models enables predictive collision avoidance by enforcing safety via a minimum-norm constrained optimization during the denoising of predicted trajectories, improving safety and task success on SafeLIBERO.
AI.motivation: Safety in VLA-driven robotic manipulation has been limited to preventing the robot's immediate next-action collisions. There is a need for predictive, long-horizon safety that anticipates and corrects potential collisions before they occur, especially under distribution shift in long-horizon tasks.
AI.method: Integrate a minimum-norm constrained optimization into the denoising process of iterative flow matching to correct safety-violating intermediate trajectories. This neuro-symbolic approach interleaves symbolic constraint satisfaction with neural trajectory generation, enabling safety corrections during trajectory refinement.
AI.result: On the SafeLIBERO benchmark, the method achieves 82.8% collision avoidance and 81.6% task success, representing improvements of 6.3% and 19.8% respectively over single-step methods. The gains are most pronounced on long-horizon tasks where distribution shift is severe.
AI.conclusion: The proposed neuro-symbolic safety guidance enables predictive collision avoidance for flow-matching VLAs by coupling symbolic constraints with neural trajectory denoising, yielding notable safety and task-performance gains, with demonstrations available on the project page.

title: Domain Knowledge Based Temporal-Spatial Graph Convolution Network for ECG Recognition
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Presented at ICONIP 2024, Auckland, New Zealand. Published in LNCS 15290, Springer, 2025
summary: In light of strides in Arti cial Intelligence (AI) and its wide spread application, challenges persist in the interpretability of AI models, particularly within specialized domains like healthcare, such as electro cardiograph (ECG) recognition. Rather than relying solely on end-to-end convolutional neural networks, this paper introduces a novel approach using a domain knowledge-based graph convolution network for ECG recognition. Key landmarks points of PRQST, vital to ECG interpreta tion, are incorporated as domain knowledge. The double-stream directed graph is employed to model both intra and inter ECG cycles. Speci cally, spatial directed graphs capture the positional relationships among key points, while temporal directed graphs delineate temporal dependencies between adjacent cycles in extended ECG sequences. Experimental re sults on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset, which speci cally classify ECG into nine categories, prove the e cacy of the proposed model. The overall average F1 score is 88.1%, the average F1 score of rare categories is 76.3%, both outperform the state-of-the-art models. The introduction of domain knowledge did enhance the detec tion performance, especially for rare categories.

AI.tldr: Introduces a domain-knowledge graph convolutional network for ECG recognition that uses PRQST landmarks and a double-stream directed graph to model intra- and inter-cycle relations, achieving strong performance on a 9-class ECG dataset.
AI.motivation: To improve interpretability and performance in ECG recognition by incorporating domain knowledge (landmarks) and explicit spatial-temporal graph structures, beyond opaque end-to-end CNNs.
AI.method: Build spatial directed graphs over key ECG landmarks (PRQST) to encode positional relationships and temporal directed graphs to capture dependencies across adjacent cardiac cycles; fuse them using a double-stream graph convolution network for ECG recognition.
AI.result: Evaluated on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset (9-class), achieving average F1 of 88.1%, rare-class F1 of 76.3%, outperforming state-of-the-art methods; domain knowledge improves detection, notably for rare categories.
AI.conclusion: Domain-knowledge graphs enhance ECG recognition by providing interpretable, physiology-aligned structure that improves accuracy and especially sensitivity for rare classes; suggests broader applicability to biomedical signal analysis.

title: Spatial-Temporal Expert Learning for Video-based Person Re-identification
summary: Video-based person re-identification (Re-ID) aims to retrieve the same identity in the query video clips from the gallery video clips. To solve this problem, exploiting fine-grained features is of great importance, especially when discriminating identities that are similar in appearance. In this paper, we propose to enhance the ability to explore fine-grained information with a novel input-aware extendable expert module. Instead of updating the network parameters with every sample in the dataset, we aim to train the experts within specific subsets that only contain similar samples and promote their ability to exploit fine-grained information within these similar samples. To achieve this goal, we incorporate two mechanisms in this module: input-aware expert selection mechanism and spatial-temporal selection mechanism. The first mechanism dynamically activates a set of experts on subsets of similar samples, pushing the experts to exploit subtle differences between these similar samples, while the second one further increases their sensitivity to the fine-grained differences in spatial and temporal aspects and allows the experts to dynamically utilize them for different input samples. In addition, to facilitate the expert module, we design an extendable scheme that allows the module to flexibly add new experts when necessary. As a result, our method achieves outstanding performance on two large-scale datasets.

AI.tldr: A novel input-aware extendable expert module for video-based person Re-ID uses input-driven expert selection and spatial-temporal mechanisms to exploit fine-grained features within subsets of similar samples, with an extendable architecture to add experts as needed, achieving outstanding results on two large-scale datasets.
AI.motivation: Improve discrimination of closely resembling identities in video-based Re-ID by focusing learning on fine-grained differences within similar sample groups, while maintaining scalability via an extendable expert framework.
AI.method: Introduce an input-aware extendable expert module with two mechanisms: (1) input-aware expert selection that activates a subset of experts on similar samples, and (2) spatial-temporal selection that enhances sensitivity to fine-grained spatial/temporal cues. The module is designed to be extendable to add new experts dynamically as needed.
AI.result: Reported outstanding performance on two large-scale datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of fine-grained, input-aware, and extendable expert modeling for video-based Re-ID.
AI.conclusion: The approach shows that combining input-conditioned expert selection with spatial-temporal fine-grained analysis in an extendable framework can improve Re-ID performance on challenging datasets, suggesting a promising direction for scalable, fine-grained representation learning.

title: Agent4cs: A Multi-agent System for Code Summarization in Large Hierarchical Codebases
comment: Accepted to the main track of the 23rd European Conference on Multi-Agent Systems (EUMAS 2026)
summary: Understanding large, complex codebases, especially those with obfuscated structures and incomplete documentation, remains a significant challenge. Existing code summarization solutions often rely on a single language model or coding assistant like Claude Code, and treat source code as flat text, underutilizing the rich interdependencies and hierarchical information within a repository. To address these shortcomings, we propose Agent4cs - a multi-agent framework that summarizes large codebases in a bottom-up fashion, where a summarization agent focuses on producing robust summaries; a keyword-extraction agent proactively identifies critical information from subfolders; and a quality-assurance agent iteratively refines the outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness. Evaluated on 7 frontier models, Agent4cs improves semantic consistency across all folder levels by average 8% compared to two structured prompting baselines with code segments. Furthermore, extensive evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate over the same baselines.

AI.tldr: Agent4cs proposes a multi-agent, bottom-up approach to codebase summarization that exploits repository hierarchy and interdependencies, outperforming baselines in semantic consistency and keyword coverage.
AI.motivation: Codebases are large, hierarchical, and often poorly documented. Existing summarization methods treat code as flat text and rely on a single model, underutilizing structural information.
AI.method: A three-agent architecture: a summarization agent generates robust summaries, a keyword-extraction agent identifies critical information from subfolders, and a quality-assurance agent refines outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness; evaluated across 7 frontier models and compared to structured prompting baselines.
AI.result: Average 8% improvement in semantic consistency across folder levels versus two structured prompting baselines; up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent, bottom-up framework leveraging hierarchical information improves codebase summarization quality and keyword coverage, with demonstrated gains across multiple models and datasets.

title: CommonRoad-Game: A Human-in-the-Loop Simulation Framework for Autonomous Driving
summary: Motion planning algorithms should be evaluated in human-in-the-loop environments to ensure they produce safe and efficient behaviors during interactions. However, existing simulation platforms often rely on recorded datasets, lack dedicated interfaces for real-time human interaction, or remain weakly integrated with an autonomous driving ecosystem. Moreover, many human-in-the-loop simulators are computationally intensive by design, making them less suitable for rapid prototyping and flexible experimentation in early-stage autonomous driving research. To address these limitations, we present CommonRoad-Game, a lightweight human-in-the-loop simulation framework tightly integrated with the CommonRoad platform, focusing on the systematic testing of motion planners with human participation and the analysis of human driving behaviors in interactive scenarios. We introduce a multi-threaded architecture with a robust synchronization mechanism that aligns simulation time with wall-clock time, enabling deterministic and temporally consistent interaction between autonomous and human-driven vehicles. In addition, the framework provides a scenario generation module that records driving logs, allowing diverse and reproducible test cases to be constructed from human-in-the-loop experiments. Experimental results demonstrate that CommonRoad-Game achieves stable temporal synchronization, supports scalable multi-agent simulation, and seamlessly integrates CommonRoad-compatible motion planners to generate interactive driving scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunfei-Bi8/CommonRoad-Game.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, real-time human-in-the-loop simulator, CommonRoad-Game, tightly integrated with CommonRoad to enable deterministic, synchronized multi-agent testing of motion planners with human participation; includes scenario generation/logging and open-source code.
AI.motivation: to overcome limitations of existing simulators (dataset-driven, lacking real-time human interaction interfaces, weak ecosystem integration, computationally heavy) and enable rapid prototyping and systematic human-in-the-loop evaluation in autonomous driving research.
AI.method: design and implement a multi-threaded architecture with robust time synchronization aligned to wall-clock time; integrate with CommonRoad; provide a scenario generation module and logging; support scalable multi-agent interaction between human-driven and autonomous vehicles; deterministic interaction.
AI.result: demonstrates stable temporal synchronization, scalable multi-agent simulation, and seamless integration with CommonRoad-compatible motion planners; provides reproducible interactive driving scenarios; source code available.
AI.conclusion: CommonRoad-Game fills a gap by delivering lightweight, real-time human-in-the-loop testing within the CommonRoad ecosystem, enabling rapid prototyping, behavioral analysis, and systematic planner testing.

title: Scaling Laws for Grid-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in High Dimensions
summary: Grid-based approaches to approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search have been absent from modern scaling analyses. We present a systematic characterization of a multiprobe grid algorithm with respect to dataset size $N$ and dimensionality $d$. Our experiments reveal a previously unreported $d$-scaling crossover on the GloVe embedding family, in which multiprobe grid search maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent while other graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based methods exhibit degrading throughput. The advantage comes with near-linear query scaling in $N$, but also with lower indexing cost than competing ANN methods. Our results suggest that grid-based methods such as multiprobe grid may be competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness dictate performance. More broadly, recent work has formalized self-attention as an ANN operation. Thus, the $N$- and $d$-scaling properties of ANN algorithms may guide cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures. Code is available at: https://github.com/weiz345/MultiProbeANN.

AI.tldr: Multiprobe grid ANN shows a d-scaling crossover on GloVe embeddings: it keeps a roughly constant dimensional scaling exponent while graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based methods degrade in throughput. It offers near-linear query scaling in N with lower indexing cost, making grid-based methods competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings and potentially informing transformer cost analyses.
AI.motivation: Fill a gap in scaling analyses for grid-based ANN methods and understand their performance across dataset size and dimensionality, particularly for modern embeddings like GloVe and in the context of self-attention as an ANN operation.
AI.method: Systematically characterize a multiprobe grid algorithm across varying dataset size N and dimensionality d; conduct experiments on GloVe embeddings; compare against graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based ANN methods; measure throughput scaling with N and d and indexing cost; provide code for reproducibility.
AI.result: Identification of a d-scaling crossover where multiprobe grid maintains an approximately constant d-scaling exponent, while other ANN methods exhibit degrading throughput as d increases. Query throughput scales near-linearly with N, and indexing cost is lower than competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Grid-based methods like multiprobe grid can be competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness matter. The observed scaling properties may inform cost analyses for efficient transformer architectures, given the framing of self-attention as an ANN operation; code is available.

title: MapDreamer: Aerial Imagery Conditioned Latent Diffusion for Lane-Level Map Generation
summary: High definition map generation is essential for autonomous driving, yet remains a labor-intensive process at scale. We present MapDreamer, a generative diffusion model that synthesizes lane-level vector maps with explicit topology directly from a single aerial image. MapDreamer learns a compact latent representation of lane centerlines and their topological relations using a variational autoencoder and predicts graphs with a transformer-based latent diffusion model. To align generated maps with the observed scene, we condition each denoising step on dense aerial features injected through cross-attention. To handle the varying number of lanes across scenes, we propose a lane cardinality module paired with background ghost lane latents, a learned buffer that prevents slot collapse during diffusion. Furthermore, we introduce a sliding-window global graph aggregation strategy that stitches local tiles into city-scale maps while preserving connectivity through encoded lane boundaries. Experiments on UrbanLaneGraph derived from Argoverse 2 show improved geometric and topological fidelity over non-generative baselines.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based model called MapDreamer generates lane-level vector maps from a single aerial image, using a VAE for lane topology latent space and a transformer-based latent diffusion model, with mechanisms to handle varying lane counts and city-scale stitching.
AI.motivation: Reduce manual HD map annotation by producing topology-aware lane maps directly from ubiquitous aerial imagery, enabling scalable, consistent maps for autonomous driving.
AI.method: Encode lane centerlines and topology with a variational autoencoder to a compact latent space; use a transformer-based latent diffusion model to predict graphs; condition denoising steps on dense aerial features via cross-attention; address variable lane counts with a lane cardinality module and background ghost lane latents; employ a sliding-window global graph aggregation to stitch local tiles into city-scale maps while preserving connectivity through encoded lane boundaries.
AI.result: The approach achieves improved geometric and topological fidelity relative to non-generative baselines on UrbanLaneGraph data derived from Argoverse 2.
AI.conclusion: MapDreamer demonstrates that diffusion-based generative modeling can produce topology-aware, scalable, lane-level HD maps from single aerial images, with effective handling of lane count variability and global connectivity.

title: When Should Service Agents Reconsider? Difficulty-Routed Control in Customer-Service Operations
summary: Autonomous customer-service agents are shifting from conversational interfaces toward operational execution roles: they retrieve firm records, apply service policies, and execute backend writes such as refunds, cancellations, exchanges, order modifications, and reservation changes. This shift creates a service-control problem: firms must keep routine service fast and low-friction while preventing operational errors on requests where customer instructions, policy constraints, firm records, and backend writes interact. We propose a difficulty-routed service-control architecture that asks when service agents should reconsider before acting. A lightweight router keeps routine sessions on a low-cost baseline path and routes operationally coupled sessions to an escalated workflow. The escalated path uses conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration to concentrate deliberation and safeguards before consequential backend writes, rather than applying additional control uniformly across all service sessions. We evaluate the architecture on human-verified retail and airline tasks from $τ^{2}$-bench. In retail, the method improves reliability consistently on service requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence shows that stronger control is directed toward conflicted requests rather than broadly applied to routine ones. Dialogue and tool-use profiles suggest that gains do not come from indiscriminate interaction expansion or broader tool chains; instead, added turns and tool calls support evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration. Case-level evidence shows that the escalated workflow preserves fallback plans, binds retrieved records to the correct action, sequences writes, and decomposes multi-entity requests. Airline results extend the same service-control logic to reservation operations.

AI.tldr: A targeted, difficulty-aware routing architecture for service-control in autonomous agents reduces backend-write errors by routing operationally coupled sessions to an escalated, conflict-aware workflow, improving reliability on conflicted retail and airline tasks without blanket interaction expansion.
AI.motivation: Reduce operational errors and latency in autonomous customer-service agents when performing backend writes by focusing deliberation only where requests conflict with policies, records, or constraints.
AI.method: Implement a lightweight router that classifies sessions into routine vs. escalated; keep routine on a low-cost baseline; escalate to a workflow with conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration; emphasize write separation, evidence gathering, and pre-write checks; evaluate on τ²-bench retail and airline tasks; analyze dialogue/tool-use patterns and case-level outcomes.
AI.result: Reliability improved on conflicted service requests; routing evidence shows control concentrated on conflicted cases; gains attributed to added turns/tool calls for evidence gathering and pre-write checks; escalated workflow preserves fallbacks, binds records to actions, sequences writes, and decomposes multi-entity requests; results extend to airline reservation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Selective, conflict-aware escalation yields stronger service-control with targeted deliberation, balancing speed and safety in backend-write operations for enterprise chat assistants.

title: BIFROST: Bridging Invariant Feature Representation for Observation-space Sim2Real Transfer
summary: Sim2real transfer for robot policy learning suffers due to mismatch between simulation and reality. Existing methods typically address each gap in isolation through separate adaptation modules, which are composed or layered when both gaps coexist. Yet the basis for attempting sim2real in the first place is that there is shared structure between a task in simulation and reality, where equivalent actions from equivalent configurations produce equivalent long term outcomes regardless of domain specific differences in rendering or physics. In this paper, we study whether we can identify and exploit this shared structure from raw observations to train a policy that enables zero shot transfer. We introduce BIFROST, which learns a shared history encoder on paired cross-domain data via cross-domain bisimulation objective: observation-action sequences leading to equivalent long-term behavior are mapped to nearby latent states, regardless of domain. Policies trained on these latent states in simulation transfer zero-shot to reality. We provide empirical evidence on sim2sim visual navigation and sim2real contact rich manipulation task and visual servoing task that BIFROST achieves effective transfer where domain adaptation and co-training baselines fail under both visual and dynamics domain gaps.

AI.tldr: BIFROST learns a cross-domain bisimulation-based shared history encoder to enable zero-shot sim2real transfer by aligning observation-action sequences with equivalent long-term behavior across domains; outperforms baselines on sim2sim and sim2real tasks.
AI.motivation: There is a shared task structure across simulation and reality; gap-specific adaptation methods treat domain gaps separately and may miss the underlying common dynamics. Exploiting this shared structure from raw observations could enable zero-shot transfer.
AI.method: Train a shared history encoder using paired cross-domain data with a cross-domain bisimulation objective. Map observation-action sequences that yield equivalent long-term behavior to nearby latent states, independent of domain. Train policies on these latent states in simulation so that they transfer zero-shot to reality.
AI.result: Empirical evidence that BIFROST achieves effective transfer where domain adaptation and co-training baselines fail under both visual and dynamics domain gaps. Demonstrated in sim2sim visual navigation, sim2real contact-rich manipulation, and visual servoing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Cross-domain bisimulation-based sharing of history representations can capture the structural similarity between simulation and reality, enabling zero-shot transfer and outperforming baselines; supports a general approach for leveraging cross-domain structure from raw observations in robotics.

title: IonSense-QKG: A Quantum-Readiness Metadata Framework for Lithium-Ion Battery Dataset Discovery
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Code and metadata artifact available at GitHub
summary:
Public lithium-ion battery datasets are increasingly used for state-of-health estimation, remaining-useful-life prediction, anomaly detection, electrochemical diagnostics, second-life analytics, and battery safety research. However, these datasets vary substantially in chemistry, modality, scale, label quality, sequence structure, access status, and preprocessing complexity. These differences directly affect whether a dataset is feasible for near-term hybrid quantum-classical machine-learning workflows.
  This paper presents IonSense-QKG, a quantum-readiness metadata framework for lithium-ion battery dataset discovery. Starting from the EV-Battery-IonSense index, the proposed framework enriches public battery dataset records with quantum-relevant metadata, including task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, and NISQ feasibility. A transparent Quantum Readiness Score is introduced to rank datasets as candidate resources for future hybrid quantum-classical battery benchmarks. The score is intended as a dataset-selection heuristic, not as evidence of quantum advantage.
  The framework demonstrates query-based discovery over enriched metadata to identify datasets suitable for compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series workflows, limited-label anomaly detection, and future battery-health benchmarking. The released artifact includes metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, link-checking utilities, and SQL-style query examples. IonSense-QKG positions dataset selection as a data-management problem and provides a reproducible foundation for data-centric quantum battery analytics.

AI.tldr: IonSense-QKG introduces a quantum-readiness metadata framework for lithium-ion battery datasets, enriching records with quantum-relevant metadata and a Quantum Readiness Score to guide near-term hybrid quantum-classical benchmarking.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient discovery and selection of public battery datasets for quantum ML workflows by accounting for dataset heterogeneity and quantum-compatibility constraints.
AI.method: Augment the existing EV-Battery-IonSense index with quantum-relevant fields (task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, NISQ feasibility); define and publish a transparent Quantum Readiness Score; implement query-based discovery and release artifacts (metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, link-check utilities, SQL-like query examples).
AI.result: A practical framework enabling dataset discovery for quantum-friendly tasks (compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series, limited-label anomaly detection, future battery-health benchmarking); includes reproducible artifacts and an accessible scoring mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Frames dataset selection as a data-management problem and provides a reproducible foundation for data-centric quantum battery analytics; the Quantum Readiness Score is a heuristic meant for resource ranking and not as evidence of quantum advantage.

title: MIBE: Multi-subject Interaction Benchmark and Evaluator for Personalized Image Generation
summary: Multi-subject personalized image generation requires the precise rendering of all requested reference identities and their specified interactions based on a guiding prompt. However, state-of-the-art models still struggle with this process, frequently omitting subjects, failing to preserve reference appearances, or misattributing interactions. Furthermore, existing metrics designed primarily for single-subject fidelity cannot reliably capture these errors, suffering severe degradation in ranking separability and failing to align with human preference as the subject count increases. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-subject Interaction Benchmark and Evaluator (MIBE), a unified framework comprising a Multi-subject Interaction Benchmark (MIB) and a Multi-subject Interaction Evaluator (MIE). MIB systematically covers diverse relation types and scene complexities through a decoupled data regime. This consists of a 60K-pair VLM-labeled Silver Set for scalable metric training and a 4K-pair double-blind Human Evaluation Gold Set covering a diverse range of state-of-the-art generators, with the Silver Set reaching 95.1% cross-VLM preference agreement. To demonstrate the utility of this benchmark, we present MIE, a lightweight, reference-conditioned evaluator trained exclusively on the Silver Set with a dual-head ranking and diagnosis objective. MIE exhibits strong cross-generator generalization on the Gold Set, achieving 0.922 overall pairwise accuracy against human preference, including 0.982 on seen generators and 0.884 on unseen generators. By outperforming a broad spectrum of baseline metrics, including CLIP and DINO variants, MIE demonstrates that diagnostic supervision can preserve ranking separability and human alignment where traditional evaluators collapse.

AI.tldr: A benchmark and evaluator for multi-subject image generation: MIB and MIE with Silver and Gold sets; MIE achieves strong human-aligned ranking and generalizes across generators, outperforming CLIP/DINO baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing single-subject metrics fail to capture errors in multi-subject generation (omissions, misattributions, interaction errors) and lack ranking separability with increasing subject count.
AI.method: MIB provides a decoupled data regime: 60K-pair Silver set labeled by video-language models for scalable metric training, and 4K-pair double-blind Gold set for human evaluation across generators. MIE is a light, reference-conditioned evaluator trained on the Silver set with a dual-head ranking and diagnosis objective to preserve ranking separability.
AI.result: MIE achieves 0.922 overall pairwise accuracy vs human preference on the Gold set, with 0.982 on seen generators and 0.884 on unseen. It outperforms baselines like CLIP and DINO variants in preserving human-aligned ranking.
AI.conclusion: Diagnostic supervision in MIE helps maintain ranking separability and human alignment in multi-subject generation, addressing shortcomings of traditional evaluators as subject count grows.

title: CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 Workshop on Creativity & Generative AI
summary: Divergent thinking is a crucial aspect of creativity, yet large language models (LLMs) tend to consistently generate similar responses to open-ended questions, in what has been termed the artificial hivemind effect. Here, we introduce CreativityNeuro, a data-free method for enhancing divergent thinking in LLMs via contrastive weight steering. We evaluate our method across multiple creativity assessments and report several main findings. On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), a vocabulary-space creativity test, CreativityNeuro improves performance by up to 14 human percentile points. Next, in a large-scale human evaluation (N=720) on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) and the Task Task, CreativityNeuro achieves significant improvements in originality, surprise, and creativity, transferring to longer-form and more open-ended tasks. Importantly, we find that across all three tasks, CreativityNeuro demonstrably reduces measures of mode collapse. Moreover, activation steering achieves comparable performance to CreativityNeuro on the DAT, but it does not transfer to the AUT and Task Task, demonstrating the effectiveness of weight-space steering in generalizing to unseen tasks. In conclusion, CreativityNeuro improves divergent thinking and reduces mode collapse without requiring behavioral data, re-training, or gradient-based fine-tuning, providing a straightforward way to enhance LLM performance in creative domains.

AI.tldr: CreativityNeuro is a data-free technique that uses contrastive weight steering to enhance divergent thinking in LLMs, reducing mode collapse and improving performance on creativity tasks without data, retraining, or gradient fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Divergent thinking in LLMs tends to produce convergent, stereotyped outputs (mode collapse). A data-free method to steer weight space can improve creativity without requiring behavioral data or retraining.
AI.method: Apply contrastive weight steering (weight-space adjustments) to LLMs; compare to activation steering; evaluate on Divergent Association Task (DAT) and human-evaluated AUT and Task Task (N=720); measure originality, surprise, and creativity; assess mode collapse; no data, no fine-tuning.
AI.result: CreativityNeuro improves DAT by up to 14 percentile points; significant improvements on AUT and Task Task across originality, surprise, and creativity; transferrable to longer-form tasks; reduces mode collapse across tasks; activation steering matches DAT but fails to generalize; weight-space steering shows better generalization.
AI.conclusion: A data-free, gradient-free, non-retraining method (weight-space steering) enhances divergent thinking in LLMs and reduces mode collapse, offering a straightforward way to augment creativity in LLMs.

title: SE(2) Navigation Mesh
summary: Global navigation for ground robots in complex multi-level environments requires representations that accurately capture traversable regions while enabling efficient path planning. Current approaches present key limitations: Point clouds and volumetric occupancy maps lack explicit surface structure for traversability estimation, whereas direct pathfinding on dense triangle meshes is computationally prohibitive. Navigation meshes mitigate these challenges through polygonal abstraction of the underlying mesh, but assume yaw-invariant traversability, rendering them unsuitable for non-circular robots in constrained spaces. We propose SE(2) Navigation Mesh (SE(2) NavMesh), a polygonal representation of traversable regions that encodes yaw-dependent traversability. Our method evaluates traversability using footprint masks and constructs a graph over yaw-specific layers with explicit translational and rotational connectivity. Grounded in this representation, we develop an A*-String Pulling-A* (ASA) pathfinding strategy that hierarchically optimizes robot position and heading. We also present an online method that incrementally updates the SE(2) NavMesh from streaming point clouds during concurrent geometry reconstruction. In simulation, the SE(2) NavMesh captures over 50% more traversable area than classical NavMeshes, and the SE(2) NavMesh + ASA pipeline consistently outperforms sampling-based baselines in constrained environments. Extensive real-world experiments on a physical robot validate real-time online generation and successful navigation across multiple environments.
