AI.tldr: Semi-CoT introduces semi-supervised chain-of-thought by generating multiple pseudo-CoTs for unlabeled questions, selecting low-entropy (high-confidence) chains as demonstrations, yielding mixed results across datasets.
AI.motivation: To exploit unlabeled data to provide reasoning supervision for CoT models, moving beyond inference-time prompts to semi-supervised training signals.
AI.method: For each unlabeled question, sample multiple pseudo-CoTs, estimate answer-level semantic entropy, select low-entropy chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations, integrate as pseudo-supervision (self-training style) under Semi-CoT.
AI.result: On AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, MultiArith, the entropy gate identifies high-precision pseudo-CoTs with pseudo-answer precision 91.36%-100%. Small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, negative transfer on AQuA, ceiling on MultiArith.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo-reasoning signals, but effective use requires stronger demonstration selection or student training; Semi-CoT demonstrates potential but is dataset-sensitive and may require improvements to achieve consistent gains.

title: Lightweight Safe Reinforcement Learning for End-to-End UAV Navigation
summary: With the rapid development of autonomous aerial systems, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed in applications such as inspection, environmental monitoring, and rescue, creating growing demand for reliable autonomous navigation. However, autonomous UAV navigation in dense environments remains challenging under sparse perception and dynamic constraints. Most reinforcement learning (RL) methods lack explicit safety mechanisms, leading to unsafe exploration, unstable training, and risky behaviors, especially during high-speed flight. Even in safe RL approaches, safety is often enforced by projecting policy outputs onto a safe action set, which may introduce instability. Meanwhile, many learning-based methods rely on dense inputs or large networks, increasing computational burden and limiting lightweight onboard deployment. Facing the above challenges, we propose a safety-constrained perception-control integrated framework for UAV navigation. A lightweight network encodes sparse observations into collision-risk-aware features using asymmetric and depthwise separable convolutions. We formulate the task as a constrained Markov decision process within a hierarchical control architecture and solve it using a Lagrangian-based safe PPO algorithm. Curriculum learning further improves training stability. Experiments with varying obstacle densities and flight speeds demonstrate higher success rates, improved safety, and better efficiency than existing reinforcement learning baselines.

AI.tldr: Safety-constrained perception-control integration for UAV navigation using a lightweight network on sparse observations, a constrained MDP with hierarchical control, a Lagrangian-based safe PPO, and curriculum learning; achieves higher success, safety, and efficiency vs RL baselines in dense environments.
AI.motivation: Address the safety, stability, and efficiency challenges of learning-based UAV navigation in dense, dynamic environments with sparse sensing, where unsafe exploration and heavy computation hinder deployment.
AI.method: Encode sparse observations into collision-risk-aware features with asymmetric and depthwise separable convolutions. Formulate navigation as a constrained MDP within a hierarchical control framework and solve with a Lagrangian-based safe PPO algorithm. Employ curriculum learning to stabilize training.
AI.result: Experiments across varying obstacle densities and flight speeds show higher success rates, improved safety, and better efficiency compared with existing RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed safety-constrained perception-control framework improves autonomous UAV navigation in dense environments and enables safer, more efficient, and potentially on-board deployable learning-based navigation.

title: The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Preprint. 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ACM SoCC 2026
summary: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

AI.tldr: Compares execution substrates for coding-agent RL; large variation in startup costs and computing workload across substrates; highlights importance of optimizing infrastructure within training loops to gain efficiency.
AI.motivation: Infrastructure overhead in RL training is often ignored yet materially affects total compute costs; identifying efficient execution substrates can yield large post-training efficiency gains.
AI.method: Empirical study comparing four substrates (single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes containers, cloud VMs). Measures cold-start latency and projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories.
AI.result: Cold-start latency varies up to 110x across substrates; projected worker-hours vary by about 1.8x for a large-scale run; substantial efficiency potential if substrate is optimized.
AI.conclusion: Future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as an integral part of the training system, not just deployment plumbing.

title: Disentangling Pictorial Cue Understanding from Language Bias in VLMs via Depth Ordering Task
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, accepted to ECCV 2026 (30 pages, 13 figures, supplementary materials included)
summary: In this paper, we study depth perception of vision-language models (VLMs) to isolate the effects of pictorial depth cues and disentangle vision and language influences on model performance. To this end, we combine depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks: the VLMs are presented with images where one object is at different depth relative to other, otherwise identical, objects, and must determine whether the odd-one-out target is closer or farther to the observer. To create stimuli, we generate 2D views from simulated and real 3D scenes while controlling the presence of individual pictorial depth cues, enabling a fine-grained analysis of cue-level contributions. Language effects are examined by varying referring expression clarity. We also introduce a novel metric to quantify vision-vs-language sensitivities. Applying this methodology, we create the Odd-One-Out Depth (O3-D) dataset with 37K real and synthetic images and 147K image-question pairs. Evaluation of 12 open-source and commercial models on O3-D shows under-utilization of depth cues and depth-ordering accuracies between 47% and 56%, with no model above chance level. At the same time, our metric reveals strong linguistic bias in the answers. Neither chain-of-thought (CoT) nor in-context learning (ICL) significantly improves performance, suggesting that static image data alone may be insufficient for depth understanding. All code, the image generation pipeline, and the O3-D dataset are publicly released at https://github.com/lyiqian/o3-d.

AI.tldr: New O3-D dataset enables probing depth perception in vision-language models; findings show limited use of depth cues, with depth-ordering accuracy around 47–56% (not above chance), and strong linguistic bias; none of the evaluated models benefit from chain-of-thought or in-context learning; dataset and code released publicly.
AI.motivation: To disentangle visual depth cue processing from linguistic influences in vision-language models, enabling fine-grained cue-level analysis and a metric for vision–language sensitivity.
AI.method: Employ depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks on 2D renders derived from synthetic and real 3D scenes; systematically manipulate the presence of individual pictorial depth cues; vary referring expression clarity; introduce a metric quantifying vision-vs-language sensitivity; create and release the Odd-One-Out Depth (O3-D) dataset (~37k real/synthetic images, ~147k image-question pairs) and evaluate 12 models.
AI.result: Models under-utilize depth cues; depth-ordering accuracy ranges 47–56%; no model performs above chance; strong linguistic bias detected in answers; CoT and ICL do not significantly improve performance; static image data may be insufficient for robust depth understanding.
AI.conclusion: Static image data alone is insufficient for reliable depth understanding in VLMs; to advance depth comprehension, richer multimodal signals or training paradigms are likely necessary; the O3-D dataset and accompanying tools are publicly available for the community.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
summary: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

AI.tldr: OPINE-World is an LLM-driven agent that learns an object-centric, programmatic world model online via a two-agent loop (environment actor and model synthesize-and-verify), enabling data-efficient, reusable reasoning and planning. It uses replay verification and a Bayesian ontology error to guide exploration and model adequacy, achieving strong performance on ARC-AGI-3 without per-game training (20/25 solved; 78.4 action-efficiency).
AI.motivation: To overcome data inefficiency and limited transfer of deep world models by enabling flexible, object-centric, programmatically specified world models that can be learned online from interaction, even when object vocabulary, goals, or actions are withheld.
AI.method: Two cooperating agents form a loop: (1) an environment agent acts, (2) a program-synthesis agent generates/edits an object-centric world model in code using LLMs and refines it via counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) with replay verification. The model supports model-based planning; exploration is guided by a Bayesian ontology-error metric estimating object-type adequacy.
AI.result: On ARC-AGI-3, OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and achieves an action-efficiency score of 78.4 relative to human performance.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates data-efficient, reusable world modeling for pixel-based environments with flexible object vocabularies, showing promising scalability of program-synthesized world models and the utility of ontology-aware exploration in autonomous agents.

title: VLA-Corrector: Lightweight Detect-and-Correct Inference for Adaptive Action Horizon
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have recently achieved strong progress in embodied intelligence. To reduce policy-call frequency while preserving temporal coherence, most generative policies adopt an action chunk mechanism, executing multiple future actions in an open-loop manner under a fixed action horizon. However, this "predict-then-blindly-execute" paradigm sacrifices closed-loop reactivity: in contact-rich physical interactions, even small local perturbations can rapidly amplify within the open-loop blind spot, leading to compounding errors and ultimately task failure. To address this limitation, we propose VLA-Corrector, a lightweight corrective inference framework for action-chunked VLA policies. Without modifying the backbone policy weights, VLA-Corrector introduces a lightweight Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) that continuously compares predicted and actual visual feature evolution, enabling online detection of visual dynamics deviations. Once persistent deviation is detected, the system triggers a truncation event, discards the remaining stale actions, and invokes corrective replanning via Online Gradient Guidance (OGG). The detect-and-correct mechanism of VLA-Corrector naturally induces an event-triggered adaptive action horizon: it preserves long-horizon execution when the current chunk remains reliable, and invokes short-horizon corrective replanning when execution begins to drift. In doing so, VLA-Corrector mitigates the trade-off imposed by static horizons between execution robustness and policy-call frequency. It can be integrated into different VLA models without further retraining the VLA backbone, interrupting compounding errors while preserving much of the efficiency benefit of action chunking and substantially improving robustness in long-horizon, contact-rich robotic manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: VLA-Corrector adds a lightweight latent-space vision monitor to action-chunked VLA policies, enabling event-triggered truncation and corrective replanning (Online Gradient Guidance) to recover from visual drift, improving robustness without retraining while preserving chunking efficiency.
AI.motivation: Open-loop action chunking in vision-language-action models sacrifices closed-loop reactivity in perturbation-prone, contact-rich tasks. A lightweight, model-agnostic correction mechanism is needed to maintain long-horizon performance without increasing policy-call frequency.
AI.method: Introduce Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) to compare predicted vs. actual visual feature evolution; detect persistent deviations; on detection, truncate the remaining actions and trigger Online Gradient Guidance (OGG) for corrective replanning. This yields an event-triggered adaptive action horizon: long horizon when reliable, short horizon when drifting. No retraining of the backbone policy is required.
AI.result: Reported substantial robustness gains in long-horizon, contact-rich robotic manipulation tasks, with preserved efficiency from action chunking and no backbone retraining required.
AI.conclusion: VLA-Corrector provides a lightweight, plug-in correction framework that interrupts compounding errors and adapts horizon length via detections of visual dynamics deviations, improving robustness while maintaining the efficiency of action chunking across VLA models.

title: Conditional Inference Trees and Forests for Feature Selection
summary: Conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) reduce split-selection bias by testing features before choosing split thresholds, but repeated permutation tests and threshold searches can make these methods computationally expensive. We study CIT and CIF as top-$k$ feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. At a fixed node, if the features and permutation budget do not depend on the node responses, Bonferroni-corrected $+1$ Monte Carlo permutation $p$-values control nodewise rejection under the complete permutation null. CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With Bonferroni correction held fixed, the CIF runtime ablations indicate that adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest measured effect on runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0--8.4$\times$ and 1.9--10.8$\times$, respectively, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Sparse high-$p$ simulations indicate that forest feature sampling can leave informative features out of many split decisions. Overall, the results support CIF as a top-$k$ feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

AI.tldr: CIF/CIT can serve as top-k feature-ranking tools with competitive downstream performance, but improvements come with computational costs tied to adaptive stopping and threshold searches; Bonferroni-corrected permutation p-values can control nodewise error under a complete permutation null; sparse high-p scenarios may miss informative features.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether CIT and CIF, known for reducing split-selection bias, are effective and efficient as top-k feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction across diverse real and synthetic benchmarks.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation on 22 classification datasets and 8 regression datasets, plus runtime ablations and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. Analysis includes permutation-based p-values under complete permutation null, fixed-budget settings, and comparisons to 16–18 baseline methods.
AI.result: CIF ranks 4th (classification, 22 datasets) and 3rd (regression, 8 datasets). Under fixed Bonferroni-corrected p-values, nodewise rejection control holds. Key runtime drivers are adaptive stopping and number of thresholds searched; disabling them or using exact search increases time by roughly 4–8x and 2–11x, while downstream score changes are ≤0.011. Sparse high-p simulations reveal potential exclusion of informative features due to forest sampling.
AI.conclusion: CIF is a competitive top-k feature-ranking method for downstream prediction. It balances accuracy and interpretability with a nontrivial computational cost, and care should be taken in high-p settings where informative features may be missed due to feature sampling.

title: Hidden-Shot: Towards One-Shot Task Generalization for Low-Level Vision Generalist Models
summary: Despite the intense engagement surrounding low-level vision generalist models, their effectiveness in zero/few-shot scenarios beyond learned tasks remains unverified. The primary challenge of developing an ideal generalist lies in achieving the ability to generalize from new unseen tasks, which also can be assessed by matched quantitative criteria. Existing methods have made some progress in prompt engineering but have not systematically explored this gap across a wide range of low-level visual tasks. Stimulated by the problem, we propose Hidden-Shot, an implicit prompt mechanism aimed at exploring low-level task adaptation in a vision generalist model. Specifically, the method extracts implicit visual task-based information, utilizes a global task-aware textural prompt, and selectively merges implicit information with in-task processing information to enhance one-shot capabilities in new tasks. The overall design performs direct injection in a cost-effective manner, while minimally altering the architecture of the original generalist model. Additionally, we introduce a data-driven evaluation framework termed C/U assessment to cover two basic scenarios, 3C4U (3 conventional and 4 unconventional tasks) for retraining existing models and 3C7U (3 conventional and 7 unconventional tasks) for training from scratch, as a comprehensive assessment to systematically test the generalization ability of low-level generalist models. Experiments on seven and ten datasets outperform the state-of-the-art vision generalist model, respectively verified by 3C4U and 3C7U framework. Our presented Hidden-Shot approach demonstrates superior performance on one-shot new tasks while maintaining consistent performance on existing tasks.

AI.tldr: Hidden-Shot leverages an implicit prompt mechanism to boost one-shot adaptation for low-level vision generalist models and introduces C/U evaluation frameworks (3C4U, 3C7U) to systematically assess generalization across conventional and unconventional tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on seven and ten datasets respectively.
AI.motivation: Current low-level vision generalist models struggle to generalize to unseen tasks in zero/few-shot settings. Prior work focuses on prompt engineering but lacks a systematic, broad evaluation across diverse tasks. A data-driven, cost-efficient adaptation mechanism and rigorous evaluation framework are needed to quantify generalization.
AI.method: Hidden-Shot extracts implicit task-based information, applies a global task-aware textural prompt, and selectively merges this with in-task processing information to enhance one-shot capabilities. The injection is cost-effective with minimal architectural changes. Evaluation is performed using C/U assessment: 3C4U (3 conventional, 4 unconventional tasks) for retraining existing models, and 3C7U (3 conventional, 7 unconventional tasks) for training from scratch.
AI.result: Empirical results show outperforming the state-of-the-art vision generalist on seven datasets under 3C4U and on ten datasets under 3C7U frameworks, validating improved one-shot generalization to new tasks while maintaining performance on existing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-Shot provides a practical, efficient mechanism for improving one-shot generalization in low-level vision generalists and introduces a comprehensive, data-driven evaluation framework (C/U) to systematically test generalization across a wide task spectrum.

title: Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning
summary: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

AI.tldr: Scaling SOLiD reduces undetected deception across model sizes and enables removal of expensive labelers, but detector performance is sensitive to distribution shifts between training and preference data.
AI.motivation: Address the high cost of monitoring and preventing deceptive responses in LLMs by using scalable lie-detection with SOLiD and testing its scalability on larger models and more realistic preference-learning tasks.
AI.method: Scale SOLiD to larger architectures (up to 405B parameters) and evaluate deception detection at a fixed detector true positive rate (TPR ≈ 99%) across diverse preference-learning settings; compare deception rates with and without human labelers in the fine-tuning phase; assess robustness to distribution shift between detector training data and preference-training data.
AI.result: Detections improve with model size: undetected deception falls from 34% at 1B parameters to 14% at 405B when TPR is 99%. Expensive human labelers can be removed from the fine-tuning pipeline without a statistically significant rise in deception. Detector performance degrades under distribution shift, increasing false positives to impractical levels.
AI.conclusion: Scaling SOLiD to larger models is promising for scalable oversight, but distribution shift poses a major challenge by inflating false positives; approaches to align detector training and preference data distributions are required for robust deployment.

title: DL-SLAM: Enabling High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting SLAM in Dynamic Environments based on Dual-Level Probability
summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have enabled significant progress in dense dynamic Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM). Prevailing methods typically discard predefined dynamic objects, ignoring that transiently static objects offer valuable geometric constraints for pose estimation. A recent work attempts to leverage this potential by employing per-pixel uncertainty maps to quantify the magnitude of motion. While this approach enables transiently static objects to enhance pose estimation, it erroneously integrates these objects into the static map, resulting in persistent artifacts. Moreover, its reliance on purely geometric information leads to ambiguous object boundaries in the uncertainty maps. To overcome these limitations, we present DL-SLAM, a monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM system built upon a novel dual-level probabilistic framework. Our method computes dynamic probability maps by combining semantic and geometric information. These pixel-level probabilities are lifted to 3D and aggregated to derive an object-level dynamic probability for each instance. Object-level probability enables the categorical pruning of dynamic Gaussians, resulting in an artifact-free static map. The static map, in turn, provides a geometrically consistent guidance to refine the pixel-wise probabilities, enhancing their reliability. Experimental results demonstrate that DL-SLAM outperforms existing approaches, improving tracking accuracy by up to 13\% while generating high-fidelity semantic maps.

AI.tldr: DL-SLAM introduces a dual-level probabilistic framework for monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM that fuses semantic and geometric cues to compute per-pixel dynamic probabilities, lifts them to 3D to derive object-level probabilities for pruning dynamic Gaussians, and uses the static map to refine pixel probabilities, yielding artifact-free maps and up to 13% tracking accuracy gains with high-fidelity semantic maps.
AI.motivation: Prevailing methods either discard dynamic objects or rely solely on geometric uncertainty maps, leading to lost constraints or artifacts from transiently static objects and ambiguous boundaries.
AI.method: Propose DL-SLAM: a monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM with a dual-level probabilistic framework. Compute per-pixel dynamic probabilities from semantic and geometric information; lift to 3D to obtain object-level probabilities per instance; prune dynamic Gaussians using object-level probabilities; use the static map to refine pixel probabilities in a loop.
AI.result: DL-SLAM outperforms existing approaches, achieving up to 13% improvement in tracking accuracy and generating high-fidelity semantic maps.
AI.conclusion: A dual-level probabilistic integration of semantic and geometric cues enables artifact-free static maps and improved pose estimation by leveraging object-level dynamics, with the static map providing geometric refinement to pixel-level probabilities.

title: On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

AI.tldr: Moderate domain-specific MoE pruning preserves in-domain utility with limited reliability decline; extreme pruning increases hallucinations; cross-domain transfer degrades utility and reliability; evaluating only utility is insufficient for high-stakes deployment.
AI.motivation: To examine how domain-specific pruning affects both utility and reliability of mixture-of-experts models, particularly in biomedical/high-stakes contexts.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of four MoE models, six pruning methods, across multiple pruning ratios, on generation and classification tasks, in-domain biomedical and cross-domain settings.
AI.result: Moderate pruning maintains in-domain utility without immediate reliability loss; reliability declines at high pruning; cross-domain performance deteriorates rapidly in both utility and reliability; pruning impacts hallucination risk.
AI.conclusion: Safe compression via MoE requires domain- and task-aware pruning with reliability assessment; focusing solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment.

title: Boosting Infrared Small Target Detection via Logit-Domain Contrast and Adaptive Shape Refinement
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Infrared small target detection (IRSTD) remains challenging due to tiny target size, low signal-to-noise ratio, severe foreground-background imbalance, and blurred boundaries in complex scenes. Existing methods usually rely on post-activation probability-domain supervision for discrimination, where weak targets and strong clutter may produce saturated and close probabilities, limiting weak-target discrimination. Meanwhile, blurred boundaries and halo-like predictions mainly stem from thermal diffusion, tiny target scale, boundary uncertainty, and insufficient explicit contour constraints. To address these issues, we propose Adaptive-Contrastive SLSIoU (AC-SLSIoU), a plug-and-play discriminative and shape-aware loss for IRSTD. Specifically, a Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) is introduced to enlarge the response gap between targets and informative hard negatives in the logit space, thereby enhancing weak-target discrimination. Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applies scale-aware annular penalties to refine target contours and suppress halo-like overflow responses. In addition, False-Alarm Focal Loss assigns larger weights to high-probability negative samples, further penalizing persistent high-confidence false alarms. Without introducing extra inference overhead, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing detectors and consistently improves both detection accuracy and shape quality. Extensive experiments and cross-backbone evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and generalization ability of the proposed method for infrared small target detection.

AI.tldr: AC-SLSIoU: a plug-and-play, discriminative and shape-aware loss for infrared small target detection (IRSTD); introduces LDMC, ABS, and False-Alarm Focal Loss; improves weak-target discrimination and contour quality without extra inference cost; demonstrated robustness across backbones.
AI.motivation: Infrared small targets are extremely small, have low SNR, and exist within clutter, causing weak discrimination and blurred boundaries. Existing post-activation supervision can saturate probabilities for weak targets and strong clutter, while boundary blur (halo) stems from diffusion, tiny targets, boundary uncertainty, and insufficient explicit contour constraints. A loss that enforces discrimination in logit space and provides explicit contour guidance without adding inference overhead is needed.
AI.method: Propose Adaptive-Contrastive SLSIoU (AC-SLSIoU) as a plug-and-play discriminative and shape-aware loss. Key components: (1) Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) to widen the gap between target responses and informative hard negatives in logit space, boosting weak-target discrimination; (2) Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applying scale-aware annular penalties to refine target contours and suppress halo-like spillover; (3) False-Alarm Focal Loss that assigns larger weights to high-probability negatives to penalize persistent high-confidence false alarms. The loss is designed to be integrated into existing detectors without adding inference overhead.
AI.result: Extensive experiments with cross-backbone evaluations show that AC-SLSIoU improves detection accuracy and shape quality across diverse IRSTD detectors, demonstrating robustness and generalization to different backbone architectures.
AI.conclusion: AC-SLSIoU effectively addresses weak-target discrimination and boundary/halo issues in IRSTD, delivering improved detection performance and contour fidelity while remaining plug-and-play with no additional inference cost.

title: EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: Grounds hypothesis generation for Earth observation in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph using a heterogeneous graph neural network to rank dataset pairings, with a three-agent LLM pipeline to filter, generate, and evaluate structured hypotheses; yields 160 hypotheses from 1,475 NASA datasets, with novel pairings rated plausibly close to real co-usages, though evaluation stability varies by judge and model.
AI.motivation: Move beyond unstructured literature for LLM-driven scientific hypothesis generation by grounding reasoning in a structured knowledge graph specific to Earth observation, enabling coherent, domain-relevant dataset pairing hypotheses.
AI.method: 1) Ground hypotheses in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. 2) Train a heterogeneous graph neural network on historical co-usage relations to rank candidate dataset pairings. 3) Deploy a three-agent LLM pipeline that filters, generates, and evaluates structured hypotheses. 4) Apply to 1,475 NASA datasets to produce hypotheses. 5) Conduct a 2x2x2 factorial evaluation across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 to assess robustness and judge variability.
AI.result: Generated 160 hypotheses spanning ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol–cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry from 1,475 NASA datasets. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages. Rankings are stable across surveyed LLMs, but absolute scores depend on the judge, indicating evaluation heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline can surface scientifically coherent yet unexplored dataset pairings grounded in a structured knowledge graph; however, single-judge LLM evaluations show limitations, underscoring the need for multi-judge validation and robust evaluation frameworks.

title: SPLC: Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) holds significant potential for crowd robot navigation in human-robot coexistence applications. However, the inherent complexity of pedestrian motion renders the design of effective reward functions for promoting socially compliant robot behaviors a persistent challenge. This paper proposes a Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation (SPLC) algorithm to eliminate the need for detailed reward design. Its core innovation lies in the introduction of a social preference feedback mechanism to automatically generate preference data through principled preference evaluation criteria. By explicitly accounting for the intricacies of pedestrian dynamics, the pipeline mitigates the reward bias and facilitates the systematic quantification of broad social norms, thereby fostering socially compliant behaviors. Extensive experiments integrating SPLC with offline RL methods demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across standard performance metrics. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the TurtleBot4 further validate the effectiveness of SPLC in practical human-robot coexistence settings. Our code and video demos are available at https://github.com/sklus949/SPLC.

AI.tldr: Introduces SPLC, a social preference learning framework for crowd robot navigation that eliminates manual reward design in offline RL by using a social preference feedback mechanism to generate preference data from pedestrian dynamics, achieving improvements over baselines and validating on TurtleBot4 with released code.
AI.motivation: Reward design for socially compliant crowd navigation is error-prone and labor-intensive; offline RL offers data-efficiency but relies on good reward signals. SPLC aims to automate preference data generation reflecting social norms to improve policy learning without handcrafted rewards.
AI.method: SPLC embeds a social preference feedback mechanism that derives preference data from principled evaluation criteria reflecting pedestrian dynamics. This data guides offline RL to learn policies without explicit reward shaping. The approach is integrated with offline RL methods and evaluated in simulation and on real-world TurtleBot4 demonstrations; code and demos are released.
AI.result: SPLC-enabled offline RL shows consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across standard performance metrics in both simulation and real-world TurtleBot4 experiments.
AI.conclusion: The social-preference-based data generation mitigates reward bias and facilitates learning socially compliant navigation; SPLC offers a practical, reproducible pathway for offline RL in crowd robot navigation, with potential for broader application and future enhancement of social norms modeling.

title: Geometry-Aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary:
We propose a novel hybrid neural architecture, the Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN), which integrates V.L.Rvachev's R-functions into the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) framework. The proposed approach combines two complementary modeling mechanisms: smooth nonlinear structure is learned by KAN branches, while known geometric or logical constraints are encoded analytically using differentiable R-functions. This enables explicit representation of discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries within a trainable neural architecture.
  The framework implements differentiable logical operations through R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions, allowing complex geometric supports to be represented analytically and incorporated directly into regression models. Several GRS-KAN variants are introduced, including additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures.
  The method is demonstrated on regression problems involving discontinuities with circular and rectangular supports. Numerical experiments show that explicit geometric encoding substantially improves predictive accuracy and boundary localization compared with standard KANs. In the considered benchmarks, geometry-aware GRS-KAN models reduce test RMSE by up to 67% while simultaneously improving interpretability through explicit analytical representation of the learned geometric structure. The agnostic variant further demonstrates the ability to automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial for a given learning task.

AI.tldr: GRS-KAN merges R-functions with KAN to encode geometry and discontinuities as differentiable priors within a neural regression model, yielding improved accuracy and interpretability; multiple variants including agnostic to auto-select priors; shows up to 67% RMSE reduction on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of standard KANs in modeling discontinuities and geometric constraints; enable explicit geometric priors that improve accuracy and interpretability.
AI.method: Integrate differentiable R-functions (R-conjunctions/disjunctions) into KAN architecture; implement additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted variants; train on regression tasks with circular/rectangular supports to encode geometry.
AI.result: Significant performance gains: substantial RMSE reduction (up to 67%), improved boundary localization and interpretability; agnostic variant can automatically decide if priors help.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware priors encoded via R-functions enhance KAN performance and interpretability; the approach provides a flexible framework for combining analytic geometric constraints with neural regression.

title: Mind the Gap: Standard 3DGS Evaluation Primarily Measures Near-Trajectory Interpolation
summary: Standard MipNeRF360-style 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) evaluation holds out every N-th frame -- but these frames have trained neighbors on both sides, so the metric measures near-trajectory interpolation rather than spatial generalization. We introduce a fair matched-count protocol that isolates this effect: both arms train on the same number of images and differ only in whether the holdout is spread evenly (interpolation) or forms a contiguous spatial sector (extrapolation). Our primary finding is a large, consistent interpolation-extrapolation gap of 3~12dB -- several times the differences typically reported between competing methods. The gap is robust to training noise, is in two cases large enough to flip a method ranking under multi-seed confirmation, and -- crucially -- persists across three representation families, including a non-Gaussian volumetric neural radiance field (NeRF), so it reflects spatial coverage rather than any one representation. Diagnostically, it is dominated by a diffuse/geometry-proxy component and tracks each view's angular distance to its nearest training view, a zero-cost signal that also guides capture planning; loss-side regularization yields only marginal gains. Standard holdouts remain useful for near-trajectory rendering but should not, alone, be read as evidence of spatial generalization. Prior work notes protocol sensitivity; ours is, to our knowledge, the first to combine matched-count paired holdout, cross-representation quantification, and a diagnostic analysis Table 1. We describe a spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit with standardized splits and baselines for 16 scenes, which we are preparing for public release.

AI.tldr: Matched-count evaluation reveals a large interpolation-extrapolation gap (3–12 dB) in 3D Gaussian Splatting across representations; spatial generalization is distinct from near-trajectory interpolation; the paper proposes a matched-count protocol, cross-representation validation, and a diagnostic angular-distance metric; emphasizes spatial coverage and cautions against using standard holdouts as evidence of generalization.
AI.motivation: To disentangle training-neighborhood interpolation from genuine spatial generalization in 3D scene representations, and to provide a fair, reproducible benchmark for spatial extrapolation.
AI.method: Introduce matched-count holdout protocol with two arms: interpolation (spatially spread holdout) and extrapolation (contiguous spatial sector), train on equal numbers of images; evaluate across three representation families including NeRF. Use zero-cost angular-distance to training views as diagnostic. Regularization effects tested.
AI.result: Consistent large gap (3–12 dB) between interpolation and extrapolation, robust to training noise, in multiple representations; can flip method ranking under multi-seed tests; gap tracks angular distance; mostly due to geometry proxy; simple loss regularization provides marginal gains; holdouts remain useful for near-trajectory rendering but not spatial generalization; introduces benchmark toolkit for 16 scenes.
AI.conclusion: Spatial generalization in 3D scene representations is not adequately captured by standard holdouts; matched-count and cross-representation diagnostics are necessary; the evaluation metric should emphasize spatial coverage and extrapolation behavior; prepared public toolkit to enable standardized evaluation.

title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation
summary: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Hawk is a training-free framework for NPU kernel generation that uses three hardware-aware knowledge modules to improve correctness and performance, achieving large gains on real workloads.
AI.motivation: NPUs have strict hardware constraints; LLMs lack hardware priors; naive code transplantation can cause runtime crashes and performance degradation.
AI.method: Three modules: Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis with Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation; Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval with 2D-Retrieval projecting queries into syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation with LLM-driven arbitration and empirical feedback to prune errors and consolidate knowledge.
AI.result: Improved generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%; up to 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines on real-world NPU workloads.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-aware, training-free knowledge integration can substantially improve NPU kernel generation; promising, but further details on generalization, overhead, and reproducibility are needed.

title: PhysMani: Physics-principled 3D World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
comment: ECCV 2026. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/vLAR-group/PhysMani
summary: Manipulating fast and dynamically moving targets in unstructured 3D environments remains challenging for embodied AI. Existing visual-language-action models and world models struggle with accurate 3D geometry and physically meaningful forecasting. We propose PhysMani, a framework that couples a physics-principled 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy model. The world model learns a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field via online optimization for fast and physically grounded future dynamics prediction. The policy model integrates the predicted 3D scene future dynamics through a learnable token based cross-attention module. We introduce PhysMani-Bench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark with 16 tasks, and demonstrate a superior success rate over strong baselines in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.

AI.tldr: PhysMani combines a physics-principled 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy, using a divergence-free velocity field and token-based cross-attention to predict and exploit 3D scene dynamics. It introduces PhysMani-Bench (16 dynamic manipulation tasks) and reports superior success rates vs baselines in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.
AI.motivation: Manipulating fast, dynamically moving targets in unstructured 3D environments is hard for current visual-language-action models and world models, which struggle with accurate 3D geometry and physically meaningful forecasting.
AI.method: A 3D Gaussian world model learns a divergence-free velocity field via online optimization for physically grounded future dynamics. A policy model ingests predicted 3D scene dynamics through a learnable token-based cross-attention module. A new benchmark, PhysMani-Bench, with 16 tasks, evaluates performance in simulation and real-world robots.
AI.result: PhysMani outperforms strong baselines on the 16-task PhysMani-Bench across both simulated and real-world experiments, demonstrating improved success rates and robust dynamic manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Coupling physics-based 3D dynamics with a future-aware policy via cross-attention yields robust manipulation of fast targets in unstructured 3D environments, with the PhysMani-Bench benchmark validating its effectiveness and generalization.

title: Token Geometry
summary: Language models learn continuous programs over discrete symbols, with the embedding table and LM-head acting as the read/write interface between them. We show that this interface has gradient geometry distinct from dense hidden weights which can be exploited to improve the Pareto frontier across supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining, while only utilizing kilobytes of optimizer state. We introduce Ember, a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that utilizes O(V + D) VRAM, instead of Adam's O(2VD), and forgoes the need to shard both token table optimizer states. We provide empirical evidence that Ember scales effectively across batch size and parameter count. We show that the optimization trajectory of tokens can be well described by a simple 1D ray, counter to the popular belief that neural net parameters navigate a heavily nonconvex landscape. We provide a principled view on the surprisingly narrow space of optimizers that suffice for Transformer training. Finally, we open-source our distributed Ember implementation that merges cleanly with existing ZeRO/FSDP setups to support further research at https://github.com/katop1234/ember

AI.tldr: Ember is a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices in language models, exploiting distinct gradient geometry of the read/write interface to improve the Pareto frontier across finetuning, RL, and pretraining, with a low memory footprint; open-source integration with ZeRO/FSDP.
AI.motivation: The embedding table and LM-head interact with discrete symbol embeddings differently from dense hidden weights, creating gradient geometry distinct from other parameters; current optimizers (e.g., Adam) incur high memory and shard-level requirements that limit scaling; there is a need for scalable, memory-efficient optimization of token-level parameters.
AI.method: Introduce Ember, an optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that achieves O(V + D) VRAM per device (vs Adam's O(2VD)), avoiding the need to shard both token-table optimizer states. Provide empirical evidence of scaling with batch size and parameter count. Characterize token optimization trajectories as a simple 1D ray. Argue a principled view on the limited set of optimizers needed for Transformer training. Release a distributed Ember implementation compatible with ZeRO/FSDP.
AI.result: Ember scales effectively across batch size and parameter count; token optimization follows a 1D ray in optimization space; memory footprint is dramatically reduced (kilobytes of optimizer state); compatible with standard distributed training frameworks (ZeRO/FSDP); provides improved Pareto trade-offs in supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining.
AI.conclusion: A principled, memory-efficient optimizer for embedding and LM-head parameters that reveals a narrow space of necessary optimizers for Transformer training; the Ember implementation is open-source to facilitate further research and integration with existing distributed training regimes.

title: MVFusion-GS: Motion-Variance Guided Temporal Attention for High-Quality Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis for static scenes. Extending it to dynamic scenes via deformation fields has recently attracted significant attention, particularly for dynamic scene reconstructionband distractor-free. However, existing deformation networks lack explicit motion awareness: they neither capture long-term motion intensity nor exploit short-term temporal coherence, leading to inaccurate foreground deformation and pseudo-static residuals in the background. We present MVFusion-GS, a method that enhances deformation networks with two complementary motion-aware mechanisms. The Motion-Variance Guided Refinement aggregates per-Gaussian deformation statistics across time to estimate motion variance and uses it to guide dynamic-static separation during deformation prediction. The MotionFormer Temporal Attention module applies Transformer self-attention over neighboring timesteps to model local motion dependencies and improve temporal consistency. Extensive experiments on both dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, showing that explicit motion awareness improves both foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction.

AI.tldr: MVFusion-GS enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting for dynamic scenes by adding two motion-aware modules: (1) Motion-Variance Guided Refinement to quantify per-Gaussian motion and separate dynamic vs static components, and (2) MotionFormer Temporal Attention to model local motion via Transformer over neighboring frames. This yields state-of-the-art results on dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free benchmarks by improving foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing deformation networks for dynamic 3D scenes lack explicit motion awareness, failing to capture long-term motion variability and short-term temporal coherence. This leads to inaccurate foreground deformation and residual static background artifacts.
AI.method: Two complementary mechanisms: (i) Motion-Variance Guided Refinement aggregates per-Gaussian deformation statistics across time to estimate motion variance and guide dynamic-static separation during deformation prediction; (ii) MotionFormer Temporal Attention applies Transformer self-attention over neighboring timesteps to model local motion dependencies and improve temporal consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free reconstruction benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating that explicit motion awareness improves both foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling motion in deformation networks via variance-guided refinement and temporal attention substantially improves dynamic 3D scene reconstruction, yielding better foreground motion handling and static background fidelity, with strong empirical evidence on standard benchmarks.

title: Safe and Adaptive Cloud Healing: Verifying LLM-Generated Recovery Plans with a Neural-Symbolic World Model
summary: As the scale and complexity of cloud-based AI systems continue to escalate, ensuring service reliability through rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery has become a critical challenge. While existing approaches integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic understanding and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for policy optimization, they often rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize the generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift with PASE, a Planning-Aware Semantic self-healing engine, a novel fault self-healing framework that reconceptualizes recovery as a neuro-symbolic program synthesis task. PASE employs an LLM as a core Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from a library of semantic primitives. A Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility through simulation, while a Meta-Prompt Optimizer, trained via DRL, learns to generate optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning process. This tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop enables dynamic, context-aware recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces. Experiments on a real-world cloud fault injection dataset demonstrate that PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios. Our framework advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance.

AI.tldr: PASE reframes fault self-healing as neuro-symbolic, plan-driven synthesis using an LLM core, with verification and meta-prompt optimization, achieving major reductions in recovery time and improved detection in unknown faults.
AI.motivation: As cloud-based AI systems scale in complexity, traditional, sequential self-healing pipelines underutilize LLM reasoning. A tight loop that plans, simulates, and adapts can enable context-aware recovery beyond predefined action spaces.
AI.method: PASE uses: (1) an LLM as Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from semantic primitives; (2) a Neural-Symbolic World Model to verify plan feasibility via simulation; (3) a Meta-Prompt Optimizer trained with DRL to learn prompts that guide the LLM’s planning; (4) a reason-plan-verify-adapt loop for dynamic recovery strategy generation.
AI.result: On a real-world cloud fault injection dataset, PASE reduces average recovery time by over 40% and improves fault-detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios compared with state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance, advancing autonomous system management for resilient cloud services.

title: A Stereo Visual SLAM System Using Object-Level Motion Estimation and Geometric Filtering Based on Cross Disparity
summary: This paper presents OCD SLAM, a dynamic stereo visual SLAM framework that extends ORB-SLAM2 by jointly addressing dynamic objects and dynamic features in the scene. Usual visual SLAM systems operating in dynamic environments often fail in the presence of moving objects, due to the static-world assumption used in pose estimation and mapping. To address this predicament, we introduce a novel geometric approach based on the discrepancy between disparity and a newly proposed notion called ``cross disparity'', which exploits both temporal and stereo inconsistency to identify dynamic feature points. Complementary to this feature-level motion analysis, OCD SLAM integrates a 3D object detection module (SMOKE) with Kalman filter-based object tracking to perform object-level motion classification, enabling robust separation of static and dynamic scene elements for accurate pose estimation. The proposed approach has been evaluated on various sequences from the KITTI Odometry and KITTI Raw datasets. Results demonstrate that OCD SLAM achieves significant improvement in trajectory accuracy compared to ORB-SLAM2 and several state-of-the-art dynamic SLAM methods. Ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the cross disparity module in the KITTI Raw dataset and show that this method is able to detect dynamic features that are missed by the 3D object detection scheme alone.

AI.tldr: A dynamic stereo SLAM called OCD SLAM extends ORB-SLAM2 to handle dynamic objects via cross disparity for feature-level dynamics and a SMOKE-based 3D object detector with Kalman tracking for object-level motion, achieving improved trajectory accuracy on KITTI datasets.
AI.motivation: To overcome the static-world assumption in visual SLAM and maintain accurate pose/mapping in scenes with moving objects by detecting dynamic features and separating static/dynamic elements.
AI.method: Introduce cross disparity, a geometric measure exploiting temporal and stereo inconsistency to identify dynamic feature points via disparity discrepancy. Combine with SMOKE-based 3D object detection and Kalman-filter object tracking for object-level motion classification, enabling robust separation of static/dynamic scene elements for pose estimation.
AI.result: On KITTI Odometry/Raw sequences, OCD SLAM achieves significant trajectory accuracy improvements over ORB-SLAM2 and other dynamic SLAM methods; ablation shows cross disparity is effective, especially in KITTI Raw, and detects dynamic features beyond 3D object detection alone.
AI.conclusion: Cross disparity plus object-level tracking provides complementary dynamic handling, enabling robust, accurate pose estimation in dynamic environments; the approach validates the benefit of integrating feature-level and object-level motion cues in SLAM.

title: Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum and Faster Hyperparameter Exploration to Tackle Class Imbalance in Federated Learning
summary: Class imbalance poses a critical challenge in federated learning (FL), where underrepresented classes suffer from poor predictive performance yet cannot be addressed by standard centralized techniques due to privacy and heterogeneity constraints. We propose FedCGNM (Federated Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum), a client-side optimizer in FL that partitions classes into a small number of groups based on minimum within-group variance, maintains a momentum per group, normalizes each group momentum to unit length, and uses the summation of the normalized group momentums as an update direction. This design both equalizes gradient magnitude across majority and minority groups and mitigates the noise inherent in rare-class gradients. We further provide a theoretical convergence analysis explicitly accounting for time-varying resampling-rates. Additionally, to efficiently optimize these rates in small-client regimes, we introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit (XAB) based algorithm that exploits federated parallelism that evaluates many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset demonstrates that FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines, with FedHOO yielding further gains in small-scale federations.

AI.tldr: FedCGNM introduces class-grouped normalized momentum for federated learning to address long-tailed class imbalance; paired with FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit rate optimizer; shows empirical improvements on benchmarks and a proprietary dataset.
AI.motivation: Class imbalance in federated learning under privacy and data heterogeneity constraints leads to poor performance on minority classes; centralized imbalance remedies are not applicable, necessitating client-side, privacy-preserving strategies.
AI.method: Partition classes into a small number of groups by minimum within-group variance; maintain a momentum per group; normalize each group's momentum to unit length; sum the normalized group momenta to form the update direction. Theoretical convergence analysis accounts for time-varying resampling rates. FedHOO uses X-armed-bandit optimization to efficiently search rate combinations in small-client regimes by exploiting federated parallelism, evaluating many two-rate combinations per client at linear cost.
AI.result: FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines across four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset. FedHOO yields additional gains in small-scale federations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FedCGNM addresses class imbalance via group-wise momentum normalization, with a convergence guarantee under varying resampling. FedHOO provides an efficient, scalable mechanism to optimize learning rates in FL, enhancing performance in limited-client settings.

title: VLAFlow: A Unified Training Framework for Vision-Language-Action Models via Co-training and Future Latent Alignment
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently advanced robotic manipulation, yet the effects of different robot-data pre-training paradigms remain difficult to compare because existing models often differ in architecture, data, action space, and evaluation protocol. We present VLAFlow (Vision-Language-Action Flow), a unified flow-matching framework for controlled comparison of VLA training objectives. Using a heterogeneous robot corpus, OXEMix, containing approximately 5,000 hours of data from DROID, OpenX-Embodiment, OpenX-Augmented, and RoboCOIN, we evaluate four paradigms under the same pi0-style architecture, shared VLM backbone, action expert, and 14-dimensional action space: action-only modeling (MindPI), language-supervised co-training (MindLPI), future latent alignment (MindWPI), and their combination (MindLWPI). Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv show that action-only pre-training is sensitive to heterogeneous data. In contrast, language supervision helps preserve vision-language generalization, while future latent alignment improves state-transition and action-outcome modeling. By combining both signals, MindLWPI achieves the most stable overall transfer performance across benchmarks. These results suggest a meta-action space view: language and future latent representations provide complementary intermediate constraints that make heterogeneous action supervision smoother and more transferable.

AI.tldr: Unified framework VLAFlow enables controlled comparison of VLA pre-training paradigms on a large heterogeneous robot dataset; combining language supervision and future latent alignment yields best transfer.
AI.motivation: To enable fair, ablation-ready comparison of VLA pre-training objectives under identical architecture/data/space, and to understand how data heterogeneity interacts with action modeling signals.
AI.method: Introduce VLAFlow with a pi0-style architecture, shared VLM backbone, action expert, 14D action space; evaluate four paradigms MindPI (action-only), MindLPI (language-supervised), MindWPI (future latent alignment), MindLWPI (combination) on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv using OXEMix (~5k hours from DROID/OpenX-Embodiment/OpenX-Augmented/RoboCOIN).
AI.result: Action-only pre-training is sensitive to heterogeneous data; language supervision preserves vision-language generalization; future latent alignment improves state-transition and action-outcome modeling; MindLWPI yields the most stable transfer across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A meta-action-space view where language and future latent representations act as complementary intermediate constraints, smoothing heterogeneous action supervision and enhancing transfer; combining both signals yields robust VLA training across diverse datasets.

title: SemHash-LLM: A Multi-Granularity Semantic Hashing Framework for Document Deduplication
summary: Large scale document deduplication must preserve semantic equivalence while remaining efficient over massive corpora. We present SemHash LLM, a multi granularity framework that unifies semantic projection hashing, attention weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM based adjudication. The method combines character, token, and document level signals through gated fusion, then applies a cascaded filtering pipeline for efficient candidate reduction. Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space, while attention weighted Min- Hash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content. Adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation further improve robustness across template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments. Experiments show that SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality with less than one percent neural verification cost.

AI.tldr: A multi-granularity SemHash LLM framework for large-scale document deduplication using semantic projection hashing, attention-weighted MinHash, boundary learning, and selective LLM adjudication; achieves <1% neural verification cost while maintaining high accuracy.
AI.motivation: Efficiently identify semantically equivalent documents in massive corpora while preserving semantics, addressing boilerplate, short text perturbations, and template pollution; reduce neural verification costs.
AI.method: Integrates semantic projection hashing in distilled LLM embedding space, attention-weighted MinHash to downweight boilerplate, gated fusion of character, token, and document signals; cascaded filtering pipeline; adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation; selective LLM adjudication.
AI.result: Empirical results show strong duplicate detection quality with <1% neural verification cost.
AI.conclusion: SemHash LLM offers robust, scalable deduplication with low neural verification, resilient to common perturbations.

title: Cross-Platform Control for Autonomous Surface Vehicles via Adaptive Reinforcement Learning
summary: Autonomous surface vehicles vary widely in hydrodynamic and actuation characteristics, yet most controllers are designed for single-platform deployment. We present an adaptive reinforcement learning approach for trajectory tracking that enables zero-shot cross-platform deployment using a single policy. Since the deployment platform's dynamics are unknown to the policy, we address cross-platform generalization with the standard partial-observability approach of conditioning on interaction history, employing a teacher-student architecture in which a learned module infers a latent representation of the platform dynamics. The policy is trained in simulation under randomized vessel dynamics and is deployed zero-shot to two real-world platforms without any fine-tuning, despite relying on a simple analytical dynamics model rather than a high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulator. In real-world experiments on two different platforms, the adaptive policy outperforms non-adaptive learning-based baselines by up to 58% in position mean absolute error while approaching the tracking accuracy of a platform-specific tuned controller.

AI.tldr: Adaptive RL policy enables zero-shot cross-platform trajectory tracking for autonomous surface vehicles by conditioning on interaction history and using a teacher-student latent dynamics module; trained in randomized simulated dynamics and deployed without fine-tuning to two real platforms.
AI.motivation: Achieve robust, cross-platform trajectory tracking for heterogeneous autonomous surface vehicles without platform-specific tuning, addressing unknown and varying platform dynamics.
AI.method: Partial-observability achieved by conditioning on interaction history; teacher-student module infers a latent representation of platform dynamics; policy trained in simulation with randomized vessel dynamics; zero-shot deployment to real platforms using a simple analytical dynamics model rather than a high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulator.
AI.result: Outperforms non-adaptive learning-based baselines by up to 58% in position mean absolute error; approaches the tracking accuracy of a platform-specific tuned controller; successful zero-shot deployment on two real platforms.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates cross-platform generalization of RL-based trajectory tracking for ASVs through latent dynamics inference and history-conditioned policies; simple dynamics models can suffice for robust zero-shot transfer, enabling scalable deployment across heterogeneous platforms.

title: How to Allocate Your Tokens? Scaling Laws with Training Steps and Batch Size
summary: We propose a scaling law that takes into account model size and training data while explicitly splitting the latter into training steps and batch size (called three-term law). Fitting the proposed law on a large set of training runs, we find that it correctly recovers the scaling of the optimal batch size. Moreover, because it makes use of training runs with suboptimal batch size, our proposed law can be robustly fit with a significantly smaller amount of training runs. We further show that the three-term law can be used to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes, and that it matches previous empirical findings related to the critical batch size.

AI.tldr: A three-term scaling law that explicitly separates training data into steps and batch size, enabling accurate prediction of optimal batch size and robust fitting from suboptimal runs.
AI.motivation: Standard scaling laws often consider model size and data quantity but do not explicitly separate data into the number of training steps and batch size. The authors aim to better capture how batch size affects learning efficiency and to reduce the number of training runs required to fit the law.
AI.method: Introduce a scaling law with three terms (model size, total training data, and an explicit representation of batch size via training steps versus batch size). Fit the law on a large collection of training runs, verify that it recovers the known scaling of optimal batch size, and extend the framework to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes and to connect with the critical batch size literature.
AI.result: The three-term law reproduces the observed scaling of the optimal batch size and can be robustly fitted with fewer runs by leveraging suboptimal batch sizes. It also yields scaling relations for suboptimal batch sizes and aligns with prior empirical findings about the critical batch size.
AI.conclusion: A three-term scaling law that splits data into steps and batch size is effective for modeling batch-size effects, enables efficient fitting with fewer experiments, and coheres with existing results on critical batch size.

title: Multi-THuMBS: Multi-person Tracking of 3D Human Meshes Beyond Video Shots
summary: Tracking multi-person 3D human meshes from in-the-wild videos is a highly challenging problem due to complex interactions, frequent occlusions, and severe truncation inherent in unconstrained environments. While recent approaches have improved robustness against these issues, they largely overlook the critical challenge prevalent in real-world footage: frequent shot changes. These abrupt transitions in camera viewpoints often cause existing methods to lose track of human identities and fail in reconstructing temporally coherent trajectories. Although several recent works have explored 3D human mesh tracking under shot changes, they are still limited to single-person scenarios, making them inadequate for real-world videos where multiple people interact and appear simultaneously. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-THuMBS (Multi-person Tracking of 3D Human Meshes Beyond Video Shots) that leverages a state-of-the-art 3D scene prior to reconstruct the two boundary frames in a single shared 3D space. Human meshes are then registered within the shared 3D space, maintaining per-person identity and motion consistency across shot changes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements in 3D human mesh recovery, camera pose estimation, and identity tracking, thereby ensuring high-fidelity motion reconstruction with consistent identity preservation across shots compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes Multi-THuMBS, a multi-person 3D mesh tracking method across video shot changes by embedding boundary frames into a shared 3D space using a 3D scene prior, enabling identity-preserving tracking and improved 3D recovery, camera pose, and tracking performance.
AI.motivation: The problem is highly challenging in unconstrained videos due to occlusions, truncation, and especially frequent shot changes that disrupt identity tracking and temporal coherence. Existing shot-change methods are typically single-person; this work targets multi-person scenarios to reflect real-world footage.
AI.method: Leverages a state-of-the-art 3D scene prior to reconstruct the two boundary frames in a single shared 3D space. Each human mesh is then registered within this shared space to maintain per-person identity and coherent motion across shot changes, enabling multi-person tracking beyond single-shot changes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show significant improvements in 3D human mesh recovery, camera pose estimation, and identity tracking, with improved identity preservation across shot changes compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables high-fidelity motion reconstruction with consistent identity preservation across shots in multi-person scenarios, addressing a key limitation of prior work in shot-change handling.

title: Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Product Improvement: A Case Study of Manga Sales in Japan
summary: Counterfactual explanation (CE) is widely used to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models and support data-driven decision-making based on model predictions. However, existing CE methods typically require two exogenously specified inputs: a desired output value (target) and a distance function that quantifies changes in explanatory variables. In regression settings, neither the validity of target specification nor the practical interpretation of the distance metric has been sufficiently addressed.
