Furthermore, most existing CE methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, even though real-world decision-making often requires explicit objective maximization. To address these limitations, we formulate CE as a profit maximization problem in management and marketing contexts and propose a framework termed profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE). PBCE eliminates the need for exogenous target specification by directly maximizing profit as the primary optimization objective. Concurrently, the distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing a clear and economically grounded interpretation.

AI.tldr: Introduces profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE) that maximizes profit directly and reinterprets distance as modification cost, removing need for target specification in regression CE.
AI.motivation: Addresses shortcomings of existing CE methods: reliance on exogenous targets and distance metrics; ambiguous interpretation in regression; disconnection from actual decision objectives.
AI.method: Formulates CE as a profit-maximization optimization; PBCE framework; target is profit; distance becomes cost of changing attributes; no external target required.
AI.result: Conceptual framework with interpretable, profit-aligned counterfactuals; demonstrates feasibility for management/marketing decisions; improves interpretability and decision quality by aligning CE with objective.
AI.conclusion: PBCE provides an economically grounded, target-free CE approach that integrates decision objectives into explanations; applicable to real-world decision making.

title: Guided Action Flow: Q-Guided Inference for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Flow-matching vision-language-action policies generate robot action chunks through an iterative transport process, creating an opportunity for test-time guidance without retraining the base policy. We study this opportunity in Guided Action Flow, an inference-time framework that keeps a pretrained SmolVLA policy frozen and uses a learned action-chunk critic to guide its reverse-time flow sampler. The critic is trained from real success and failure rollouts, can condition on task-description features from the frozen SmolVLA language pathway, and is used only through action gradients during sampling. We evaluate the approach on LIBERO manipulation tasks. A single-task critic improves success from 68.0% to 82.0% on one seed window and from 82.0% to 86.0% on another. A multi-family task-description critic improves validation success from 46.0% to 56.0%, while the locked held-out test gain is positive but modest, from 65.0% to 67.5%. These results support the feasibility of Q-guided inference for frozen flow-matching VLA policies, while showing that critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance remain the central bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: Inference-time Q-guided action-flow on frozen SmolVLA improves success without retraining; results show feasibility but generalization/uncertainty remain bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Enable test-time guidance for flow-matching VLA policies without retraining, leveraging a learned action-chunk critic trained on real outcomes and task descriptions.
AI.method: Freeze pretrained SmolVLA; train an action-chunk critic using real success/failure rollouts; apply critic gradients to guide reverse-time flow sampling; conditioning on language-path task descriptions; evaluate on LIBERO tasks; compare single-task vs multi-family critics.
AI.result: Single-task critic: 68.0%→82.0% and 82.0%→86.0% on two seeds. Multi-family critic: validation 46.0%→56.0%; held-out test gain: 65.0%→67.5% (positive but modest). Overall demonstrates feasibility of Q-guided inference; critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance are the central bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time critic-guided guidance can boost frozen flow-matching VLA policies; improvements needed in generalization and uncertainty handling; future work could explore uncertainty-aware sampling and richer task descriptions.

title: Don't Let Gains FADE: Breaking Down Policy Gradient Weights in RL
summary: Reinforcement learning post-training dramatically improves LLM reasoning, but suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. Advantage functions offer an appealing fix: they reshape the training objective, reweight which rollouts drive learning, and are trivial to implement. Yet a proliferation of methods makes it unclear which advantage to use and when. We cut through the confusion with a unifying framework that decomposes any advantage into its positive and negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes. On the sign axis, imbalanced updates collapse either entropy or weight geometry. On the difficulty axis, hard-problem focus sharpens signal but costs sample size. Both trade-offs shift during training: exploration favors balance and hard focus; exploitation favors suppression and medium focus. This motivates FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), a self-adapting advantage that reads training dynamics to schedule the gradient weight automatically. FADE reaches peak pass@1 20k steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2k steps earlier at the 32B , while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.

AI.tldr: A dynamic, self-adapting advantage (FADE) improves RL post-training for LLMs by decomposing advantages into positive/negative gradient mass along two axes, balancing exploration/exploitation and entropy/weight geometry, yielding faster peak performance and better accuracy-diversity trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Address training instability and diversity collapse in RL post-training for LLMs, and clarify which advantage to use.
AI.method: Decompose any advantage into positive/negative gradient mass along sign and difficulty axes; analyze trade-offs (balance vs hard focus; suppression vs medium focus) and their evolution during training; introduce FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy) that automatically schedules gradient weight based on training dynamics.
AI.result: FADE achieves earlier peak performance (pass@1 20k steps sooner on 7B, 2k steps sooner on 32B) and attains best accuracy-diversity trade-off across pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME compared to static baselines.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, self-adapting gradient weighting improves stability, efficiency, and diversity in RL post-training for LLMs; FADE outperforms static baselines across scales and metrics.

title: Online Segment 3D Gaussians via Launching Virtual Drones
summary:
Interactive segmentation of 3D Gaussians offers a compelling opportunity for real-time manipulation of 3D scenes, thanks to the real-time rendering capability of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). However, existing methods require a time-consuming per-scene setup - typically tens of seconds or even minutes - before interactive segmentation can begin on a raw 3DGS scene. This setup involves multi-view mask preparation, mask lifting, and feature distillation, creating a major bottleneck for online applications.
  To address this limitation, we aim to completely eliminate the setup stage for interactive 3DGS segmentation while keeping the segmentation time practical (under 1 second). In this work, we present SAGO (Segment Any Gaussians Online), a novel setup-free framework for interactive 3DGS segmentation. By introducing virtual drones, our method reframes the 3D segmentation problem as an online Next-Best-View (NBV) planning task formulated within a Markov process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAGO can extract clean 3D assets directly from 3D Gaussians with sub-second latency, thereby enabling a broad range of downstream applications such as object manipulation and scene editing. Moreover, our method achieves over a 50x speedup compared to the previous setup-free 3DGS segmentation frameworks.

AI.tldr: SAGO eliminates the setup stage for interactive segmentation of 3D Gaussian Splatting by reframing the task as an online Next-Best-View planning problem with virtual drones, achieving sub-second latency and over 50x speedup vs prior setup-free methods.
AI.motivation: Current interactive 3DGS segmentation relies on lengthy per-scene preprocessing (mask preparation, mask lifting, feature distillation), hindering real-time, online use; a setup-free solution is highly desirable for interactive editing and real-time manipulation.
AI.method: Introduce virtual drones and model the 3D segmentation problem as an online Next-Best-View planning task within a Markov decision process, enabling setup-free, real-time segmentation directly from existing 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes.
AI.result: Empirical evidence shows sub-second segmentation latency and the ability to extract clean 3D assets directly from 3D Gaussians; the approach delivers >50x speedup over previous setup-free 3DGS segmentation frameworks.
AI.conclusion: SAGO provides a practical, setup-free segmentation framework for 3DGS, enabling immediate interactive editing and downstream applications such as object manipulation and scene editing; it significantly accelerates the workflow and broadens applicability.

title: Scaling with Confidence: Calibrating Confidence of LLMs for Adaptive Test Time Scaling
summary: Training large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced their performance on reasoning and question-answering tasks. However, prevailing RL reward designs typically prioritize response correctness, neglecting to incentivize models to express their confidence accurately. This leads to a critical problem: performance gains are often accompanied by poor calibration between confidence and accuracy, misleading models to overconfidently hallucinate when uncertain. To address this limitation, we propose $\textbf{C}$orrectness and $\textbf{C}$onfidence $\textbf{C}$alibration $\textbf{R}$einforcement $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textbf{C3RL}$), a novel RL algorithm integrating correctness, calibration and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards together. Comprehensive evaluation across 8 text and multimodal datasets demonstrates that C3RL enhances calibration without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method in both performance and calibration metrics. Utilizing the well-calibrated verbalized confidence from C3RL, we further introduce $\textbf{C}$onfidence-based $\textbf{A}$daptive Test Time $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{CAS}$), an adjustable inference-time strategy that allocates computational resources based on response confidence. Experiments show that CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing the inference budget by up to 12.33 times. We believe the synergy of C3RL and CAS paves the way for deploying more reliable and resource-efficient LLMs. The code, data and models will be released.

AI.tldr: Introduces C3RL RL objective with correctness, confidence calibration, and reference accuracy rewards plus CAS adaptive inference; improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy; CAS reduces compute; code/data/models will be released.
AI.motivation: RL reward designs typically optimize for response correctness but ignore calibration, leading to overconfident, miscalibrated outputs and hallucinations; need calibration-aware RL and cost-aware inference for reliable LLMs.
AI.method: C3RL integrates three rewards: correctness (alignment with ground-truth-ish reference), calibration (penalize miscalibrated confidence outputs), and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards; trains LLMs with RL to jointly optimize these objectives. Additionally, Confidence-based Adaptive Test Time Scaling (CAS) uses the model's verbalized confidence to allocate computation dynamically at inference, enabling adjustable compute.
AI.result: Evaluations on 8 text and multimodal datasets show improved calibration without sacrificing accuracy; outperforms current state-of-the-art on both performance and calibration metrics. CAS further surpasses majority voting on in-domain and out-of-domain data and reduces inference budget by up to 12.33x. The approach claims synergy between C3RL and CAS for reliable, resource-efficient LLMs.
AI.conclusion: C3RL and CAS enable more reliable, resource-efficient LLM deployment; code, data, and models will be released.

title: Choreographing the Way of Water: A Computational Framework for Aquatic Robotic Art
summary: Robotic choreography in open water is governed by nonlinear fluid dynamics, which impose significant challenges due to environmental disturbances and nonlinear system dynamics. This paper presents the cyber-physical architecture of Way of Water, a vertically integrated framework that orchestrates a fleet of autonomous surface vessels as a distributed choreographic platform. Moving beyond the surface-pixel paradigm, these vessels use laminar nozzles and multi-zone lighting to extend their expressive range from the 2D water plane into the 3D volumetric domain. Our primary contribution is the Way of Water Studio, a browser-based, timeline-compositing authoring paradigm that treats the fleet as a DAW-like instrument for music-responsive choreography. The Studio encapsulates Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation and Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection presented through a visual timeline, broadening access to high-performance aquatic robotics for non-programmer artists. Grounding the Studio is the full cyber-physical stack: a custom holonomic chassis, a state-estimation and control stack tuned for the aquatic domain, and an LTE/MQTT fleet link with RTK-GPS time synchronization. We report on the system's validation across two distinct deployments: an 18-vessel Swan Lake interpretation at Lake Zurich and an 8-vessel Time Space Existence 2025 Venice Biennale demonstration at Forte Marghera, establishing a foundational reference for the design and deployment of fluidic robotic swarms.

AI.tldr: A browser-based, DAW-like studio orchestrates a fleet of autonomous surface vessels for expressive 3D water choreography, using Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation and Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection, validated on two large-scale deployments.
AI.motivation: Open-water robotic choreography is hindered by nonlinear fluid dynamics and disturbances. There is a need for accessible, high-performance tools to choreograph heterogeneous aquatic swarms and extend expression from 2D water planes into 3D volumetric space, enabling non-programmer artists to work with large fleets.
AI.method: Way of Water Studio is a browser-based, timeline-compositing authoring paradigm that treats the fleet as a DAW-like instrument. It leverages Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation and Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection, within a full cyber-physical stack (custom holonomic chassis, state estimation/control tuned for aquatic domains, LTE/MQTT fleet linking with RTK-GPS time synchronization). The system also uses laminar nozzles and multi-zone lighting to extend expressivity into 3D space.
AI.result: Validation across two deployments: an 18-vessel Swan Lake interpretation at Lake Zurich and an 8-vessel Time Space Existence 2025 Venice Biennale demonstration at Forte Marghera, establishing a foundational reference for design and deployment of fluidic robotic swarms.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a scalable, accessible platform that broadens access to high-performance aquatic robotics for artists, providing a practical workflow and reference architecture for planning, designing, and deploying expressive robotic swarms in open-water environments.

title: Unveiling the Non-Monotonic Effect of Privacy on Generalization under Byzantine Robustness
summary: Recent work has established a fundamental trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. We show that this trilemma does not universally extend to generalization error, but instead depends critically on the privacy regime. Specifically, in the high-noise regime (strong privacy), we prove that increasing privacy reduces the generalization error, i.e., there is no tension between robustness and privacy. In the low-noise regime (weaker privacy), however, the tension between robustness and privacy reappears and increasing privacy indeed degrades generalization. Our theory explains this surprising non-monotonic behavior of the generalization error via matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. We corroborate and further analyze these theoretical findings with empirical evaluations.

AI.tldr: Generalization in Byzantine-robust distributed learning with local DP is regime-dependent: strong privacy can improve generalization, while weak privacy can harm it; a non-monotonic, regime-based trade-off is demonstrated via matching stability bounds and empirical validation.
AI.motivation: Address the extension of the robustness/privacy/trade-off literature from optimization error to generalization error, and show that the previously claimed universal trilemma does not hold uniformly across privacy regimes.
AI.method: Derive matching lower and upper bounds on algorithmic stability for Byzantine-robust distributed learning under local DP. The analysis distinguishes high-noise (strong privacy) and low-noise (weak privacy) regimes and supports results with empirical experiments.
AI.result: High-noise regime: increasing privacy reduces generalization error (no robustness-privacy tension). Low-noise regime: increasing privacy degrades generalization (tension reappears). The bounds explain non-monotonic behavior and align with empirical findings.
AI.conclusion: Generalization error under robustness and LDP exhibits a regime-dependent, non-monotonic trade-off; practitioners should consider privacy strength relative to the noise regime, and the stability bounds provide a theoretical explanation for observed behavior.

title: DRDN: Decoupled Representation Dynamic Network for From-Scratch ViT Class-Incremental Learning
comment: 10 pages, IEEEtran journal format. Preprint submitted to IEEE Transactions on Multimedia
summary:
Dynamic expansion methods for class-incremental learning (CIL) protect task-specific knowledge by growing dedicated tokens or subnetworks, yet our analyses suggest that classification supervision alone does not sufficiently preserve task-agnostic shared backbone representations over long incremental sequences. We identify two intertwined challenges: cross-task confusion from sequential training on predominantly current-task data, which biases decision boundaries toward recent tasks; and under-optimized shared representations in the backbone that cap long-term discriminability as tasks accumulate.
  We propose the Decoupled Representation Dynamic Network (DRDN), which addresses these challenges via two orthogonal mechanisms. For shared backbone representations, DRDN continuously applies masked image modeling (MIM) at every incremental step, with reconstruction gradients routed exclusively through the backbone, encouraging it to retain general visual structure beyond class-discriminative cues. For task-specific discrimination, DRDN employs hierarchical task token expansion across all transformer layers, with a modified per-task attention rule that reduces inter-task interference. We support this design with accuracy degradation analysis and cross-task confusion rate measurements.
  In the from-scratch ViT CIL setting (no external pretraining), DRDN consistently improves over strong token-expansion baselines with comparable backbone scale. On CIFAR100-B0 (10 steps), DRDN achieves 77.19% average accuracy, outperforming DKT by 1.36 points and DyTox by 3.53 points, with an advantage that grows at longer incremental sequences. Multi-seed validation confirms stability (+/-0.31%). The MIM decoder is active only during training, adding no inference-time parameters or computation.

AI.tldr: DRDN decouples backbone representation maintenance from task-specific discrimination in class-incremental learning via (i) masked image modeling (MIM) with gradients routed through the backbone, and (ii) hierarchical task token expansion with per-task attention to reduce interference, yielding improved long-sequence accuracy without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Classification supervision alone struggles to preserve task-agnostic backbone representations over long incremental sequences, leading to cross-task confusion and under-optimized shared representations as tasks accumulate.
AI.method: Two orthogonal mechanisms: (1) continuous masked image modeling (MIM) at every incremental step with reconstruction gradients routed exclusively through the backbone to retain general visual structure; (2) hierarchical task token expansion across all transformer layers with a modified per-task attention rule to reduce inter-task interference, supported by accuracy degradation and cross-task confusion analyses.
AI.result: In the from-scratch ViT CIL setting, DRDN consistently outperforms strong token-expansion baselines with similar backbone scale. On CIFAR100-B0 (10 steps), DRDN achieves 77.19% average accuracy, beating DKT by 1.36 and DyTox by 3.53. Multi-seed validation shows stability within ±0.31. The MIM decoder is active only during training, contributing no inference-time cost.
AI.conclusion: DRDN effectively addresses both cross-task confusion and stagnating shared representations, delivering improved long-term discriminability in CIL without additional inference-time computation.

title: Spatial Support Matters: Geometry-Aware Graph Fusion for Rainfall Field Reconstruction
summary: Fine-scale rainfall reconstruction is critical for urban flood modeling, but real rainfall sensing systems observe the field through incompatible spatial supports: gauges measure points, microwave links measure paths, and radar/satellite products measure gridded areas. These differences in measurement support impose geometrically distinct constraints on the rainfall field, yet existing heterogeneous graph approaches reconcile such sources in feature space, giving each its own embedding while discarding the geometry of its support. We propose a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network that represents each observation according to its support type (0D point, 1D line, or 2D grid) as a distinct node layer, and fuses them through cross-support message passing into a point-support prediction layer from which the field is reconstructed. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, allowing the same trained model to reconstruct the field at user-defined target locations or display grids. On Singapore data, the proposed method reduces RMSE by 23.2\% over the classical interpolation baseline, inverse-distance weighting, and consistently outperforms other neural architectures such as convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study using data from Sydney, Australia lets us characterize when multi-support fusion helps: the available skill appears to depend on gauge spacing relative to the spatial correlation length of the field, so fusion delivers the largest gains where the field is under-sampled relative to its correlation length and little when it is already resolved. Code and models will be open-sourced upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware, multi-support heterogenous GNN fuses 0D point gauges, 1D lines, and 2D grids for fine-scale rainfall reconstruction, enabling inductive, resolution-flexible field estimation and showing substantial RMSE gains on Singapore data (≈23% over baselines) with insights on when fusion helps (gauge spacing vs spatial correlation).
AI.motivation: Different rainfall sensing modalities observe the field at incompatible supports (points, lines, grids), causing geometric constraints that are not captured by feature-space fusion. There is a need to preserve and exploit observation geometry to improve fine-scale rainfall reconstruction.
AI.method: Introduce a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network. Represent each observation as a distinct node layer corresponding to its support type (0D/1D/2D). Use cross-support message passing to fuse information into a point-support prediction layer, from which the field is reconstructed. Employ an inductive masked-node formulation to decouple prediction resolution from sensing resolution, enabling reconstruction at user-defined target locations/grids. Train/evaluate on Singapore data; generalize with Sydney data.
AI.result: The method reduces RMSE by 23.2% compared to classical baselines (interpolation, inverse-distance weighting) and outperforms other neural architectures like convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study indicates fusion gain depends on gauge spacing relative to the field's spatial correlation length; largest gains occur when the field is under-sampled. Code and models will be open-sourced upon acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware multi-support fusion effectively leverages the observation geometry to improve fine-scale rainfall reconstruction, offering resolution-flexible, cross-support integration with practical inductive capabilities and clear gains in under-sampled regimes.

title: Bridge-WA: Predicting Where and How the World Changes for Robotic Action
summary: General-purpose vision-language-action models benefit from large vision-language priors, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating action-relevant scene changes. Existing world-action models often rely on large generative world models or dense future rollouts, which are expensive and spend capacity on visual details weakly coupled to control. We present Bridge-WA, a lightweight world-action framework that distills a frozen future-change teacher into three compact priors: future tokens for intended outcomes, change maps for intervention support, and motion-flow maps for local transition direction. A WorldBridge conditions the action transformer on these priors through multi-source attention memories and spatial-temporal biases, while the teacher model is removed at inference. Across VLABench, RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-Plus and real-robot evaluations, Bridge-WA improves task success, progress, and robustness, with particularly clear gains under out-of-distribution visual shifts. By focusing action generation on where and how the scene will change, Bridge-WA suppresses nuisance appearance factors such as background, lighting, and distractors, leading to better generalization without deployment-time dense future-image generation. Code and visualizations are available at: https://hcplab-sysu.github.io/BRIDGE-WA .

AI.tldr: Bridge-WA introduces a lightweight world-action framework that distills a frozen future-change teacher into three compact priors—future tokens for outcomes, change maps for intervention cues, and motion-flow maps for local transitions. A WorldBridge conditions the action transformer with these priors via multi-source attention memories and spatio-temporal biases; the teacher is discarded at inference. This yields robust, generalizable action planning without dense future-image generation, improving performance across multiple benchmarks and real-robot tests.
AI.motivation: To enable robust and generalizable vision-language-action control by explicitly modeling action-relevant scene changes while avoiding expensive dense future-image generation and nuisance appearance factors (background, lighting, distractors).
AI.method: Distill a frozen future-change teacher into three compact priors (future tokens, change maps, motion-flow maps). Use WorldBridge to condition the action transformer on these priors through multi-source attention memories and spatial-temporal biases. Remove the teacher model at inference. Evaluate on VLABench, RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-Plus, and real-robot setups.
AI.result: Bridge-WA yields higher task success, progress, and robustness across diverse datasets, with pronounced gains under out-of-distribution visual shifts. By focusing generation on where/how the scene will change, it suppresses nuisance appearance factors and avoids deployment-time dense future-image generation, enhancing generalization. Code and visualizations are released.
AI.conclusion: Bridge-WA offers an efficient, robust approach to vision-language-action modeling by leveraging compact priors that capture future outcomes, interventions, and local transitions, enabling better generalization and deployment efficiency.

title: Towards Learning Representations of Policies in Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
summary:
We investigate the problem of learning useful policy representations (embeddings) in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. We make three contributions: First, we introduce methods of creating datasets of policies for a given game. Second, we propose methods to learn policy representations. Third, we introduce downstream tasks to evaluate the effectiveness of such representations.
  We evaluate each dataset method, embedding method, and downstream task on Kuhn and Leduc Poker. Although our methods are very basic, we demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning policy representations in games. Our code is available at https://github.com/VitamintK/ssl-project for others to extend.

AI.tldr: Proposes a self-supervised learning framework to learn policy embeddings in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games, with three components (dataset construction, representation learning, downstream evaluation); evaluated on Kuhn and Leduc Poker; shows embeddings capture behavioral signals; among first SSL comparisons in game policy representations; code released.
AI.motivation: Policy representations can enable transfer, generalization, and efficient evaluation in imperfect-information games. Self-supervised learning leverages unlabelled policy data to learn compact, informative embeddings without requiring extensive labeling or handcrafted features.
AI.method: Three-part framework: (1) propose concrete methods to generate datasets of policies for a given game; (2) develop self-supervised learning approaches to produce policy representations from these datasets; (3) define downstream tasks to evaluate the usefulness of the representations. Empirical evaluation on Kuhn and Leduc Poker.
AI.result: Learned embeddings exhibit meaningful behavioral structure across the tested datasets and embedding methods. Demonstrates, for the first time in this context, a systematic comparison of self-supervised techniques for learning policy representations in games. Code is made available for further extension.
AI.conclusion: SSL-based policy representations are feasible in small imperfect-information games and provide a foundation for more advanced methods and broader domains. The study uses fairly basic methods, leaving room for stronger SSL objectives and larger-scale evaluations.

title: Bridging 3D Gaussians and Semantic Occupancy for Comprehensive Open-Vocabulary Scene Understanding from Unposed Images
comment: Hu Zhu, Bohan Li, and Xianda Guo contributed equally. Corresponding author: Wenjun Zeng
summary: Comprehensive 3D scene understanding from sparse, unposed images requires a model to recover renderable geometry, open-vocabulary semantics, and free/occupied 3D space without relying on external camera calibration. Recent feed-forward Gaussian methods improve pose-free reconstruction and semantic rendering, but their Gaussian primitives are mainly optimized through image-space objectives and remain weakly constrained in unobserved regions. We propose \textit{COVScene}, a pose-free semantic Gaussian framework that couples renderable Gaussian primitives with a dense semantic occupancy field through differentiable volumetric lifting. Instead of converting Gaussians to voxels only at evaluation time, COVScene lifts the predicted semantic Gaussians inside the training computation graph, so volumetric regularization provides gradients to Gaussian opacity, geometry, and semantic features. The framework combines a semantic-aware Geometry Transformer, multi-task Gaussian decoding, geometric foundation distillation, and occupancy entropy regularization to support novel view synthesis, open-vocabulary semantic querying, and semantic occupancy prediction within a single representation. Experiments on ScanNet and ScanNet++ show that COVScene maintains competitive rendering quality, improves open-vocabulary segmentation, and achieves stronger semantic occupancy prediction than the self-supervised baseline without direct voxel-level supervision.

AI.tldr: COVScene is a pose-free semantic Gaussian framework that jointly learns renderable Gaussian primitives and a dense semantic occupancy field via differentiable volumetric lifting, enabling open-vocabulary semantic querying and semantic occupancy prediction without voxel supervision.
AI.motivation: To achieve comprehensive 3D scene understanding from sparse, unposed images without camera calibration, addressing limitations of prior Gaussian approaches that rely on image-space objectives and poorly constrain unobserved regions.
AI.method: Introduce differentiable volumetric lifting that integrates semantic Gaussians into the training graph, coupling renderable Gaussians with a dense semantic occupancy field. The method combines a semantic-aware Geometry Transformer, multi-task Gaussian decoding, geometric foundation distillation, and occupancy entropy regularization to support novel view synthesis, open-vocabulary semantics, and semantic occupancy within a single representation.
AI.result: On ScanNet and ScanNet++, COVScene maintains competitive render quality, improves open-vocabulary segmentation, and achieves stronger semantic occupancy prediction than a self-supervised baseline without voxel-level supervision.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified, pose-free representation for rendering, open-vocabulary semantics, and semantic occupancy, enabling robust 3D understanding from sparse, unposed imagery.

title: Autonomous discovery of traffic laws with AI traffic scientists
summary: Universal traffic laws describe recurrent patterns in congestion, mobility and driving behavior across cities, providing a scientific basis for transportation planning, management and control. Their discovery, however, remains expert-driven, requiring candidate regularities to be identified from heterogeneous observational evidence or validated through intervention experiments. Although autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems have advanced scientific discovery in controlled laboratory settings, extending them to complex transportation domains remains a challenge. Here we present TrafficSci, an agentic AI system that formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow integrating evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. Across four case studies spanning population, network, control and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets. TrafficSci provides a route for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled domains to complex urban systems.

AI.tldr: TrafficSci autonomously discovers traffic laws via an iterative, auditable AI workflow, revalidating known laws and revealing a new intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving across multiple scales and cities.
AI.motivation: Addresses the need for automated, auditable discovery of universal traffic laws beyond expert-driven identification, enabling scalable AI-driven discovery in complex urban transport systems.
AI.method: An agentic AI system (TrafficSci) implements an iterative workflow: evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation, spanning population, network, control, and trajectory scales to discover universal traffic laws.
AI.result: TrafficSci autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, with statistical consistency across eight cities and two trajectory datasets.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the feasibility of AI-driven, auditable scientific discovery in complex urban systems and provides a framework potentially extensible to other domains.

title: Actuator Reality Shaping for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robot Learning
summary: Sim-to-real transfer in robot learning is often limited by discrepancies between the ideal actuator dynamics assumed during policy training and the nonlinear, hardware-dependent behavior of physical motors. While conventional approaches attempt to bridge this gap by increasing simulator fidelity through system identification, domain randomization, or learned actuator models, we introduce an alternative paradigm: actuator reality shaping. Instead of modifying the simulator to match the real world, our method shapes the closed-loop behavior of physical actuators to match the idealized second-order reference dynamics used in simulation. By equipping each joint with a two-degree-of-freedom feedforward--feedback controller, we decouple reference-response shaping from robust stabilization, thereby providing a standardized actuator interface for reinforcement learning policies. As a result, policies trained only with the prescribed reference model can be deployed zero-shot on real hardware without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models. We validate the approach on a single-joint high-gear-ratio servo under external loads and a 7-DOF robotic arm reaching task, where actuator reality shaping substantially reduces sim-to-real tracking error and improves zero-shot task performance compared with standard servo-control and representative real-to-sim-to-real baselines. We further demonstrate zero-shot transfer on a wheeled-legged robot driving over a slope and a humanoid robot walking, suggesting that actuator reality shaping can serve as a reusable interface for robot learning across diverse hardware platforms.

AI.tldr: Actuator reality shaping enforces an ideal second-order reference on hardware via 2-DOF controllers, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real RL transfer without actuator models.
AI.motivation: Bridging sim-to-real gaps caused by nonlinear, hardware-specific actuator dynamics by shaping hardware response rather than increasing simulator fidelity.
AI.method: Attach a two-degree-of-freedom feedforward–feedback controller to each joint to shape the closed-loop dynamics toward a prescribed second-order reference, decoupling reference shaping from stabilization and creating a standardized actuator interface for RL policies. Policies trained against the reference model transfer zero-shot to real hardware without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models.
AI.result: Actuator reality shaping substantially reduces sim-to-real tracking error and improves zero-shot task performance compared with standard servo-control and representative real-to-sim-to-real baselines, demonstrated on a single-joint servo with loads, a 7-DOF arm, a wheeled-legged robot, and a humanoid.
AI.conclusion: Actuator reality shaping provides a reusable interface for robot learning across diverse hardware platforms, enabling zero-shot transfer and reducing reliance on accurate actuator models or high-fidelity simulators.

title: The risk of KV cache compression
summary: Transformer inference on long sequences is expensive because softmax attention repeatedly reads from a large KV cache. The prevalent approach to this bottleneck is KV cache compression, which replaces the full cache with a compact summary. Despite its practical importance, the design of such summaries is largely driven by empirical experimentation. On the theoretical side, existing results show that KV cache compression can be impossible in the worst case, but offer little systematic guidance for designing algorithms in regimes where accurate compression is possible. We bridge this gap by characterizing the minimax risk of KV cache compression in terms of the intrinsic compressibility of a cache, revealing when and how accurate compression is possible. These results yield novel design principles for KV cache compression under causal masking that map efficiently to prefill and autoregressive decoding while achieving minimax-optimal risk. We instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm and report promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments. Overall, our results provide a principled avenue for practical KV cache compression with theoretical guarantees.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the minimax risk of KV cache compression for transformer inference on long sequences, derives principled design guidelines under causal masking based on intrinsic compressibility, and presents a practical algorithm with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation on LongBench.
AI.motivation: Transformer attention on long sequences incurs high cost due to re-reading a large KV cache. KV cache compression is used but lacks theory-guided design; there is evidence of impossibility in the worst case, so a systematic framework is needed for regimes where compression is feasible.
AI.method: Characterize the minimax risk of KV cache compression in terms of the cache's intrinsic compressibility; develop design principles that map to prefill and autoregressive decoding under causal masking; instantiate these principles into a practical algorithm and analyze its theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: Shows that accurate KV cache compression is possible in regimes with high intrinsic compressibility, achieving minimax-optimal risk; provides design principles that translate into efficient prefill and decoding strategies; and reports promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments.
AI.conclusion: Offers a principled framework for KV cache compression with theoretical guarantees, and delivers a practical algorithm that balances compression accuracy with decoding efficiency for long-sequence transformer inference.

title: Multi-Resolution Flow Matching: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Staged Sampling
comment: The code is available at https://github.com/Xingyu-Zheng/MrFlow
summary: Hardware-agnostic strategies for accelerating text-to-image diffusion, such as timestep distillation and feature caching, can reduce inference time without custom kernels or system-level optimization. Among them, multi-resolution generation strategies have recently received broad attention, attaining more than 5x speedup without any training. However, the design of performing upsampling in the latent space, together with the selective modification of partial regions, causes these methods to exhibit noticeable blurring or artifacts. To this end, we propose MrFlow, a training-free multi-resolution acceleration strategy for pretrained flow-matching models built upon a staged low-to-high-resolution pipeline. MrFlow first rapidly generates the main structure at low resolution, then performs super-resolution in the pixel space using a lightweight pretrained GAN-based model, subsequently injects low-strength noise to enable high-frequency resampling, and finally refines the details at high resolution. Quantitative and qualitative results on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image show that MrFlow exploits the quadratic token reduction and reduced step requirement of low-resolution sampling to achieve 10x end-to-end acceleration while keeping OneIG within a 1% gap relative to that before acceleration, significantly surpassing other training-free acceleration strategies, and requiring no training or runtime dynamic identification whatsoever. MrFlow can further be directly combined orthogonally with pre-trained timestep distillation strategies, achieving even higher generation acceleration of up to 25x.

AI.tldr: MrFlow is a training-free multi-resolution acceleration for pretrained flow-matching diffusion models, achieving up to 25x speedups by a staged low-to-high-res pipeline that uses low-res structure, GAN-based pixel-space super-resolution, noise injection, and high-resolution refinement; compatible with pre-trained timestep distillation, with minimal quality loss (≤1% OneIG gap).
AI.motivation: Mitigate blurring/artifacts and latency in multi-resolution diffusion acceleration that upsampling in latent space introduces, by providing a training-free, architecture-agnostic method that preserves image quality while delivering substantial speed gains.
AI.method: A staged pipeline: (1) generate main structure at low resolution to exploit reduced tokens/steps; (2) perform pixel-space super-resolution via a lightweight pretrained GAN; (3) inject low-strength noise to enable high-frequency resampling; (4) refine details at high resolution. Optional orthogonal combination with pretrained timestep distillation.
AI.result: On FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image, MrFlow yields ~10x end-to-end acceleration with OneIG within 1% of the unaccelerated baseline. It outperforms other training-free strategies and requires no training or runtime dynamic identification. When combined orthogonally with timestep distillation, acceleration increases to up to ~25x.
AI.conclusion: MrFlow provides a practical, training-free acceleration framework for pretrained flow-matching diffusion models, achieving substantial speedups with controlled quality loss by leveraging low-to-high-resolution generation, GAN-based pixel-space super-resolution, and strategic noise for high-frequency sampling; it complements existing acceleration methods.

title: Diverse Evidence, Better Forecasts: Multi-Agent Deliberation Under Information Asymmetry
summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used for forecasting future events, as deliberation among multiple LLMs is believed to improve reasoning and calibration. Yet existing approaches overlook a critical design choice: what information each agent receives. When all agents are given identical evidence, deliberation collapses into herding rather than genuine belief revision, leaving multi-agent systems little better than a single agent. We identify this as a fundamental gap and propose designed information asymmetry to close it: by partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets, each agent holds exclusive knowledge that can only reach others through deliberation. We theoretically show that this decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation, and instantiate it in InfoDelphi, a framework combining relevance-aware evidence routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. On PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions derived from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12--18% in Brier score and 4--8 percentage points in accuracy. More detailed experiments confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing diversity of input as the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning.

AI.tldr: We propose InfoDelphi, a multi-agent reasoning framework that injects designed information asymmetry by partitioning evidence into shared and private subsets to reduce inter-agent error correlation, achieving significant gains on PolyGym (12–18% in Brier score, 4–8 PP in accuracy).
AI.motivation: In standard multi-agent LLM deliberation, giving agents identical evidence leads to herding and limited belief revision; there is a gap to enable genuine, diverse reasoning among agents.
AI.method: Partition evidence into public/shared and disjoint private subsets; implement relevance-aware routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation; provide theoretical justification that this reduces inter-agent error correlation; instantiate as InfoDelphi.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on PolyGym (375 binary forecasting items) shows InfoDelphi outperforms strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12–18% in Brier score and 4–8 percentage points in accuracy; removing information asymmetry eliminates most gains; diversity of input is key.
AI.conclusion: Designed information asymmetry closes the gap in multi-agent reasoning, with input diversity enabling more accurate forecasts; InfoDelphi provides a practical framework and guideline for future multi-agent systems.

title: CoFL-S: Spatially Queryable Sector Flow Fields for Local Language-Conditioned Navigation
summary: Vision-Language Navigation has increasingly emphasized high-level instruction reasoning, memory, global map construction, and instruction decomposition, while the low-level action representation remains comparatively underexplored. We propose CoFL-S, a low-level vision-language-action framework that predicts a language-conditioned flow field over the robot's local visible sector and generates continuous trajectories by rolling out the predicted field. To train this low-level representation, we convert each VLN-CE episode, originally a whole-episode instruction paired with an action sequence, into frame-level local supervision with aligned sub-instructions and matched action, trajectory, and dense flow-field targets. For evaluation, we introduce a continuous-time Habitat benchmark that isolates low-level action interfaces from instruction decomposition and executes all methods through a shared velocity-command controller, enabling decomposition-independent closed-loop comparison across different planner frequencies rather than fixed discrete forward-and-turn transitions in VLN-CE. Under matched encoders and training settings, CoFL-S consistently outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark, and zero-shot real-world closed-loop deployment further shows its advantage over both baselines beyond simulation.

AI.tldr: CoFL-S introduces a low-level, language-conditioned flow-field representation for continuous-time vision-language navigation (VLN-CE), transforming episode-level supervision into frame-level local targets and evaluating via a continuous-time Habitat benchmark. It outperforms action-token/chunk baselines and shows zero-shot real-world gains.
AI.motivation: The field has focused on high-level reasoning, memory, and map construction in VLN, while low-level action representations remain underexplored. A robust, continuous, low-level policy is needed to enable smooth real-time control and fair cross-planner comparisons.
AI.method: CoFL-S predicts a language-conditioned flow field over the robot’s local visible sector and rolls out continuous trajectories by following this field. Training converts each VLN-CE episode into frame-level supervision with aligned sub-instructions and matched actions, trajectories, and dense flow-field targets, enabling dense, frame-level learning.
AI.result: Under matched encoders/training, CoFL-S outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark. Zero-shot real-world deployment also surpasses baselines.
AI.conclusion: A low-level flow-field representation improves continuous-time VLN-CE control, enabling frequency-independent evaluation and better real-world transfer, suggesting stronger generalization and smoother control than existing action-based baselines.

title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

AI.tldr: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM) with Least-Recently-Updated (MHM-LRU) improves retention and end-to-end accuracy in long-context LLMs by partitioning memory into independent heads with a stage-wise select-then-update rule; achieves substantial gains across long token ranges and model families.
AI.motivation: End-to-end performance of recurrent memory agents degrades as context length grows due to a memory retention bottleneck. Treating memory as a monolithic text block makes updates risky and content overwriting likely, hindering retention.
AI.method: Introduce MHM: partition memory into multiple independent heads; a stage-wise select-then-update strategy updates exactly one head per step while other heads are shielded from overwriting. MHM-LRU instantiation enforces uniform head utilization with zero token overhead, as a lightweight training-free design.
AI.result: Experiments on long-context benchmarks show substantial gains in both retention and end-to-end accuracy across 100K–1M token contexts. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, memory retention rises from <30% to 73.96%. Gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimization of memory (MHM/MHM-LRU) is a practical and cost-efficient path to reliable long-context recurrence, addressing the retention bottleneck without additional training.

title: Boosting Ultrasound Image Classification via Attribute-Guided Dual-Branch Framework
summary: Ultrasound image classification is essential for computer-aided diagnosis. However, current methods often neglect clinical priors, leading to poor generalization in challenging scenarios and a lack of interpretability that limits clinical adoption. To address these issues, we aim to develop a medical-prior module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines to enhance both diagnostic performance and interpretability. In this paper, we propose an attribute-guided dual-branch framework for ultrasound classification that introduces domain-agnostic medical attribute priors, improving generalization while offering interpretable evidence. Specifically, a baseline branch follows conventional architectures and predicts image categories via a fully connected classifier. An attribute-guided branch injects domain-agnostic attributes as priors and produces human-interpretable decision cues. Finally, an adaptive decision module fuses the two branches in a data-dependent manner to yield the final prediction. Experiments across diverse ultrasound classification tasks demonstrate that our approach can be integrated into multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhaobo253-crypto/AttrGuide.

AI.tldr: Proposes an attribute-guided dual-branch framework for ultrasound image classification that injects domain-agnostic medical attribute priors to boost generalization and provide interpretable decision cues, with an adaptive fusion module to combine branches; demonstrates compatibility with multiple backbones and SOTA methods, with code released.
AI.motivation: Current ultrasound classifiers neglect clinical priors, leading to limited generalization in challenging scenarios and poor interpretability, hindering clinical adoption.
AI.method: Baseline branch uses conventional architecture and classifier; attribute-guided branch injects domain-agnostic attributes as priors to generate interpretable cues; adaptive decision module fuses branches in a data-dependent way to produce final prediction; architecture compatible with different backbones; low overhead.
AI.result: Empirical results across diverse ultrasound classification tasks show improved accuracy and interpretability; method is easily integrable into existing pipelines and SOTA methods with low overhead; code available.
AI.conclusion: The attribution-guided dual-branch framework effectively leverages medical priors to improve generalization and interpretability in ultrasound classification, with broad compatibility and practical applicability; future work could explore broader priors or more rigorous interpretability evaluation.

title: Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment
summary:
In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

AI.tldr: Incremental, source-aware expert bank for multi-source ECG with a frozen backbone and margin-based fusion; achieves near offline performance in source-aware settings and remains robust without source labels.
AI.motivation: In multi-source ECG deployment, raw data retention is often impractical. There is a need to assimilate new data domains with minimal parameter interference and under conditions where source metadata may be unavailable during deployment.
AI.method: Freeze a 1024-d ECGFounder backbone; build an incremental expert bank where each new domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert. Train a lightweight router on retained training features and domain labels from observed sources; fuse the two most likely experts using a validation-calibrated margin rule rather than selecting a single routed expert.
AI.result: Source-aware expert selection achieves Macro-F1 0.7915±0.0036, closely matching an offline independent-head reference at 0.7885±0.0009. Without source IDs, an MLP router attains 0.7756±0.0027 and top-2 margin fusion yields 0.7782±0.0022; the top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small (+0.0026) with a 95% CI including zero. Across three domain orders, top-2-to-oracle gap remains 0.0111–0.0133. No raw ECGs are replayed; training features are retained for router updates, so the method is not memory-free.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates strong retention of source-specific experts and robust performance under missing source IDs, but autonomous source inference remains the principal bottleneck. The design supports practical deployment where raw data cannot be retained, though it trades memory efficiency for retained features.

title: NEUROSYMLAND: Neuro-Symbolic Landing-Site Assessment for Robust and Edge-Deployable UAV Autonomy
summary: Safe landing-site assessment in unstructured environments remains a key challenge for autonomous UAV deployment, as vision-only learning approaches often degrade under terrain variability and provide limited transparency in safety decisions. We present NEUROSYMLAND, a neuro-symbolic landing-site assessment system that integrates lightweight perception with explicit safety reasoning. The framework constructs a probabilistic semantic scene graph from onboard visual input and evaluates candidate landing regions using symbolic constraints capturing terrain flatness, obstacle clearance, and spatial consistency, enabling structured reasoning under perceptual uncertainty while maintaining edge-feasible execution. Across 72 simulated landing scenarios spanning diverse terrains, NEUROSYMLAND achieves 61 successful assessments, outperforming four competitive baselines (37-57 successes). To evaluate deployability, we further conduct 100 hardware-in-the-loop trials with randomized initial poses, profiling end-to-end latency, stage-wise execution time, and system-level metrics including CPU/GPU utilization, memory footprint, and power consumption. Results demonstrate improved robustness and interpretability with bounded edge-resource usage. Profiling shows that symbolic reasoning contributes only a small fraction of end-to-end latency, while the main computational cost arises from perception and PSSG construction. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying the landing-site assessment stack on edge-constrained UAV hardware, and all source code, datasets, prompts, and symbolic rule refinement examples are released in an open-source repository

AI.tldr: Neuro-symbolic landing-site assessment (NEUROSYMLAND) combines lightweight perception with explicit symbolic safety reasoning to evaluate landing regions under perceptual uncertainty, enabling edge-deployable and interpretable decision-making; demonstrated in simulation and hardware-in-the-loop with open-source release.
AI.motivation: Vision-only methods struggle with terrain variability, safety transparency, and edge-resource constraints in unstructured landing environments. A neuro-symbolic approach promises interpretable, robust safety reasoning under perceptual uncertainty while remaining compute-efficient for UAV edge hardware.
AI.method: Construct a probabilistic semantic scene graph (PSSG) from onboard imagery and evaluate candidate landing regions using symbolic constraints that encode terrain flatness, obstacle clearance, and spatial consistency. This enables structured reasoning under uncertainty and yields edge-feasible decisions. The system is evaluated in 72 simulated scenarios and 100 hardware-in-the-loop trials, with profiling of latency, execution time, CPU/GPU usage, memory, and power; all source materials are released as open-source.
AI.result: In 72 simulated landing scenarios spanning diverse terrains, NEUROSYMLAND achieved 61 successful assessments, outperforming four baselines (37–57 successes). In 100 hardware-in-the-loop trials with randomized poses, end-to-end latency and resource usage were measured; symbolic reasoning contributed a small fraction of latency, with perception and PSSG construction as primary cost. The results indicate improved robustness and interpretability with bounded edge resources, and demonstrate feasibility of deploying the stack on edge-constrained UAV hardware. The authors also release source code, datasets, prompts, and symbolic-rule refinements publicly.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic framework provides interpretable safety reasoning for landing-site assessment under perceptual uncertainty and is feasible on edge hardware, with perception and PSSG construction as the main computational bottlenecks. Future work could strengthen uncertainty quantification, provide more comprehensive ablations, and explore real-world deployment challenges.

title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: Two-stage learning pipeline combines wind estimation from onboard data with a reinforcement learning flight controller to mitigate turbulence effects on small multirotors; wind estimator uses attention-augmented gated RNN trained in simulated von Karman turbulence; wind-aware PPO controller significantly improves tracking and shows robustness to wind disturbances.
AI.motivation: Enable accurate wind perception and robust control for small multirotors operating in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulence degrades trajectory tracking and defeats conventional feedback control.
AI.method: Stage 1: wind estimation from onboard kinematics/dynamics using an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with shear and veer. Stage 2: a proximal policy optimization (PPO) controller that consumes the estimator's output (freezing the estimator during RL) to improve trajectory tracking. Extensive ablations separate kinematic benefits from wind-perception benefits and evaluate performance across wind regimes, including out-of-distribution winds.
AI.result: Wind estimator achieves horizontal wind RMSE 0.40 m/s and direction error 3.2 degrees on unseen regimes; generalizes to vertical ascent with skill score 0.861; PPO controller reduces horizontal tracking error by 48% vs wind-blind PD baseline across 4–12 m/s winds; evals show 100% success; ablation indicates wind perception contribution grows with wind speed; controller degrades gracefully under 13–15 m/s OOD winds where baseline fails.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a wind-perception module into a frozen estimator feeding a PPO controller substantially improves wind-robust trajectory tracking for small multirotors, with greater benefits at higher wind speeds and reasonable robustness to out-of-distribution winds; the kinematic component alone provides some benefit, while wind perception accounts for most gains in stronger winds.

title: Plug-and-Play Volumetric Reconstruction for Compressive Sensing Light-Sheet Microscopy
summary: We investigate volumetric reconstruction for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM), where fast volumetric imaging is achieved by encoding multiple axial planes into each camera exposure. To recover the underlying volume from highly multiplexed measurements, we propose a plug-and-play (PnP) framework that flexibly incorporates any user-specified denoiser into the reconstruction process. Building on a slice-based formulation, we further introduce an axial-coupled model that exploits correlations between adjacent slices to improve volumetric continuity. For efficient computation, we derive a Woodbury-based update for the data-consistency step in both the slice-based and axial-coupled formulations, and employ a Gauss-Seidel sweep for the denoising step in the axial-coupled model. Under a weakly convex regularization assumption, we establish subsequential convergence of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully recovers cellular structures from compressed measurements, and provide practical insights into the comparative performance of commonly used denoisers within the PnP framework under the CS-LSM setup.

AI.tldr: A plug-and-play (PnP) framework for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM) reconstructs 3D volumes from multiplexed measurements, using slice-based and axial-coupled models, Woodbury-based data updates, Gauss-Seidel denoising, and convergence guarantees under weakly convex regularization; validated on synthetic and zebrafish-heart data with insights on denoiser performance.
AI.motivation: Enable fast volumetric imaging in CS-LSM by enabling robust reconstruction from highly multiplexed measurements, while exploiting slice correlations for volumetric continuity and allowing flexible, user-specified denoisers within a convergent framework.
AI.method: Develop a PnP reconstruction framework for CS-LSM with two formulations: a slice-based model and an axial-coupled model that leverages inter-slice correlations. Implement a Woodbury-based update for the data-consistency step and apply a Gauss-Seidel sweep during the denoising step (axial-coupled). Provide subsequential convergence guarantees under weakly convex regularization. Validate on synthetic data and real zebrafish-heart data; compare common denoisers within the PnP framework.
AI.result: The framework successfully recovers cellular structures from compressed CS-LSM measurements and yields practical insights into how various denoisers perform within PnP-CS-LSM, highlighting trade-offs between reconstruction fidelity and continuity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach offers a flexible, efficient, and convergent reconstruction pathway for CS-LSM, with axial coupling improving volumetric continuity and a tunable denoiser integration via PnP. Future work could explore broader denoiser choices, deeper convergence analysis, and application to diverse biological specimens.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Goggles is a gradient-editing module that enforces an epistemic frame during finetuning to combat negation neglect; it achieves ~91% fictional tagging after applying to new documents and preserves capabilities, suggesting a path to training on misaligned data without absorbing it.
AI.motivation: Negation Neglect arises when finetuning on documents annotated as fictional; models continue to believe core claims; need a mechanism to decouple data annotations from learned beliefs.
AI.method: Train a Goggles module to edit the gradients (LoRA finetuning) to impart a chosen epistemic frame; one Goggles instance per base model/frame/LoRA; apply frozen to unseen documents; re-train Goggles on the same documents to encode fictional annotations; evaluate across frames (e.g., AI safety eval); test with GPQA and TruthfulQA.
AI.result: With Goggles, the model flags content as fictional about 91% of the time on previously annotated docs after training; preserves or matches baseline capabilities on GPQA and TruthfulQA; the frame can persist under some continued finetuning, though interventions may revert when pushes toward the claim occur.
AI.conclusion: Goggles demonstrates a promising path to train models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the misaligned behaviors, by gradient-level interventions that impart and retain an epistemic frame.

title: Real-Time Visual Intelligence on Low-Cost UAVs: A Modular Approach for Tracking, Scanning, and Navigation
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Project repository available at: github.com
summary: Autonomous drones are rapidly transforming modern warfare and civil applications alike. This paper presents the development of an integrated intelligent drone system designed to serve as a personal assistant. Leveraging the DJI Tello drone platform, we implemented a modular architecture that integrates three core artificial intelligence functionalities: facial detection, facial recognition, and depth estimation from monocular vision. A web-based interface enables seamless drone control and real-time video monitoring, while a Python-based server processes visual data and executes inference pipelines using lightweight neural models optimized for embedded systems. Unlike existing commercial solutions, this system emphasizes accessibility, low-cost hardware, and open-source technologies. The system demonstrates robust performance in real-world conditions, including person tracking, indoor scanning, and autonomous line following using virtual sensors. This project validates the applicability of advanced AI techniques in real-time robotic systems and illustrates the feasibility of deploying them on constrained hardware, providing a foundation for future research in autonomous UAVs for military, rescue, and surveillance missions.

AI.tldr: Modular, open-source autonomous drone system on DJI Tello with facial detection, facial recognition, and monocular depth estimation; web interface and Python server; lightweight embedded models; demonstrations include tracking, indoor scanning, and line following; emphasizes accessibility and low-cost hardware for future UAV research.
AI.motivation: Make AI-enabled drones accessible, affordable, and open for research and practical applications; validate deployment of AI on constrained hardware.
AI.method: Modular architecture integrating three AI functionalities; web-based control and real-time video; Python-based server with inference pipelines; models optimized for embedded systems; real-world evaluation.
AI.result: Robust performance in real-world conditions; validated feasibility of deploying AI on constrained hardware; provides foundation for future UAV research in military, rescue, surveillance contexts.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of integrated AI on constrained UAV hardware and serves as a foundation for further research; open-source, low-cost approach broadens accessibility for diverse applications while highlighting need for ethical and privacy considerations.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.
