AI.tldr: Certified sensing clocks establish when world-model predictions stay valid by using drift-aware validity envelopes, offering guaranteed re-sensing schedules and empirical validation across seeds, with limitations in short-horizon regimes.
AI.motivation: Provide formal guarantees for when a learned world model's predictions remain valid, enabling reliable deployment through scheduled sensing bounded by a certified horizon.
AI.method: Audited equivariant world model is used to derive deadlines for no-sensing intervals. Calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes replace on-manifold Lyapunov rates to produce deployed guarantees. The approach is validated on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model; a cue-conditioned theorem-bed isolates scheduling rules to compare deployment distributions against exact mixtures; and limits are explored via short-horizon regimes and partial-reset exploration.
AI.result: The clock controls valid, held-out intervals across seeds and data shards and reduces eventful-tail violations relative to a baseline scheduler. In cortured tests, conformal horizons match deployed clocks in short-horizon regimes; spectral-term benefits are not universally superior in budgeted settings.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a certified sensing-clock primitive and a drift-aware deployment method, emphasizing that spectral clocks do not universally dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

title: Domain Generalization via Text-Anchored Information Bottleneck
summary: Visual recognition models often fail when deployed in new environments. Domain Generalization (DG) addresses this by learning representations that remain invariant to environment-specific variations. Recent approaches increasingly rely on large vision-language models, assuming that preserving their expressive visual representations improves robustness. However, we show that such visual expressiveness can instead propagate spurious cues that tie representations to the training environments, hindering invariant learning. We therefore discard visual guidance and instead treat the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance, naturally acting as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations. Extensive experiments across diverse backbones exhibit state-of-the-art performance and further analyze what makes guidance effective for robust generalization. These findings shift the focus of DG from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance.

AI.tldr: Discards visual guidance from vision-language models for domain generalization; uses language embeddings as the primary source of invariance, acting as an information bottleneck to preserve semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations. Achieves state-of-the-art results across diverse backbones; analyzes why guidance helps for robust generalization.
AI.motivation: Domain Generalization aims to learn representations that are invariant to environment-specific variations. The abstract argues that relying on highly expressive visual features from vision-language models can propagate spurious cues tied to training environments, hindering invariant learning, and proposes a language-centric approach to enforce invariance.
AI.method: Treat the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance, using it as an information bottleneck to preserve core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations; perform extensive experiments across diverse backbones; analyze the effectiveness of guidance for robust generalization.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance in domain generalization across diverse backbones; empirical evidence that replacing visual guidance with language-space supervision improves robustness; provides analysis of what makes guidance effective for robust generalization.
AI.conclusion: DG should shift focus from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance; a language-space bottleneck yields robust domain-invariant representations and preserves core semantics.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW introduces skill evolution for persistent, reusable agent skills in workflow-based image generation, using typed graph editing, staged tool exposure, auto-reversion of invalid edits, and a region-VLM verifier to guide repair; it outperforms a verifier-only baseline across multiple configurations and user studies.
AI.motivation: Agents need to recall prior workflow patterns, constraints, and user preferences across runs to improve reliability and efficiency in recurring visual workflows.
AI.method: Formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing with stage-specific tools; automatically reverts invalid edits; employs a region-level vision-language model verifier to convert visual failures into actionable repairs; develops a progressively disclosed skill library by distilling trajectories, errors, and verifier feedback into reusable Agent Skills.
AI.result: Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation score among six configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline; human annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is effective for improving reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction and can scale across agent models and backbones.

title: The Moving Eye: Enhancing VLA Spatial Generalization via Hybrid Dynamic Data Collection
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown remarkable promise in generalized robotic manipulation. However, their spatial generalization remains fragile. We argue that simply increasing the number of viewpoints is insufficient. Models often fall into the trap of Shortcut Learning, latching onto spurious correlations (e.g., fixed relative poses between objects or between the camera and robot base) rather than learning true spatial relationships. In this work, we propose a data-centric solution to enhance VLA spatial generalization. We utilize a dual-arm setup where one arm performs manipulation while the other serves as a mobile environmental camera. We systematically evaluate three data distribution patterns: Fixed, Multi-Fixed, and Moving Views. Our findings reveal that a hybrid strategy, combining continuous camera motion with diverse static viewpoints, yields the best performance by substantially reducing spurious correlations while maintaining training stability. Our experiments demonstrate that this strategy mitigates spurious correlations, enabling VLAs to generalize to unseen camera poses and object configurations where simply adding more static viewpoints fails. Crucially, we reveal that the susceptibility to shortcut learning and the struggle with spatial generalization are universal characteristics shared across diverse architectures. Consequently, all evaluated models (ACT, Diffusion, and VLA models including Pi0 and Gr00t) benefit significantly from our mixed data strategy.

AI.tldr: A data-centric strategy with a dual-arm system and mixed camera viewpoints reduces shortcut learning and improves spatial generalization for Vision-Language-Action models, outperforming purely static viewpoints across architectures.
AI.motivation: VLA models exhibit fragile spatial generalization due to shortcut learning from spurious correlations (e.g., fixed object-camera poses). A data-centric remedy is sought to encourage robust spatial reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce a dual-arm setup where one arm manipulates and the other acts as a mobile environmental camera. Compare three viewpoint distributions—Fixed, Multi-Fixed, and Moving Views—and test a hybrid approach that combines continuous camera motion with diverse static viewpoints across architectures (ACT, Diffusion, Pi0, Gr00t).
AI.result: The hybrid moving-plus-static view strategy substantially reduces spurious correlations, enabling generalization to unseen camera poses and object configurations. It also stabilizes training and improves performance across all evaluated models, indicating universal susceptibility to shortcut learning and generalization challenges across architectures.
AI.conclusion: A mixed data strategy that blends moving and diverse static viewpoints mitigates shortcut learning and enhances spatial generalization in VLA systems, with benefits that transfer across architectures and model families.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: EFE uses LLM-driven evolutionary search to automatically discover Python-based preprocessing transformations for structured data, enabling integration into ML pipelines to boost performance and interpretability in time-series forecasting and tabular prediction.
AI.motivation: Leverage LLMs as open-ended search operators to automate feature engineering for structured data, aiming to improve model accuracy and interpretability while simplifying pipeline design.
AI.method: Represent candidate transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface; use evolutionary search guided by dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream validation feedback to refine candidates; instantiate in two settings: EFE-Time for time-series with invertible, dataset-specific normalizations; EFE-Tab for compact, interpretable features for tabular data.
AI.result: For time-series, EFE-Time yields improvements of 3%+ in forecasting error metrics (MASE, WQL, MAE) on average across datasets, with up to 19% improvement on the COVID-Deaths dataset, notably compatible with Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact, interpretable feature programs that improve or match existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods, and are particularly effective with decision-tree models that benefit from small, interpretable feature sets.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven evolutionary feature engineering can enhance both accuracy and interpretability in structured-data tasks, and can be integrated into existing ML pipelines to augment traditional preprocessing and feature engineering approaches.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models What to See and Where to Look
comment: The paper has been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing VLAs' training relies heavily on text-centric visual question answering and chain-of-thought reasoning data, which emphasizes linguistic reasoning rather than action-grounded planning. As a result, the learned representations capture semantic knowledge but lack spatial dependencies crucial for reliable trajectory prediction. We propose DriveTeach-VLA, a framework that explicitly teaches VLAs what to see and where to look. Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving-specific perceptual priors into the vision encoder, while 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. Together, they form a vision-guided learning pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO). DriveTeach-VLA achieves the state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ShivaTeam/DriveTeach-VLA.

AI.tldr: DriveTeach-VLA integrates driving-specific vision priors and 2D trajectory-guided prompts to teach vision-language-action models what to see and where to look, enhancing end-to-end action-grounded planning for autonomous driving and achieving SOTA on NAVSIM and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Current VLA training relies on text-centric visual QA and chain-of-thought data, which emphasize linguistic reasoning over spatial, trajectory-relevant perception, leading to representations with insufficient spatial dependencies for reliable trajectory prediction.
AI.method: Introduce Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) to inject driving priors into the vision encoder; introduce 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) to provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories; a vision-guided learning pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO). The model is trained end-to-end on driving data; prompts guide attention and policy optimization.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes datasets; code released at https://github.com/ShivaTeam/DriveTeach-VLA.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly aligning perception with driving-relevant spatial priors and trajectory-guided prompts, DriveTeach-VLA closes the gap between semantic understanding and spatial trajectory reasoning, yielding improved end-to-end driving performance.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: Generic TB-Coverage: a coverage-aware MoE expert pruning method that profiles per-expert utility on separate generic corpora (WikiText2, C4) and enforces a fixed-budget cross-corpus coverage to prune without downstream calibration data; yields better zero-shot accuracy and lower perplexity degradation than baselines at 25–75% retention.
AI.motivation: MoE models have substantial redundant routing across experts. Pruning without task-specific calibration is challenging and single aggregated scores bias retention toward experts tied to dominant calibration patterns. A cross-corpus, coverage-aware approach using generic data aims to preserve diverse high-utility experts and improve robustness across tasks.
AI.method: Profile per-expert utility separately on each corpus (WikiText2 and C4) and enforce a fixed-budget coverage rule to preserve high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. No downstream calibration data used. Evaluate across two MoE models and multiple budgets (25%, 50%, 75%).
AI.result: Improved average accuracy on six zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity; reduced perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. Gains are largest at aggressive pruning (25% and 50%). Effective under fixed budgets with no downstream calibration data.
AI.conclusion: Cross-corpus coverage preserved by per-corpus utility profiling provides a robust generic-data prior for MoE pruning, enabling effective pruning without task-specific calibration data.

title: HEFT: Heavy-Payload Full-size Humanoid Teleoperation with Privileged Motion Guidance and Windowed Payload Curriculum
summary: General motion tracking and teleoperation offer a promising path to scalable humanoid skill acquisition, yet most existing frameworks are validated on compact platforms or without real payload interaction, leaving full-size humanoids with real payloads largely unexplored. Scaling to full-size humanoids introduces two compounding challenges: their larger inertia and tighter balance margins make tracking highly sensitive to noise, drift, and retargeting errors from commodity VR trackers, while their payload potential remains largely underutilized. We present HEFT, a heavy-payload full-size humanoid teleoperation framework that addresses both challenges. HEFT learns from deployable noisy VR references with physically plausible reconstructed references through Privileged Motion Guidance (PMG), and uses a Windowed Payload Curriculum (WPC) with expert-guided payload caps to acquire robust heavy-payload tracking. We deploy HEFT on L7, a 175cm, 65kg humanoid. The robot tracks motions including turns, forward/backward locomotion, and squats under payloads up to 24kg.

AI.tldr: HEFT enables robust heavy-payload teleoperation for full-size humanoids by combining Privileged Motion Guidance (physically plausible reference reconstruction) and a Windowed Payload Curriculum to handle noise and inertia; demonstrated on the L7 humanoid with up to 24 kg payloads for turning, locomotion, and squats.
AI.motivation: Extend teleoperation from compact platforms to full-size humanoids with real payloads, addressing large inertia, tight balance margins, and underutilized payload potential; overcome VR tracker noise, drift, and retargeting errors.
AI.method: Privileged Motion Guidance to produce physically plausible reconstructed references from deployable noisy VR signals; Windowed Payload Curriculum with expert-guided payload caps to gradually train robust heavy-payload tracking; deployment on L7 (175 cm, 65 kg) for high-payload tracking up to 24 kg; evaluating motion tasks like turning, forward/backward locomotion, squats.
AI.result: HEFT achieves tracking of turns, locomotion, and squats under payloads up to 24 kg on L7; demonstrates feasibility of heavy-payload full-size humanoid teleoperation using the proposed framework.
AI.conclusion: Combines PMG and WPC to address noise, drift, and retargeting in full-size humanoid teleoperation with payloads; enables scalable skill acquisition by leveraging heavy payload capabilities, validated on a real full-size humanoid.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: A simple, interpretable topological mask for Graph Transformers using a log-transform of symmetrically normalized adjacency to gate attention; assigns per-head structural radii for multi-hop propagation, achieving state-of-the-art on 13 of 20 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Graph data have sparse, structured interactions; vanilla self-attention is dense and lacks topology; need a lightweight, interpretable mechanism to inject graph structure without changing the Transformer architecture.
AI.method: Compute symmetric normalized adjacency A_hat. Apply a logarithmic transform to create a topology-aware gating signal. Use different powers of A_hat for different heads to give each head a defined structural radius, enabling multi-hop information within a single layer. Interprets a standard Transformer encoder as one-step message passing on a complete graph, and uses X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention.
AI.result: Across 20 node-, edge-, and graph-level benchmarks, achieves state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remains competitive in one-layer configurations; demonstrates interpretability and simplicity without modifying the Transformer backbone.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can adapt self-attention to graph data effectively while preserving Transformer architecture; code available for reproducibility.

title: Unified Panoramic-Gaussian Representation for Monocular 4D Scene Synthesis
summary: 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos has made significant progress in recent years. However, existing methods are typically constrained by view interpolation. As a result, they struggle to infer unseen regions beyond the observed views. In this paper, we reformulate the task as 4D scene synthesis with unseen regions, which extends beyond traditional interpolation settings. Camera-conditioned video generation enables unseen region synthesis by guiding generation along specified cameras. However, these methods lack explicit 3D priors and are optimized with random camera trajectories. This design leads to severe inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations. To address this limitation, we build a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance. While this design improves cross-view consistency, the panoramic representation alone fails to model dynamic content effectively. Object motion in panoramic space introduces scale and shape distortions. To address this, we propose PanoGaussian, a unified Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills the panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture dynamic physical priors of the 4D scene. Experiments demonstrate that PanoGaussian achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations.

AI.tldr: Introduces PanoGaussian for 4D scene synthesis from monocular video, combining panoramic trajectory guidance with a dynamic Gaussian representation to handle unseen regions and large viewpoint changes.
AI.motivation: Overcome view interpolation limitations and lack of explicit 3D priors in camera-conditioned video generation, which cause inconsistencies under large camera deviations; enable synthesis of unseen regions.
AI.method: Unified training/inference framework using panoramic trajectory guidance. Uses a panoramic representation for cross-view consistency, but introduces PanoGaussian to distill this into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation that encodes dynamic physical priors of the 4D scene.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate consistent 4D scene synthesis under large viewpoint variations, indicating improved cross-view consistency and dynamic content modeling over purely panoramic approaches.
AI.conclusion: PanoGaussian provides a robust, unified representation that pairs panoramic guidance with explicit dynamic priors to synthesize consistent 4D scenes with unseen regions across wide camera trajectories.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: Proposes a robust listwise Plackett–Luce objective for ranking-label uncertainty in LLM alignment, with an exact decomposition into nominal loss plus worst-case correction; tractable optimization via sorting; shows convexity/weak convexity guarantees and empirical robustness improvements offline and online.
AI.motivation: Existing robust LLM alignment largely tackles pairwise or dataset-level robustness; there is a need for listwise robustness under ranking-label uncertainty (ambiguity, noise) in candidate lists.
AI.method: Introduce a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett–Luce objective that conditions on the candidate list. The worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting scores in ascending order, enabling O(K log K) inner optimization. The objective decomposes into nominal PL loss plus a worst-case correction. The offline setting yields a convex objective with convergent projected subgradient methods (O(ε^-2) samples). The online setting with policy-generated lists yields weak convexity and O~(ε^-2) Moreau-envelope stationarity.
AI.result: Offline experiments show the robust correction preserves performance with clean labels and improves robustness under noise. Online alignment shows more reliable reward-model-ranked candidate expansion and improvements in both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robust listwise PL objective provides tractable, theoretically grounded robustness for ranking-label uncertainty in LLM alignment, with strong offline/online guarantees and empirical gains under noise and in online deployment.

title: ACID: Action Consistency via Inverse Dynamics for Planning with World Models
summary: Decision-time planning with action-conditioned world models has become a popular paradigm for embodied control. However, the standard planning cost judges a candidate solely by how close its predicted terminal state lies to the goal, leaving the realizability of the intermediate transitions unchecked -- a predicted trajectory can look convincing while the environment rollout drifts away from it. In this paper, we propose ACID, a decision-time planning framework that introduces cycle action consistency: the action inferred backward from a predicted transition by an inverse dynamics model should recover the one that was conditioned on. We fold this per-step residual into the planning cost via a scale-invariant adaptive weight. Across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks spanning rigid and deformable manipulation, articulated control, and visual navigation, ACID consistently improves planning and matches the baseline's accuracy with substantially less planning compute.

AI.tldr: ACID introduces cycle action consistency into decision-time planning with action-conditioned world models. It uses an inverse dynamics model to ensure that the backward-inferred action from a predicted transition matches the conditioned action, incorporating this as a per-step, scale-invariant residual in the planning cost. This yields improved planning performance with much lower compute across diverse models and tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard planning costs only consider terminal-state proximity, allowing intermediate transitions to drift and yielding trajectories that look plausible but are not realizable in the environment. A need exists to enforce consistency of transitions at every step to prevent such drift and improve real-world feasibility and efficiency.
AI.method: ACID integrates cycle action consistency by introducing an inverse dynamics model that infers the action from a predicted state-transition and enforces that it matches the conditioned action. The per-step residual from this cyclic consistency is folded into the planning objective with an adaptive, scale-invariant weight, enabling robust, planning-time computation across multiple world models.
AI.result: Empirically, ACID improves planning performance and matches the baseline accuracy while significantly reducing planning compute across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks, covering rigid/deformable manipulation, articulated control, and visual navigation.
AI.conclusion: Cycle-action consistency is a effective regularizer for decision-time planning, enabling more faithful planned trajectories and more efficient planning across diverse domains without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: Formalizes chain-of-thought as discrete curves in hidden-state space, introduces effective dimension d_rho, links flatter eigenvalue spectra to harder tasks, and shows kinematic trajectory features can predict correctness early; achieves 0.93 AUC on MATH500 and transfers to diverse questions.
AI.motivation: To understand the internal geometry of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories and connect geometric properties to task difficulty and solution quality in LLMs.
AI.method: Models CoT as discrete curves in R^d and analyzes spectral, positional, and kinematic functionals. Defines effective dimension d_rho to quantify trajectory complexity. Examines eigenvalue spectra and their relation to task difficulty, and extracts kinematic features (mean position, dispersion, velocity, speed, etc.) to predict correctness before completion. Empirical evaluation on MATH500; explores cross-question transfer and potential for early stopping.
AI.result: Found that flatter eigenvalue spectra (lower energy concentration in top eigenmodes) associate with harder tasks. d_rho correlates with difficulty; kinematic features can predict correctness within the first 20% of generated tokens; AUC of 0.93 distinguishes easy vs hard problems on MATH500; signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty.
AI.conclusion: The shape of an LLM’s internal reasoning trajectory is a meaningful indicator of task hardness and solution quality, offering a principled lens on CoT behavior and practical avenues for early stopping and model self-assessment.

title: Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for Enhanced Audiovisual Video Captioning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced video understanding, achieving precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning remains a formidable challenge. Most existing approaches suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence, failing to accurately bind auditory events to visual entities or capture complex causal dynamics. To address these deficiencies, we propose TCA-Captioner, a framework specifically engineered to enhance Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for audiovisual video captioning. We first introduce the Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) framework, an iterative refinement strategy that generates high-fidelity, meticulously grounded training data. Leveraging a curated high-density human interaction dataset, TCA-Captioner is optimized to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions. Furthermore, we present TCA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark utilizing a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate and quantify model proficiency in audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives.

AI.tldr: A framework for temporally coherent audiovisual captioning that uses an Observer-Checker-Corrector refinement to generate grounded training data and a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol benchmark to assess audiovisual binding and temporal reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: To address modality detachment and temporal incoherence in audiovisual captioning, by strengthening cross-modal binding and temporal reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce OCC iterative refinement to create high-density grounded data from a human-interaction dataset; train TCA-Captioner; propose TCA-Bench with Decoupled Evaluation Protocol for isolating audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows superior temporal coherence and audiovisual synchronization, surpassing baselines and establishing a new standard.
AI.conclusion: TCA-Captioner demonstrates strong temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual captioning; the OCC framework and TCA-Bench provide data-quality improvements and diagnostic tooling.

title: DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

AI.tldr: Introduces DRL-CLBA, a clean-label backdoor attack for speech classification that uses DDPG-driven trigger optimization and deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers; achieves high attack success and resists several defenses.
AI.motivation: Speech classification models are vulnerable to backdoor attacks. Clean-label backdoors avoid label poisoning, but existing sample-specific attacks often rely on poisoned labels and can be detected. This work proposes a clean-label backdoor attack for speech to reveal and exploit remaining vulnerabilities.
AI.method: Utilizes Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient reinforcement learning to optimize target samples toward trigger-bearing anchors embedded via deep audio steganography in the model's latent space. This creates feature-space anchors and enables label-migration-free poisoning of target samples.
AI.result: Evaluated on three datasets and four DNNs, DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate and can bypass some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates robustness against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral-signature defenses.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems to clean-label backdoors, indicating a need for defenses that address anchor-based, latent-space backdoors and steganography-based triggers.

title: LIME: Learning Intent-aware Camera Motion from Egocentric Video
summary: Autonomous robots often need to move their camera before they can act: to inspect an object, reveal an occluded region, or obtain a view that responds to a user's intent. While vision-language navigation translates instructions to base motion and vision-language-action policies map instructions to manipulation actions, language-conditioned camera motion remains comparatively underexplored as a first-class action. We formulate language-conditioned camera motion generation: given a current RGB observation and a free-form natural-language intent, predict a relative target camera pose for the next observation. This task is inherently non-trivial: viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intentions, and a valid motion may operate at different semantic granularity, from entering a room to looking around a corner, inspecting a visible object, or revealing an occluded detail. To model this structure, we mine multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video, pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative SE(3) target poses. We propose LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator that combines an auto-regressive observation-gain output with a continuous flow-matching pose head. This design lets the model jointly predict what the next view should reveal while representing multi-hypothesis target views. Across experiments and downstream robotic tasks, we show that LIME can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception.

AI.tldr: A vision-language camera-motion generator (LIME) that predicts the next camera pose conditioned on natural-language intent, using an autoregressive observation-gain head and a continuous flow-matching pose head, trained on egocentric video to capture multi-intention viewpoints.
AI.motivation: To treat camera motion as a first-class action in language-conditioned robotics and address the gap where viewpoint changes driven by latent intents are not well modeled. The goal is to enable active perception through pose-controlled viewpoint changes that align with user intent and perceptual needs.
AI.method: LIME combines an autoregressive observation-gain decoder with a continuous SE(3) flow-matching pose head. It mines multi-intention supervision from egocentric video by pairing plausible intents and observation gains with relative target poses, enabling multi-hypothesis predictions of next views.
AI.result: Experiments across tasks show LIME can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception, and improving downstream perception/interaction performance.
AI.conclusion: Language-conditioned camera motion is a viable first-class action for autonomous perception. LIME provides a practical framework that learns from passive video to predict semantically aligned camera poses and supports multi-intention viewpoint mapping.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: BOUNDARY_SYNC quantifies inter-agent coupling via CAF; text and image channels show homogenization (CAF<1); group size and cross-model results suggest controlled coupling; coupling is prompt-driven and stateless.
AI.motivation: to quantify how inter-agent communication shapes outputs and to enable design choices in multi-agent systems, balancing homogenization vs. diversification and preventing unwanted convergence.
AI.method: controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9.9k API calls); measure CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline; test text and image channels; ablations (no-communication, prompt perturbations); group sizes K=3 and K=5; cross-model replication; statelessness analysis; within-modality baselines; CI reported.
AI.result: CAF_text ≈ 0.803 (CI 0.740–0.873); CAF_image ≈ 0.834 (CI 0.811–0.858); homogenization dominates; K=5 homogenization, K=3 diversification (CAF 1.14 and 1.06; CIs pending); cross-model replication shows wide range (0.034–0.803); DeepSeek artifacts; coupling driven by prompt context, not cumulative updating; monotonic convergence under continual prompts.
AI.conclusion: Inter-agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable via prompt design; has clear implications for multi-agent system design, enabling or mitigating homogenization and diversification through prompt strategies and group composition.

title: HistoSeg++: Delving deeper with attention and multiscale feature fusion for biomarker segmentation
comment: Published in the Proceedings of ICBBE 2025. The Version of Record is available at https://doi.org/10.1145/3794209.3794211
summary: Segmentation of biomarkers in medical images is frequently viewed as a first step towards medical image analysis in any bioinformatics or biomedical application. Despite progress, existing methods still struggle to capture information at multiple scales and to perform upsampling effectively across different datasets. These shortcomings often result in suboptimal generalization capabilities. Recently, architectures belonging to the Nested-UNet family excel in capturing multiscale contextual information and upsample them effectively. In this work, We propose a novel Nested-UNet architecture that effectively captures multi-scale contextual information. It includes inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, along with channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, leading to improved segmentation performance. Additionally, the architecture integrates an edge-aware loss to emphasize boundary accuracy by assigning greater importance to edge regions. Tested extensively on three publicly available benchmark datasets. Our method demonstrates a generalization performance superior to existing Nested-UNet methods. Code: https://github.com/saadwazir/histosegplusplus

AI.tldr: A multi-scale biomarker segmentation model based on Nested-UNet with inner/outer attention, squeeze-and-excitation recalibration, and edge-aware loss, achieving better cross-dataset generalization than prior Nested-UNet methods.
AI.motivation: Segmentation of biomarkers requires robust multi-scale context fusion and precise boundary delineation; existing methods struggle with upsampling and generalization across datasets.
AI.method: Propose a Nested-UNet variant featuring inner and outer attention units during upsampling, channel-wise recalibration via squeeze-and-excitation modules, and an edge-aware loss; evaluated on three public datasets with code release.
AI.result: Demonstrates superior generalization performance over existing Nested-UNet baselines on three publicly available benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: Integrating multi-scale attention, channel recalibration, and edge-focused loss improves biomarker segmentation accuracy and cross-dataset generalization, leveraging the Nested-UNet framework.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: A case study of reformalizing the Jordan Curve Theorem across multiple proof assistants, analyzing pipeline design choices in cross-system translations.
AI.motivation: To understand practical challenges and design decisions when reformalizing formal proofs across proof assistants, and to compare concrete translation pipelines (Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, HOL Light→Agda).
AI.method: Three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem were performed from Mizar to Lean, HOL Light to Lean, and HOL Light to Agda. The study documents encountered challenges, encoding/representation choices, library alignments, and translation strategies, and analyzes how这些 design choices affect effort and feasibility.
AI.result: Successful reformalizations in all three target systems. The paper identifies key pipeline design choices that influence practicality (e.g., how to map concepts across libraries, choices between automation vs manual proof steps, and representation of topology notions).
AI.conclusion: Reformulating proofs across proof assistants is feasible with careful pipeline design. The study highlights actionable guidelines for bridging libraries, choosing encoding strategies, and balancing automation with human guidance to improve cross-system reformalizations.

title: WorldSample: Closed-loop Real-robot RL with World Modelling
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can overcome the demonstration-coverage limitation of imitation learning (IL) by allowing robots to improve through trial-and-error interaction beyond the states observed in demonstrations. However, deploying RL on real robots remains constrained by high interaction costs, since each physical rollout is costly and reflects only one realized action-outcome path. To address this challenge, we propose WorldSample, a physically grounded data augmentation framework for real-robot RL that closes a real-synthetic loop between physical rollouts, world-model generation, and policy improvement. Grounded on real rollouts, WorldSample generates high-fidelity synthetic transitions through a post-trained world model, which greatly lowers the visual hallucination. Specifically, rather than simply using these transitions as real-world experience, WorldSample introduces Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to regulate the training process through sample selection and scheduling, balancing useful augmentation against value overestimation and mitigating the hallucination-induced noise. Experiments on robot manipulation tasks involving contact-rich and precise tasks show that WorldSample improves policy success rate by 28% while reducing training steps by 59% compared with baselines. Furthermore, WorldSample improves world model visual fidelity by 19.4dB in PSNR and 0.47 in SSIM over demonstration-only post-training, validating the effectiveness of the real-synthetic loop for both policy and world model performance.

AI.tldr: WorldSample introduces a real-robot reinforcement learning framework that uses real rollouts to train a world model, generates high-fidelity synthetic transitions to augment data, and applies Policy-Paced Learning to regulate augmentation. It achieves notable gains: +28% policy success, -59% training steps, and improves world-model visual fidelity (PSNR +19.4 dB, SSIM +0.47) over demonstration-only post-training.
AI.motivation: RL on real robots is data-inefficient and costly due to expensive physical rollouts; imitation learning often misses state-action coverage. A real-synthetic loop can leverage limited real data to train accurate world models and improve policies with reduced physical interactions.
AI.method: Collect real rollouts to train a grounded world model; use the world model to generate high-fidelity synthetic transitions; apply Policy-Paced Learning to select and schedule augmented data to avoid value overestimation and noise; evaluate on contact-rich, precise manipulation tasks.
AI.result: Policy success rate improved by 28% and training steps reduced by 59% compared with baselines; world-model visual fidelity improved by 19.4 dB PSNR and 0.47 SSIM over demonstration-only post-training.
AI.conclusion: A real-synthetic loop with policy-paced data augmentation effectively improves both policy performance and world-model fidelity in real-robot RL, reducing data requirements and mitigating hallucination-induced errors.

title: SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: SINA is an open-source image-to-netlist tool that converts circuit schematic images (IC and PCB) into machine-readable netlists using DL-based component detection, connected-component labeling, OCR for designators, and a Vision-Language Model for assignment, including crossing-wires detection; achieves 96.67% accuracy, 2.72x better than prior methods.
AI.motivation: The lack of machine-readable representations of circuit designs in schematic images limits AI-driven EDA; current methods struggle to generalize across IC/PCB schematics and to distinguish connections from crossings.
AI.method: SINA is a fully automated pipeline combining (i) deep learning-based component detection, (ii) connected-component labeling for connectivity inference, (iii) OCR for component reference designator extraction, (iv) a Vision-Language Model for reliable reference designator assignment, and (v) dedicated crossing-wires detection; validated on IC- and PCB-level schematics with graph-isomorphism checks.
AI.result: Netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, approximately 2.72 times higher than state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: SINA delivers a robust, generalizable image-to-netlist solution for IC/PCB schematics, enabling simulation, verification, and AI-based modeling by correctly inferring connectivity, distinguishing wire crossings, and producing valid netlists.

title: ICDepth: Taming Video Diffusion Models for Video Depth Estimation via In-Context Conditioning
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://xuanhuahe.github.io/ICDepth/
summary: Monocular video depth estimation requires temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization across diverse scenarios, yet existing methods struggle to achieve all three simultaneously. Discriminative models excel at per-frame accuracy but suffer from temporal drift due to limited context windows, while generative methods improve consistency and generalization at the cost of extensive training data (10M+ samples) and lack of geometric precision. In response to these issues, we introduce \textbf{ICDepth}, a framework that adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning (ICC), leveraging their rich spatial-temporal priors. To address key challenges in transferring ICC from generation to dense prediction, we propose: (1)~\textbf{SAND-Attention}, which ensures precise spatial-temporal alignment via shared RoPE and enforces unidirectional attention to prevent noise contamination; (2)~\textbf{SRFM}, which injects DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to enhance geometric precision. ICDepth achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with remarkable data efficiency, trained on only 0.8M frames ($6$--$13\times$ less than competing generative methods), while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.

AI.tldr: ICDepth adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers via In-Context Conditioning (ICC) for video depth estimation, introducing SAND-Attention and SRFM to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, temporal consistency, and generalization with only 0.8M training frames.
AI.motivation: Monocular video depth estimation demands temporal consistency, geometric precision, and broad generalization. Discriminative per-frame methods suffer from temporal drift; generative approaches need vast data and can lack geometric accuracy. Transferring ICC from generation to dense prediction is challenging.
AI.method: Employ ICC on pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers. Introduce SAND-Attention with shared RoPE and unidirectional attention to ensure precise spatio-temporal alignment and avoid noise contamination; introduce SRFM to inject DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to enhance geometric precision.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with high data efficiency (0.8M frames, 6–13× less than competing generative methods) and strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.
AI.conclusion: ICDepth demonstrates that adapting diffusion-based ICC with targeted attention and semantic priors can deliver accurate, temporally consistent, and data-efficient video depth estimation, bridging the gap between discriminative and generative approaches.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: A meta-benchmarking framework reorganizes 452 public benchmarks into 41 O*NET work activities and 38 banking domains, using a multiplicative weighting (discrimination × coverage × recency) over a rolling window to scale Elo-based cross-benchmark scores, enabling domain-level comparisons without raw score normalization; demonstrated on 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026; aims to improve reproducibility and governance in model evaluation.
AI.motivation: Public LLM leaderboards optimize average performance and miss domain-specific cognitive demands; financial-services work requires targeted evaluation (e.g., compliance reasoning, multi-turn interaction). A framework that aggregates benchmarks by standardized work activities and banking domains offers governance-friendly, reproducible, and interpretable scoring.
AI.method: Aggregate 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities partitioned into 38 BIAN banking domains; apply a multiplicative weight (discrimination × coverage × recency) computed over a rolling model window; use weights to scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament to produce cross-benchmark comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalization; compute domain scores as weighted averages of activity Elo scores; provide a point-in-time snapshot (288 models, 25 organizations, June 2026) and discuss taxonomy, design decisions, limitations.
AI.result: Demonstrates a reproducible, cross-benchmark comparison framework with domain-level interpretation; suppresses saturated legacy tests automatically through weighting; yields cross-benchmark comparable work-activity scores without normalisation; applied to a snapshot of 288 models across 25 orgs at a June 2026 point-in-time.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a transparent, governance-friendly approach to evaluating model work-activity capabilities across financial-domain domains, enabling reproducible benchmarking and targeted governance; adaptable to other sectors; future work could refine weighting schemes and expand benchmarks.

title: Learning to Move Before Learning to Do: Task-Agnostic pretraining for VLAs
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of expert demonstrations -- triplets of observations, instructions, and actions that are costly to collect at scale. We argue that this bottleneck stems from conflating two distinct learning objectives: acquiring physical competence (how to move) and acquiring semantic alignment (what to do). Crucially, only the latter requires language supervision. Building on this Decomposition Hypothesis, we propose Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP), a two-stage framework that first learns transferable motor priors from cheap, unlabeled interaction data -- including discarded off-task trajectories and autonomous robot play -- via a self-supervised Inverse Dynamics objective. A lightweight second stage then grounds these priors in language using minimal expert data. On the SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on over 1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, yielding a 10% absolute gain over standard behavior cloning. On a real-world WidowX platform, TAP retains 25% success under camera perturbations where internet-scale baselines collapse to 0%, demonstrating that task-agnostic pretraining produces robust, transferable physical representations and offers a scalable path forward for Embodied AI.

AI.tldr: Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP) decouples physical competence from semantic alignment, learning transferable motor priors from unlabeled interaction data and grounding them in language with minimal expert data; it achieves strong data efficiency on SIMPLER and robustness on WidowX, suggesting scalable embodied AI pretraining.
AI.motivation: Address the bottleneck in Vision-Language-Action models caused by scarce expert demonstrations, which conflates learning how to move with what to do. The Decomposition Hypothesis argues that only semantic alignment requires language supervision, while physical competence can be learned from unlabeled interaction.
AI.method: Two-stage framework. Stage 1 pretrains transferable motor priors from cheap, unlabeled interaction data (incl. off-task trajectories and autonomous play) via a self-supervised Inverse Dynamics objective. Stage 2 uses minimal expert data to ground these priors in language, enabling task instructions to drive behavior.
AI.result: On the SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on over 1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, with a 10 percentage-point improvement over standard behavior cloning. In real-world WidowX experiments, TAP maintains 25% success under camera perturbations where internet-scale baselines drop to 0%, demonstrating robust, transferable physical representations and scalability of the approach.
AI.conclusion: Task-agnostic pretraining yields robust, transferable motor representations that can be effectively grounded with limited language supervision, offering a scalable path to more data-efficient and robust Embodied AI systems.

title: MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction
summary: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

AI.tldr: A multimodal framework for cold-start PPI prediction that fuses region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, using graph attention, bridge reconstruction, and pair-level gating to outperform baselines in novel settings.
AI.motivation: Address cold-start PPI prediction where proteins lack observed network edges; leverage complementary sequence and biomedical knowledge graph information to compensate for missing topology.
AI.method: A multimodal architecture (method) with: (1) region-aware sequence encoding that uses structurally informed sequence regions; (2) graph attention encoders over four knowledge graphs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA); (3) a bridge reconstruction objective to regularize graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations; (4) a pair-level gating module to adaptively fuse sequence and graph signals for each protein pair.
AI.result: In two benchmark settings (novel-old and novel-novel), method consistently surpasses competitive sequence-only, network-only, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses cold-start PPI prediction by integrating multi-source protein information, yielding robust gains across standard classification metrics and settings.

title: Structure-Aware Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has demonstrated remarkable potential in novel view synthesis. In contrast to small-scale scenes, large-scale scenes inevitably contain sparsely observed regions with excessively sparse initial points. In this case, supervising Gaussians initialized from low-frequency sparse points with high-frequency images often induces uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives, degrading both efficiency and quality. Intuitively, this issue can be mitigated with scheduling strategies, which can be categorized into two paradigms: modulating target signal frequency via densification and modulating sampling frequency via image resolution. However, previous scheduling strategies are primarily hardcoded, failing to perceive the convergence behavior of scene frequency. To address this, we reframe the scene reconstruction problem from the perspective of signal structure recovery and propose SIG, a novel scheduler that synchronizes image supervision with Gaussian frequencies. Specifically, we derive the average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations, and then regulate the training image resolution and the Gaussian densification process based on scene frequency convergence. Furthermore, we introduce Sphere-Constrained Gaussians, which leverage the spatial prior of initialized point clouds to control Gaussian optimization. Our framework enables frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training, achieving state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin in both efficiency and rendering quality in large-scale scenes. The code is available at: https://github.com/weiyixue999/Signal_Structure_Aware_Gaussian

AI.tldr: A structure-aware frequency scheduler (SIG) for 3D Gaussian Splatting that jointly tunes image resolution and Gaussian densification based on scene frequency convergence; enhanced by Sphere-Constrained Gaussians leveraging point-cloud priors; achieves state-of-the-art efficiency and rendering quality in large-scale scenes; code released.
AI.motivation: Large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting suffers from sparsity in observed regions leading to uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives; existing scheduling strategies are hardcoded and do not adapt to convergence behavior.
AI.method: Derive average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations; regulate training image resolution and Gaussian densification based on scene frequency convergence; introduce Sphere-Constrained Gaussians to exploit spatial priors of initialized point clouds.
AI.result: Frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training; substantial improvements in efficiency and rendering quality on large-scale scenes; state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: SIG provides a dynamic, frequency-aware scheduling framework and principled Gaussian control; code available at the provided repository.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav is an on-policy Vision-Language Navigation framework that uses a three-stage dual-supervision cycle to align exploratory trajectories with language instructions via hindsight reasoning, enabling dense training signals from semantically unlabeled movement and reducing reliance on expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: On-policy exploration broadens state coverage but causes semantic mismatch between executed visual streams and the original instruction, creating a need for semantic supervision during training. The work seeks to bridge this gap by generating instruction signals that match the agent's actual path.
AI.method: 1) Oracle-guided on-policy exploration to sample a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback. 2) A hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level instruction based on collected visual observations. 3) A second imitation pass trains on the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration, forming a dual-supervision loop.
AI.result: Phi-Nav achieves competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while using a fraction of the expert demonstrations required by existing baselines, demonstrating effective semantic alignment between exploration and language.
AI.conclusion: Semantic supervision is essential for effective on-policy VLN; Phi-Nav demonstrates that hindsight-grounded, dual-imitation training can transform unlabeled exploratory movements into valuable training signals, reducing data requirements.

title: Learning Agile Intruder Interception using Differentiable Quadrotor Dynamics
summary: This paper presents a methodology for learning a control policy to intercept an intruder using the 3D direction unit vector to the intruder and the interceptor state. Prior deep reinforcement learning approaches assume either relative position or distance to the intruder is available, but this information is not readily accessible in real-world applications that employ passive, monocular camera sensors. Instead, we propose a solution that leverages an analytical policy gradient method using differentiable quadrotor dynamics to learn agile interception at speeds up to 10 m/s. The proposed approach outperforms baseline methods that utilize simplified point mass dynamics by an average of 30%.

AI.tldr: Differentiable-policy-gradient approach for quadrotor interception using 3D direction to intruder and interceptor state, suited for monocular sensing; achieves agile interception up to 10 m/s and outperforms simplified point-mass baselines by ~30%.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where monocular cameras cannot provide direct relative position or distance to intruders, making RL methods that rely on such signals impractical; leverage differentiable quadrotor dynamics to enable end-to-end learning from limited observations.
AI.method: Analytical policy gradient optimization with differentiable quadrotor dynamics, using the 3D unit direction to the intruder and the interceptor's state as observations to learn a control policy.
AI.result: Policy achieves agile interception at speeds up to 10 m/s and provides about 30% improvement over baselines that use simplified point-mass dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that differentiable dynamics combined with analytical policy gradients can learn effective interception policies under monocular sensing constraints, outperforming traditional simplified-dynamics baselines and offering practical viability for real-world UAV interception tasks.

title: DeadPool: Resilient LLM Training with Hot-Swapping via Zero-Overhead Checkpoint
summary: State-of-the-art large language model (LLM) training takes tens of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) for months and encounters failures across the software and hardware stack. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms either impose non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency, particularly under scenarios where a small subset of compute nodes experience permanent failures. %The tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency forms a space forms a Pareto frontier We present DeadPool to simultaneously address both optimization objectives. DeadPool incorporates a fault-tolerance mechanism that restores LLM training via hot-swapping, namely by replacing failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the complete job. The hot-swapping of DeadPool is enabled by two ideas: First, it exploits an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy. Second, it introduces a communicator reconstruction protocol that replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime. DeadPool efficiently overlaps the in-memory checkpointing with computation, thus introducing zero overhead during error-free execution. Upon permanent node failures, DeadPool can rebuild memory states with minimal recomputation by leveraging in-memory checkpoints.
