We evaluate DeadPool across scales (up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs) and LLMs (up to 65B parameters), and observe zero checkpoint overhead with hot-swapping recovery completing in under 40 seconds. These results show that DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost.

AI.tldr: DeadPool adds zero-overhead fault tolerance to large-scale LLM training by hot-swapping failed nodes with spare ones using off-critical-path in-memory checkpoints and a runtime communicator reconstruction protocol, enabling recovery in under 40s up to 512 GPUs and 65B-parameter models.
AI.motivation: To overcome the heavy overhead of fault-tolerance in failure-free periods and the long recovery latency when nodes permanently fail during extensive LLM training, especially at large cluster scales.
AI.method: Introduce two mechanisms: (1) off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing to provide spatial redundancy that is overlapped with computation, and (2) a runtime communicator reconstruction protocol that substitutes failed nodes with spares without terminating the job. Training state is preserved in-memory to enable fast recovery and minimal recomputation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and LLMs up to 65B parameters shows zero overhead during error-free execution and recovery from permanent failures in under 40 seconds.
AI.conclusion: DeadPool demonstrates simultaneous zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost, addressing both core objectives of fault tolerance for large-scale LLM training.

title: LASER: A Corrective Lens for LVLMs via Visual Attention Preservation and Sink Suppression
comment: The 19th European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV 2026)
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit strong reasoning ability but suffer from visual forgetting during long-horizon decoding, where attention progressively drifts away from visual evidence. Existing methods largely treat this issue as a late-stage attention decay problem or attempt to mitigate it through heuristic reminders or post-hoc attention lifting. Through systematic empirical analysis, we find that performance degradation under visual forgetting is largely driven by two overlooked factors: early-stage attention decay disrupts evidence acquisition, and attention concentration on a subset of task-irrelevant visual sink tokens. Motivated by these insights, we propose LASER, a post-training framework that regulates both the visual attention trajectory and intra-visual token attention distribution during reasoning. Technically, LASER introduces two complementary rewards: a Visual Grounding Reward, which encourages the model to maintain attention on semantically salient visual tokens throughout decoding, and a Sink Suppression Reward, which penalizes excessive attention concentration on visual sink tokens. Together, these rewards preserve early-stage grounding while preventing attention collapse onto uninformative regions. Extensive experiments on eight benchmark datasets demonstrate that LASER consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating attention-aware training as an effective remedy for visual forgetting.

AI.tldr: LASER is a post-training framework for LVLMs that regulates visual attention during long-horizon reasoning via two rewards: Visual Grounding and Sink Suppression, improving eight-benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: Visual forgetting arises from early-stage attention decay and concentration on a subset of task-irrelevant visual sink tokens; existing remedies focus on late-stage attention or heuristic cues and do not regulate the entire attention trajectory.
AI.method: LASER introduces two complementary rewards in post-training: a Visual Grounding Reward to maintain attention on semantically salient visual tokens during decoding, and a Sink Suppression Reward to penalize excessive attention to visual sink tokens, thereby shaping both the attention trajectory and intra-token distribution.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on eight benchmark datasets show LASER consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating attention-aware training as an effective remedy for visual forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Attention-aware post-training with Visual Grounding and Sink Suppression rewards effectively mitigates visual forgetting in LVLMs by preserving early grounding and preventing attention collapse onto uninformative regions.

title: Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction
summary: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

AI.tldr: Mastermind proposes a dual-loop framework that learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies (planner) separate from task-specific execution (executor). It enables transferability across executors, achieving high pass rates on CyberGym tasks and improving multiple LLMs.
AI.motivation: Strategy learning, not full action trajectories, is a compact, concrete, and reusable unit for repository-scale SE agents. A learned planner can generalize across executors, addressing the brittleness of end-to-end prompting.
AI.method: Train a planner via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and milestone-based GRPO to acquire reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies. An experience loop maintains task-local strategy records to guide attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing frozen executors to benefit from strategy improvements. Evaluation uses CyberGym with 260 training tasks and 200 held-out tasks, testing with GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 mini, and GLM-5.1.
AI.result: With GPT-5.5 as executor, Mastermind achieves 84.5% pass rate, surpassing open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini from 45.0% to 60.0% and GLM-5.1 from 58.5% to 71.0%.
AI.conclusion: Learning high-level, transferable strategies is effective for repository-scale SE agents, and decoupling strategy learning from execution yields cross-model gains.

title: QuadRocket: An Aerial Robotic Testbed for Adaptive Thrust-Vector Control of Rocket-Like Vehicles
comment: Paper accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
summary: This paper presents QuadRocket, a quadrotor-based rocket prototype that provides a low-cost, low-risk platform for validating advanced thrust-vector control strategies for launch vehicle-type systems. The prototype consists of a cylindrical main body mounted on top of a quadrotor through a universal joint, forming a flying inverted pendulum with non-negligible inertia. For control design, the coupled system is modeled as a single axisymmetric rigid body actuated by a vectored force applied along its longitudinal axis. A reduced-attitude representation on the two sphere is adopted to explicitly exploit the vehicle's axial symmetry and to decouple yaw from the thrust-vector direction. On this model, we derive an adaptive backstepping controller that achieves almost global trajectory tracking in the presence of unknown constant disturbances, while a control-point transformation mitigates non minimum-phase behavior. The quadrotor is then treated as a thrust vector actuator, and a dynamic-surface-based attitude controller is designed to track the desired thrust-vector, accounting for actuation dynamics and avoiding explicit differentiation of virtual control signals. The complete architecture is evaluated in simulation and validated experimentally in an indoor motion-capture arena. Results demonstrate accurate trajectory tracking, effective disturbance compensation, and confirm the suitability of the QuadRocket as a versatile testbed for thrust-vector-controlled robotic vehicles.

AI.tldr: QuadRocket is a low-cost quadrotor-based rocket prototype that enables thrust-vector control research for launch-vehicle-type systems by modeling the system as a single axisymmetric rigid body and applying adaptive backstepping plus dynamic-surface-based attitude control; validated in simulation and indoor experiments.
AI.motivation: Demonstrate a versatile, low-risk, low-cost testbed for validating advanced thrust-vector control strategies for launch vehicles, addressing challenges such as coupling, non-minimum-phase behavior, and disturbances.
AI.method: Model the coupled quadrotor-rocket as a single axisymmetric rigid body actuated by vectored force along the longitudinal axis; adopt a reduced-attitude representation on the two-sphere to decouple yaw from thrust-vector direction; derive an adaptive backstepping controller with a control-point transformation to mitigate non-minimum-phase behavior; treat the quadrotor as a thrust-vector actuator and design a dynamic-surface-based attitude controller accounting for actuation dynamics without differentiating virtual controls; evaluate in simulation and validate experimentally in an indoor motion-capture arena.
AI.result: The architecture achieves accurate trajectory tracking and effective disturbance compensation in both simulation and experiments, demonstrating the feasibility and usefulness of QuadRocket as a testbed for thrust-vector-controlled robotic vehicles.
AI.conclusion: QuadRocket provides a versatile, low-cost platform for validating thrust-vector control strategies for launch-vehicle-type systems, enabling rigorous testing and development of axisymmetric, vectored-thrust control approaches.

title: CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data
summary: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway--ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

AI.tldr: CALM learns interpretable cross-modal associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from disjoint populations by projecting both modalities into a shared latent space; it aligns class-conditional distributions and preserves group separability, enabling generalization to unseen paired data and providing interpretable pathway-ROI links, demonstrated on autism with immune/metabolic pathways.
AI.motivation: Address the scarcity of paired imaging-genetics data by leveraging large unimodal datasets to study cross-modal brain-structure–genetics interactions in neuropsychiatric disorders.
AI.method: CALM uses linear projections to map brain ROI features and genetic pathway features into a shared latent space. It optimizes simultaneous alignment of class-conditional latent distributions and maximizes group separability. The learned projections yield interpretable associations between pathways and ROIs. Trained on unimodal datasets, CALM generalizes to unseen paired data and is robust to a paired baseline; it was evaluated on autism data, revealing relevant pathways.
AI.result: CALM outperforms state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines on unimodal datasets for cross-modal prediction; demonstrates stability of learned associations relative to a paired baseline; identifies immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions in autism, aligning with literature.
AI.conclusion: CALM enables leveraging large unimodal repositories to study cross-modal brain-phenotype interactions in neuropsychiatric disorders, providing interpretable pathway–ROI associations and generalizable cross-modal mappings across disparate datasets.

title: Consistent Scene Understanding in 3D Gaussian Splatting via Multi-Cue Mask Refinement
summary: Reliable instance-level scene understanding is a fundamental prerequisite for object-level interactions and high-fidelity 3D representations. While current methods often leverage 2D foundation segmentation models to obtain these priors, their 2D-centric design typically yields fragmented masks and inconsistent predictions across different views. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework that produces consistent 2D instance masks to guide the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) feature fields. Our framework consists of three main stages. (1) Multi-Cue Extraction that generates synergistic semantic, geometric, and structural priors from input images. (2) Multi-Cue-Guided Mask Merging process that consolidates fragmented masks using a composite merge score derived from semantic, depth, and edge cues. (3) Cross-View Mask Matching that establishes globally consistent identity assignments across all viewpoints. By transforming viewpoint-specific segments into coherent 3D primitives, our approach enables stable 3D instance segmentation and effective downstream editing tasks. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves cross-view consistency and segmentation stability over existing baselines while maintaining high-fidelity photometric reconstruction.

AI.tldr: A three-stage framework to produce consistent 2D instance masks to guide 3D Gaussian Splatting, achieving cross-view consistent 3D instance segmentation and editable 3D scenes by merging semantic, geometric, and structural cues across views.
AI.motivation: Current 2D foundation-based priors yield fragmented masks and inconsistent predictions across views, hindering stable 3D scene understanding and editing.
AI.method: Stage 1: Multi-Cue Extraction to pull semantic, geometric, and structural priors. Stage 2: Multi-Cue-Guided Mask Merging using a composite score from semantic, depth, and edge cues to unify masks. Stage 3: Cross-View Mask Matching to assign globally consistent identities across viewpoints; integrates with 3D Gaussian Splatting feature fields to produce coherent 3D primitives.
AI.result: Empirical results show improved cross-view consistency and segmentation stability relative to baselines while preserving photometric reconstruction fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline provides stable 3D instance segmentation and facilitates downstream editing by converting view-specific segments into coherent 3D primitives, outperforming 2D-centric baselines in consistency.

title: SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

AI.tldr: SimWorlds introduces a multi-agent, Blender-based pipeline to generate editable, physics-consistent dynamic 4D scenes from text, plus 4DBuildBench; it uses a planner-coder-reviewer workflow, deterministic layered verification, and runtime-state tools, and outperforms prior dynamic Blender baselines.
AI.motivation: Dynamic 4D scene synthesis from natural language is underexplored and hard due to the need to coordinate layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera/lighting, and verifying motion from video.
AI.method: Propose SimWorlds: a Blender-aware framework with a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and runtime-state inspection tools to catch mechanism failures not visible in rendered frames; introduces 4DBuildBench for evaluation of visual fidelity and physical consistency.
AI.result: Empirical results show SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines on the introduced benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The work advances editable, physics-grounded dynamic 3D content generated from text and provides a benchmark to assess fidelity and physical consistency; potential applications include video generation data and embodied AI training.

title: Controllable Sim Agents with Behavior Latents
summary: Realistic traffic simulation requires agents that imitate logged behavior and can also be steered along interpretable axes. Such controllability enables engineers to isolate variables, reproduce specific edge cases, and test autonomous systems without real-world risk. We introduce Controllable Neural Variational Agents (CNeVA), a controllable simulated-agent framework that learns to infer a per-agent Gaussian behavior latent from per-channel discounted returns via a closed-form conjugate variational update, conditioning a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained on a mixed channel-mask curriculum for classifier-free guidance. To tackle scarcity in reward signals, we propose soft eligibility gates that replace hard binary thresholds with smooth exponential decay, preserving the gradient signal for near-threshold agents. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, CNeVA attains competitive realism on the benchmark while exposing per-channel controllability that the higher-ranked imitation models lack. Speed- and acceleration-based steering produces monotone responses without stall-induced reward hacking. Safety controllability is monotone and substantial with the introduction of soft eligibility. We manage to achieve steerable map compliance under a context-residual return measure. Furthermore, our experiment demonstrates that steering metrics must be read alongside physical-plausibility guardrails to avoid reward-hacking confounds.

AI.tldr: Controllable Neural Variational Agents (CNeVA) for realistic, steerable traffic simulation, with per-channel latent behavior and soft eligibility, achieving competitive realism on Waymo while enabling interpretable control and reducing reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Need for traffic simulators that imitate logged behavior while being steerable along interpretable axes to study edge cases, test autonomous systems safely, and isolate variables.
AI.method: Introduce per-agent Gaussian latent inferred from per-channel discounted returns via a closed-form conjugate variational update; condition a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained with a mixed channel-mask curriculum for classifier-free guidance; implement soft eligibility gates to replace hard thresholds, preserving gradients; evaluate on Waymo Open Motion Dataset with context-residual return measures and steerability across channels.
AI.result: CNeVA achieves competitive realism on Waymo; exposes per-channel controllability lacking in higher-ranked imitators; produces monotone speed/acceleration-based steering with no stall-induced reward hacking; soft eligibility provides substantial safety controllability; demonstrates steerable map compliance under context-residual returns; highlights need to read steering metrics alongside physical-plausibility guardrails to avoid reward-hacking confounds.
AI.conclusion: A unified framework combining per-channel controllable latent variables, differentiable guidance, and softened rewards yields realistic, steerable, and safer traffic agents; emphasizes guardrails and multi-metric evaluation to prevent reward hacking.

title: Message Passing Based Two-Timescale Bayesian Learning for Joint Channel and Memory Hardware Impairments Tracking
summary: Hardware impairments in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. This paper employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model the intra-slot memory of the hardware impairments and proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework for joint channel and impairment tracking. Owing to small-scale fading, the wireless channel varies rapidly across slots, whereas hardware impairments drift slowly due to hardware aging and environmental variations. To capture these distinct physical timescales, a fastvarying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are assigned to the sparse channel and the network parameters, respectively. Based on a multi-slot factor graph formulation, a message-passing algorithm is developed. Specifically, the inter-slot messages admit closed-form updates, while the intra-slot factor graph, due to its complex recurrent structure, is partitioned into a channel tracking module and an impairments calibration module. The channel tracking module performs sparse channel estimation via turbo orthogonal approximate message passing (Turbo-OAMP), and the impairments calibration module updates the impairment parameters via a specially designed deep approximate message passing (DAMP) procedure, with the two modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation (EP) until convergence. Simulation results show that the proposed framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions.

AI.tldr: A two-timescale Bayesian deep learning framework with RGRU-based impairment memory and Turbo-OAMP/DAMP message passing on a multi-slot factor graph jointly tracks fast-varying channels and slow-drift hardware impairments, achieving lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators.
AI.motivation: Hardware impairments cause intra-slot memory and inter-element coupling, degrading channel estimation. Existing methods treat channel and impairment separately, failing to exploit distinct physical timescales and memory structures.
AI.method: Introduce a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model intra-slot impairment memory. Use a fast-varying Markov prior for the sparse channel and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior for network parameters. Construct a multi-slot factor graph with two modules: channel tracking via Turbo-OAMP and impairments calibration via DAMP, with expectation propagation (EP) to exchange extrinsic information iteratively.
AI.result: Simulation shows the proposed MP-TTBDL framework achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators across various online impairment scenarios and SNR conditions, demonstrating robustness to hardware-induced memory and slow impairment drifts.
AI.conclusion: Jointly exploiting fast and slow timescales with structured message passing and RGRU-based impairment modeling yields robust, accurate channel estimation in the presence of hardware impairments, outperforming traditional decoupled compensation schemes.

title: Beyond Pixel Diffs: Benchmarking Image Change Captioning for Web UI Visual Regression Testing
summary: Visual regression testing (VRT) is a standard quality assurance step in modern software release pipelines. On every change, it re-renders user interface (UI) screenshots, compares each one against an approved baseline image, and routes any detected difference to a human reviewer who decides whether it is an intended update or an unintended regression. A widely used approach, especially in open-source and continuous-integration pipelines, is pixel-level comparison, which is semantically blind and treats rendering noise and genuine defects identically, producing large volumes of false positives that force developers and testers to spend substantial time and effort manually reviewing flagged differences at every release cycle. Industry tools apply machine learning to VRT, but lack public evaluation. More critically, no dataset or benchmark exists to support natural language descriptions of UI changes, a capability that tells testers what changed in words instead of leaving them to interpret a binary flag or a highlighted region. To address the gap, we propose a new task, Web UI Image Change Captioning (WUICC), which sits at the intersection of VRT and image difference captioning (IDC), and release WUICC-bench, its first dataset and benchmark for the task. We evaluate eleven representative IDC methods, together with two zero-shot general-purpose LLMs. We find that: (1) these methods tend to struggle in the Web UI domain due to its layout diversity, dense text, and fine-grained changes, and (2) yet the trained methods already suppress non-meaningful visual noise far more selectively than the pixel-level comparison VRT relies on, providing a solid foundation for future domain-specific research.

AI.tldr: Introduce WUICC: a new Web UI Image Change Captioning task with WUICC-bench dataset; evaluate IDC methods and LLMs; find domain challenges but potential for noise suppression.
AI.motivation: Need for natural language UI change descriptions to complement pixel-level VRT; lack of dataset/benchmark for text-based UI change captions; improve test automation efficiency.
AI.method: Define the WUICC task, assemble WUICC-bench dataset of Web UI image diffs with captions; evaluate 11 IDC methods and 2 zero-shot LLMs on the task; analyze performance with respect to layout diversity, dense text, and fine-grained changes.
AI.result: IDC methods face challenges in Web UI domain; while trained methods suppress non-meaningful visual noise more selectively than pixel diffs, they still underperform in capturing fine-grained, layout-rich UI changes; LLMs provide baseline zero-shot captions; results indicate clear domain gap.
AI.conclusion: WUICC provides the first dataset and benchmark for Web UI image change captioning; offers a foundation for future domain-specific research and improvement of VRT workflows through natural language descriptions.

title: Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts
summary: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

AI.tldr: WM-SAR outperforms engineering LLM correctors by repairing planning graphs via backward-subgraph amplification, enabling efficient, localized fixes with strong stabilization.
AI.motivation: As planning graphs scale to thousands of steps, failures occur inside; full-graph replay is costly, consumes context, and hurts long-context retrieval; a in-place world-model correction is needed.
AI.method: Compare two corrector families: engineering local-region repair (scan & fix) vs WM-SAR (identify subgraph causing amplification of errors and repair only that causal subgraph; experiment on graph simulations and LLM repairs; test under realistic token budgets).
AI.result: WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors; achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region; provides cleaner repair targets to LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Focusing repair on causal subgraphs is effective for scalable, robust world-model correction in long-horizon planning; reduces token usage and improves stability; suggests direction for future work on automated causal subgraph extraction.

title: Embodied.cpp: A Portable Inference Runtime of Embodied AI Models on Heterogeneous Robots
summary: Embodied AI models now span vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs), but practical deployment remains fragmented across model-specific Python stacks, backend assumptions, and robot-side glue code, especially on heterogeneous edge devices. Existing inference runtimes are designed mainly for request-response serving and therefore do not satisfy the runtime contract of embodied deployment: multi-rate execution inside closed-loop control, latency-first batch-1 inference on heterogeneous hardware, and extensible embodied interfaces beyond fixed token I/O. We present Embodied.cpp, a portable C++ inference runtime for embodied models. Based on an architectural analysis of representative VLA models and WAMs, Embodied.cpp captures a shared execution path and organizes it into five layers: input adapters, sequence builders, backbone execution, head plugins, and deployment adapters. The runtime provides modular multi-rate execution, latency-first fused inference, and extensible operator and I/O support, enabling deployment across heterogeneous devices, robots, and simulators through one backend abstraction. We evaluate Embodied.cpp on two VLA models, HY-VLA and pi0.5, and on a preliminary WAM benchmark using a LingBot-VA Transformer block. The VLA deployments achieve successful closed-loop execution with 100.0% and 91.0% task success rates, respectively. The WAM benchmark reduces block memory from 312.2 MiB to 88.1 MiB. These results show that Embodied.cpp improves deployment efficiency while preserving high accuracy across diverse embodied model architectures.

AI.tldr: A portable C++ runtime, Embodied.cpp, enables multi-rate, latency-focused, extensible deployment of embodied AI models across heterogeneous hardware, achieving high task success on VLA models and significant memory reduction on a WAM benchmark.
AI.motivation: Eliminate fragmentation of embodied AI deployment across model stacks and hardware by offering a unified runtime with a fixed four-layer architecture and backend abstraction.
AI.method: Architectural analysis of representative VLA and WAM models; five-layer design (input adapters, sequence builders, backbone, head plugins, deployment adapters); modular multi-rate execution, latency-first fused inference, extensible operators/I/O; evaluation on HY-VLA, pi0.5, LingBot-VA Transformer block.
AI.result: VLA deployments achieve 100.0% and 91.0% task success; WAM memory footprint reduced from 312.2 MiB to 88.1 MiB.
AI.conclusion: Embodied.cpp demonstrates deployment efficiency and preserved accuracy across diverse embodied architectures, enabling a unified backend for robots and simulators; further validation on more models and real-world tests recommended.

title: Revisiting Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication
summary: Decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) is a popular framework for distributed applications with streaming data. To tackle the communication bottleneck, previous studies have investigated D-OCO with compressed communication and proposed several algorithms that are variants of online gradient descent (OGD). However, for D-OCO with exact communication, the best existing algorithms are variants of follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In this paper, for the first time, we propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. Compared with OGD-type algorithms, our algorithms are more elegant in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. The key insight is that the dual update mechanism of FTRL allows us to make a simple application of the technique for average consensus with communication compression. More specifically, our first algorithm considers the full-information setting, and can match the existing regret bounds. Our second algorithm is designed for the bandit setting, and can significantly improve both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

AI.tldr: Two FTRL-type algorithms for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication: a full-information variant matching existing regret bounds and a bandit variant with significantly improved regret and communication costs.
AI.motivation: Reduce communication bottlenecks in D-OCO while preserving strong theoretical guarantees; leverage FTRL dual updates to enable efficient consensus under compression and extend to bandit feedback.
AI.method: Develop two FTRL-based algorithms that use dual updates to perform average consensus with compressed communication. The full-information variant achieves regret bounds comparable to OGD-based methods; the bandit variant uses gradient estimation to improve regret and reduce communication.
AI.result: The framework yields two algorithms with theoretical guarantees: the full-information version attains regret bounds matching existing OGD-based results under compression; the bandit version achieves notably better regret and lower communication costs than prior bandit/communication-constrained D-OCO methods.
AI.conclusion: FTRL-based approaches offer elegant algorithmic design and analysis for compressed D-OCO, delivering matching performance in full-information settings and improved efficiency in bandit settings compared with OGD-based methods.

title: ReQuest: Rethinking-based Question-Aware Frame Selection for Long-Form Video QA
summary: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced video understanding, yet long-form video QA remains challenging under fixed input token budgets, where uniform sampling can be inefficient for evidence localization. We propose ReQuest , an uncertainty-driven, question-adaptive keyframe selection pipeline that aligns question intent with relevant video content through selective computation. ReQuest integrates (i) a lightweight question-aware selector distilled from MLLM-generated supervision, (ii) Re-thinking Routing that triggers additional inference only when the model is uncertain with a length-adaptive criterion, and (iii) uncertainty-guided adaptive non-maximum suppression that selects temporally diverse frames while adjusting spacing based on question difficulty. As a plug-andplay method, ReQuest improves long-video QA without modifying or fine-tuning the underlying MLLM. Experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate consistent accuracy gains with competitive computational cost, with particularly strong improvements in medium and long video regimes.

AI.tldr: A plug-and-play, uncertainty-driven, question-adaptive keyframe selection framework (ReQuest) for long-form video QA that reduces compute while improving accuracy by selectively routing inference based on question difficulty and uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Long-form video QA under fixed token budgets suffers from inefficient evidence localization with uniform sampling. There is a need to align model attention with question intent and to trigger extra inference only when necessary to save computation.
AI.method: ReQuest comprises three components: (i) a lightweight, question-aware selector learned from MLLM supervision; (ii) Re-thinking Routing that adds inference only when the model shows uncertainty, guided by a length-adaptive criterion; (iii) uncertainty-guided adaptive non-maximum suppression to choose temporally diverse frames with spacing tuned to question difficulty. It is designed as a plug-and-play method that does not require fine-tuning the base MLLM.
AI.result: Empirical results on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench show consistent accuracy gains with competitive computational cost, with particularly strong improvements for medium- and long-duration videos, across multiple datasets.
AI.conclusion: ReQuest provides a practical, uncertainty-aware, question-adaptive framework for long-video QA that improves accuracy without requiring fine-tuning of the underlying MLLM and scales well with video length.

title: Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, Accepted to the 8th epiDAMIK ACM SIGKDD International Workshop on Epidemiology meets Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery (epiDAMIK 2026)
summary: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented small language model uses FCA as a symbolic verification loop to validate and expand knowledge; evaluated on a rare ataxia dataset; seed size impacts evaluation metrics; incidence judgments improve some scores, but positive object-attribute identification remains challenging.
AI.motivation: Ontology construction requires deciding valid objects, attributes, and relations. LMs can propose structures but may be unsupported or inconsistent. The paper proposes a retrieval-augmented SLM with FCA as a verification loop to ensure verified, inspectable knowledge expansion.
AI.method: From seed attributes, FCA derives implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also performs incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, producing accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections for inspection.
AI.result: In a rare ataxia setting built from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs achieve relation F1 of 0.29–0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22–0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower scores reflect the stricter evaluation where missing or extra relations affect several implications.
AI.conclusion: Ablations show incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores, but identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even with fixed candidate objects and attributes.

title: VT-WAM: Visual-Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires policies to react to local deformation, pressure, slip, and friction, yet these cues are temporally sparse and often invisible in visual observations. Existing visual-tactile policies usually feed tactile observations directly into action prediction, but rarely model tactile deformation dynamics during action generation. In this paper, we introduce VT-WAM, a Visual-Tactile World Action Model that jointly learns future visual prediction, tactile deformation prediction, and action prediction within a unified flow matching framework. In particular, VT-WAM introduces (1) Asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention to bridge a first-frame visual anchor with temporal tactile dynamics, and (2) contact-gated Action-Visual-Tactile Attention Guidance (AVTAG) to encourage action queries to rely on tactile evidence during contact phases. Across six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, VT-WAM achieves a 71.67% average success rate, outperforming Fast-WAM by 26.67% and OmniVTLA by 35.84%. Ablations demonstrate that modeling tactile deformation dynamics and guiding contact-phase tactile attention are both important for contact-rich tasks. Project website: https://vt-wam.github.io/.

AI.tldr: VT-WAM presents a unified Visual-Tactile World Action Model that jointly predicts future visuals, tactile deformations, and actions for contact-rich manipulation. It introduces asymmetric MoT attention and contact-gated AVTAG guidance, achieving strong real-world performance across six tasks and showing the importance of tactile dynamics modeling and tactile attention during contact.
AI.motivation: Address the sparsity and invisibility of tactile cues in deformations, pressure, and slip for contact-rich manipulation, and the limitation of prior visual-tactile policies that predict actions without explicitly modeling tactile deformation dynamics.
AI.method: Proposes VT-WAM within a flow-matching framework to jointly forecast future visuals, tactile deformation fields, and actions. Key components include (1) Asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention linking a first-frame visual anchor with temporal tactile dynamics, and (2) contact-gated Action-Visual-Tactile Attention Guidance (AVTAG) that biases action queries to rely on tactile evidence during contact phases.
AI.result: Evaluated on six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, achieving 71.67% average success rate, outperforming Fast-WAM by 26.67% and OmniVTLA by 35.84%. Ablations indicate tactile deformation dynamics modeling and contact-phase tactile attention guidance are both important for performance.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating tactile deformation dynamics and contact-phase tactile attention within a unified visual-tactile world model enhances performance on contact-rich manipulation; the proposed attention mechanisms are effective architectural components for integrating visual and tactile information in action generation.

title: UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing
summary: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

AI.tldr: UniWind combines physics-based priors with state-aware corrections for wind power forecasting to separate meteorological effects from operational state, achieving robust cross-farm generalization.
AI.motivation: Wind power is shaped by future meteorology but also by site-specific states (shutdowns, curtailment). Pure physical models lack cross-farm adaptivity, while data-driven models confound meteorology with operational states. A hybrid method could leverage physics and adapt to latent states.
AI.method: 1) Physical Prior Estimator creates a site-calibrated prior by monotonic warping conditioned on site and a shared physical power curve, plus a physical upper-bound constraint forming a soft power envelope. 2) Latent State Encoder learns operating-state embeddings. 3) State-aware Power Corrector uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert corrections to transform the prior into final forecasts.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 20+ real-world datasets shows high accuracy and robustness, with full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot performance demonstrating generalization across locations and conditions.
AI.conclusion: UniWind effectively integrates physics priors with latent state routing to separate meteorological effects from state-induced deviations, achieving accurate, robust wind power forecasts and strong cross-farm generalization.

title: InterCMDM: Block-Causal Diffusion for Autoregressive Human Interaction Generation
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026, Project website: https://yu1ut.com/InterCMDM-HP/
summary: Text-conditioned human interaction generation must capture both long-range temporal causality within each individual and tightly coupled coordination between partners. Existing interaction diffusion models typically denoise full sequences using bidirectional attention, which obscures causality and hinders streaming and long-horizon generation. Autoregressive alternatives enforce causality but often suffer from temporal drift, leading to coordination degradation and unstable interaction dynamics over time. We propose InterCMDM, a block-causal latent diffusion framework for autoregressive two-person interaction generation. InterCMDM introduces a Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer that maintains separate causal streams for each person while modeling inter-person dependencies via unified dual-stream attention with multi-task attention masks. These masks unify interaction modeling within a single attention mechanism and support diverse coordination behaviors, including simultaneous actions, reactive responses, leader-follower dynamics, and independent motion. By training a single model across these mask configurations as a form of data augmentation, InterCMDM enables controllable interaction generation by simply selecting the desired attention mask at inference time. Finally, a block-wise diffusion objective enables stable latent rollout over long sequences without repeated decode-encode cycles. InterCMDM achieves state-of-the-art performance on InterHuman and Inter-X, improving text-motion alignment, realism, and long-horizon continuity.

AI.tldr: InterCMDM is a block-causal latent diffusion framework for two-person interaction generation that uses a Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer with mask-based attention to control coordination, enabling stable long-horizon, autoregressive generation and achieving state-of-the-art results on InterHuman/Inter-X.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion methods either denoise full sequences with bidirectional attention (hurting causality and streaming) or use autoregressive models that suffer from temporal drift, degrading coordination over time. There is a need for a model that preserves causality, supports long-horizon generation, and offers controllable coordination styles.
AI.method: Introduce InterCMDM: a block-causal latent diffusion pipeline with a Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer. It maintains separate causal streams per person, uses unified dual-stream attention with multi-task masks to model intra- and inter-person dependencies. Masks enable different coordination modes and can be varied at inference. A block-wise diffusion objective stabilizes latent rollout across long sequences. Training uses multiple mask configurations as data augmentation.
AI.result: The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on InterHuman and Inter-X, with improved text-motion alignment, realism, and long-horizon continuity. It enables controllable interaction generation by selecting the desired attention mask at inference time.
AI.conclusion: InterCMDM provides a controllable, stable, long-horizon two-person interaction generator by combining block-causal diffusion with dual-stream attention and mask-based control, addressing causality and drift issues present in prior diffusion and autoregressive approaches.

title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
comment: Equal contribution: Thomas Fontanari and Simone Petruzzi
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

AI.tldr: DLMs implicitly encode a diffusion-timesteplike latent in residual streams; this signal is decodable and steerable, enabling controlled modulation of denoising progress and model confidence, with a structured, interpretable activation-space geometry.
AI.motivation: Clarify how diffusion language models, which are not timestep-conditioned, represent denoising progress and how such representations are used downstream.
AI.method: Probe internal activations across layers to extract a latent timestep signal; demonstrate decodability; steer the model along a low-dimensional subspace tied to the inferred timestep to modulate denoising progress; analyze the geometry of the representation in activation space.
AI.result: A latent diffusion-timestep signal exists in the residual streams of DLMs and is decodable across layers; steering along its low-dimensional subspace systematically alters perceived denoising progress, changing model confidence and entropy; the representation exhibits structured, interpretable geometry in activation space.
AI.conclusion: DLMs internally track denoising progress via a decodable latent signal in residual streams, which can be manipulated to control behavior; this sheds light on how denoising progress is processed in these models and reveals an interpretable geometric structure of the latent representation.

title: SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication
summary: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

AI.tldr: SCAPE enables aggressive sparsification in Adam-family optimizers for LLM pre-training by using first-moment-based sparse masks, distributed mask generation aligned with optimizer sharding, and one-step mask-delay; it preserves model quality at high sparsity and yields substantial speedups (up to 3.26x per step on 1.8B models, up to 43.3% wall-clock time reduction for 500M) in Megatron-LM implementations.
AI.motivation: Communication dominates pre-training cost in data-parallel/sharded LLM training. Existing sparsification or quantization methods either destabilize modern optimizers at high sparsity or are bounded by bit-width and runtime overhead. A stable, high-sparsity approach is needed that integrates with Adam-family optimizers and sharding.
AI.method: SCAPE derives sparsity masks from first-moment statistics rather than raw gradients, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, delays mask usage by one step to overlap communication with computation, and reconstructs second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer to avoid an extra collective. Implemented in Megatron-LM and evaluated on GPT-345M (OpenWebText) and Llama-500M (SlimPajama-6B) using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista; comparisons include dense AdamS/AdamW.
AI.result: SCAPE maintains training stability, validation loss, and downstream accuracy at 90% and 99% sparsity. For Llama-500M, it reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3% with quality comparable to dense optimizers; for Llama-1.8B, it achieves up to 3.26× speedup per step over dense AdamS.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE demonstrates that high sparsity can be achieved without loss of model quality in LLM pre-training by leveraging first-moment statistics and careful orchestration of mask generation and synchronization with optimizer sharding, enabling substantial communication savings with minimal overhead; supports broader adoption in Megatron-LM and similar systems.

title: RTE-FM-Dehazer: Radiative Transfer Equation Inspired Flow Matching for Real-World Image Dehazing
summary: Single-image dehazing aims to recover a clear scene from a hazy image and is generally formulated as an image-to-image translation task; however, it faces two limitations. Its performance depends heavily on the haze-formation priors embedded in the model. Prevailing methods adopt the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), whose assumptions of single scattering and homogeneous media are often violated, leading to residual haze and color drift. Moreover, large-scale real hazy/clear pairs are impractical to collect, and existing synthesis approaches fail to reproduce the full complexity of natural haze. To address these issues, we present RTE-FM-Dehazer, a novel dehazing approach, together with a scalable data pipeline. Unlike the ASM, the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) jointly accounts for both scattering and absorption, naturally accommodating the non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media that characterize real hazy scenes. Motivated by the structural similarity between the RTE diffusion-absorption term and the ODE in flow matching, we introduce a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE, to steer the flow matching trajectory at each step. Next, leveraging modern vision-language models, we build an automated pipeline and release P-HAZE, a dataset of 50000 realistic hazy/clear pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RTE-FM-Dehazer, trained solely on P-HAZE, effectively eliminates artifacts like residual haze and color drift, exhibits strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Proposes RTE-FM-Dehazer for single-image dehazing using Radiative Transfer Equation with a diffusion-absorption regularizer, trained on a scalable P-HAZE dataset of 50k hazy/clear pairs, achieving strong generalization and state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM) in dehazing, including single scattering, homogeneous-media assumptions, residual haze and color drift, and the lack of realistic large-scale hazy/clear datasets.
AI.method: Use the Radiative Transfer Equation to model scattering and absorption (non-homogeneous, multiple scattering). Introduce a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE to guide the flow-matching trajectory. Build an automated pipeline with vision-language models to create P-HAZE, a dataset of 50,000 hazy/clear image pairs. Train solely on P-HAZE.
AI.result: RTE-FM-Dehazer reduces artifacts like residual haze and color drift, demonstrates strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading performance on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The approach shows that incorporating physically grounded RTE modeling with a diffusion-absorption regularizer and scalable data generation yields robust dehazing with superior generalization, supported by the high-quality P-HAZE dataset.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera automates safety testing of autonomous LLM agents with a three-stage pipeline (taxonomy-driven risk discovery, combinatorial executable safety cases, and adaptive sandbox execution with evidence-based verification); evaluates on four agent frameworks, reveals high attack susceptibility, and provides Vera-Bench with 1600 cases; code released.
AI.motivation: Current safety testing targets handcrafted violations and relies on hard-coded rules, which are costly to extend as agents evolve. A scalable, automated framework is needed to test non-deterministic agents against emerging risks.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: (1) literature-driven exploration to build taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool environments; (2) combinatorial generation of executable safety cases across taxonomy dimensions, each with a concrete safety goal, initial state, and deterministic verification predicate based on observable artifacts; (3) adaptive execution in isolated sandboxes with a control agent guiding multi-turn interactions and evidence-grounded verifiers evaluating outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four production frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code) showing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates at 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. Release of Vera-Bench comprising 1600 executable safety cases across 124 risk categories and three execution settings.
AI.conclusion: A modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous, scalable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems; Vera is publicly released (code: Vera).

title: DL-VINS-Factory: A Modular Framework for Learned Visual Front-Ends in Visual-Inertial SLAM
summary: Deep-learning features excel in visual matching, yet their practical value in tightly coupled visual-inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM) remains insufficiently characterized. We present DL-VINS-Factory, a unified framework that integrates learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with either Lucas--Kanade (LK) optical-flow tracking or LightGlue (LG) descriptor matching. All front-ends share a sliding-window Ceres back-end, with optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure, and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization. We benchmark the system across the four datasets covering indoor, unstructured outdoor, aggressive-motion, and visually degraded conditions. Results show that learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM, but are not universally superior to classical tracking. Relative to the corresponding GFTT+LK baseline, ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by $5\%$ in monocular odometry and by $7\%$ in stereo with loop-closure. On NTU-VIRAL, where aggressive aerial motion increases inter-frame viewpoint change, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by $12\%$. In Botanic Garden dataset, optical-flow tracking remains preferable, but learned keypoints still improve over the baseline GFTT, in which SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale camera ATE by $29\%$, while RaCo+LK reduces RGB camera ATE by $38\%$. On SubT-MRS, learned front-ends display varying degree of improvement based on individual cases. With TensorRT acceleration on a Jetson AGX Orin, all valid configurations run in real time between $29$--$47$ FPS in monocular mode and $18$--$33$ FPS in stereo mode for the EuRoC and NTU-VIRAL datasets. AnyLoc further confirms roughly $2$--$7\times$ more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2. The implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/limshoonkit/DL-VINS-Factory-ROS2/.

AI.tldr: Unified DL-VINS-Factory framework combines multiple learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with either LK optical-flow tracking or LightGlue descriptor matching for visual-inertial SLAM, achieving real-time performance on embedded hardware with mixed gains across datasets; open-source implementation available.
AI.motivation: Assess whether learned front-ends can be viable in tightly coupled VI-SLAM, quantify dataset-dependent benefits over classical tracking, and provide a configurable, open-source benchmarking platform.
AI.method: Integrate multiple learned feature extractors with LK or LightGlue within a sliding-window Ceres back-end, optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure, and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization. Evaluate on four datasets (EuRoC, NTU-VIRAL, Botanic Garden, SubT-MRS) with TensorRT acceleration on a Jetson AGX Orin to measure ATE/loop-closure performance and real-time FPS.
AI.result: Learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM but not universally superior to classical tracking. Specific gains: ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC monocular ATE by 5% and stereo ATE by 7% (with loop closure) vs GFTT+LK. On NTU-VIRAL stereo with aggressive motion, ALIKED+LG reduces loop-closed ATE by 12%. Botanic Garden favors optical-flow tracking, but learned keypoints outperform GFTT (SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale ATE by 29%; RaCo+LK reduces RGB ATE by 38%). SubT-MRS results vary by case. Real-time: 29–47 FPS monocular, 18–33 FPS stereo on EuRoC/NTU-VIRAL with Jetson AGX Orin. AnyLoc yields 2–7x more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2. Open-source at provided repository.
AI.conclusion: DL-VINS-Factory demonstrates that learned front-ends can complement classical tracking in VI-SLAM, offering dataset-dependent benefits and practical real-time performance, and provides a flexible, open-source benchmarking framework for further investigation.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP recovers training mixture proportions from released weights by merging base and fine-tuned models to form pseudo-checkpoints, extracting geometric features, and predicting domain proportions; achieves low MAE on BERT and GPT-2, outperforming membership inference.
AI.motivation: Public release of foundation models with undisclosed data recipes creates an access asymmetry. Existing inference methods operate at the sample level and cannot reveal global training composition; there is a need to recover the overall domain mixture used during training.
AI.method: WARP interpolates between base and fine-tuned models via model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the training trajectory. It then extracts geometric features from the resulting weight space footprints and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with average MAE as low as 0.046 (BERT) and 0.104 (GPT-2), outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: WARP enables estimation of global training data distributions from released weights, exposing the training data footprint and enabling comparison across models and releases; it outperforms baselines that rely on sample-level inference.

title: MedStreamBench: A Time-Aware Benchmark for Streaming and Proactive Medical Video Understanding
summary: Existing medical video benchmarks primarily evaluate whether a model produces the correct answer, but rarely assess whether it answers at the right time. In real clinical settings, AI systems must decide not only what to predict, but also when to answer, defer judgment, or proactively raise alerts. This creates a critical gap between benchmark evaluation and deployment requirements. We present MedStreamBench, a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding. MedStreamBench integrates 22 medical datasets and 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings: retrospective, present, future, and proactive. Unlike conventional benchmarks that assume full-video access, MedStreamBench restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows and supports both single-turn and streaming evaluation. We further introduce a proactive monitoring setting that requires models to determine whether and when clinically relevant alerts should be triggered. Beyond answer correctness, MedStreamBench evaluates temporal behavior through responsiveness and post-evidence stability. Experiments on leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models reveal a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Venn2024/MedStreamBench.

AI.tldr: MedStreamBench introduces time-aware medical video understanding by aggregating 22 datasets (5419 QA instances) across retrospective, present, future, and proactive settings, with temporally bounded evidence windows and streaming evaluation to assess when to answer or raise alerts.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks typically evaluate correctness without timing; clinical AI requires determining when to answer, defer, or issue alerts, creating a gap between offline evaluation and deployment.
AI.method: Assembles 22 medical datasets totaling 5419 QA instances across four temporal settings (retrospective, present, future, proactive); supports single-turn and streaming evaluation; introduces a proactive monitoring setting for alert triggering; evaluates responsiveness and post-evidence stability in addition to accuracy.
AI.result: Experiments reveal a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making; performance declines significantly in streaming and proactive settings, indicating the challenge of temporally aware decision-making and the need for such benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: MedStreamBench provides a time-aware evaluation framework for medical video understanding, highlighting the importance of temporal reasoning and alerting in deployment and offering a standardized platform for evaluating models in clinically realistic scenarios.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: A multimodal LLM-based MMIR-TCM framework for tongue diagnosis that integrates Memory-SAM for tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured tongue diagnosis, and a Qwen3-based RAG for evidence-grounded decision support, evaluated on a new large-scale MedTCM dataset using a domain-specific metric TDEU; claims state-of-the-art performance against GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
AI.motivation: Address subjectivity and reproducibility in Tongue Diagnosis (TD) in TCM, and bridge the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning amid a lack of large, standardized multimodal datasets.
AI.method: Three-stage architecture: (1) Memory-SAM for robust tongue extraction (training-free); (2) fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured tongue-diagnosis generation; (3) Qwen3-based RAG for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. Validation on MedTCM, a newly introduced large-scale multimodal dataset; introduction of TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric.
AI.result: MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash, across comprehensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates effective integration of multimodal LLMs with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation to improve diagnostic accuracy in TCM tongue-based tasks, aided by a new dataset (MedTCM) and a domain-specific metric (TDEU).

title: PixGS: Pixel-Space Diffusion for Direct 3D Gaussian Splat Generation
summary: Recent advances in 3D content generation from text or images have achieved impressive results, yet view inconsistency from 2D generators and the scarcity of high-quality 3D data remain significant bottlenecks. Existing solutions typically adapt large-scale pre-trained text-to-image latent diffusion models to generate 3D Gaussian Splats (3DGS). However, these approaches often rely on training complex cascade pipelines that are computationally expensive and scalability-limited. Most critically, the quality of generated 3D assets is inherently constrained by each component capacity and compressed latent space, leading to decoding artifacts and accumulated errors. To address these limitations, we propose PixGS, a single-stage pipeline for direct high-quality 3DGS generation, which leverages recent advances in pixel-space diffusion to bypass lossy latent compression while still benefiting from the vast 2D generative priors. By directly denoising 3D Gaussian attributes at each timestep, our method enables precise, splat-level regularization of both appearance and geometry. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive supervision strategy that incorporates surface normals, depth, and high-frequency structural information, which is often overlooked in prior works. Experiments demonstrate that PixGS outperforms current state-of-the-art methods while maintaining a fast inference speed (1s on a single A100 GPU), offering a robust and efficient alternative to multi-stage generation pipelines.
