AI.tldr: PixGS is a single-stage pixel-space diffusion pipeline for direct high-quality 3D Gaussian Splats generation, enabling fast inference (≈1s on an A100) and outperforming SOTA while avoiding lossy latent compression and multi-stage cascades.
AI.motivation: To overcome view inconsistency in 3D generation and the scarcity/quality limits of high-quality 3D data. Existing latent diffusion methods for 3DGS rely on multi-stage cascades and compressed latent spaces, which introduce artifacts and limit quality. A pixel-space approach aims to leverage 2D priors without lossy compression.
AI.method: A single-stage pipeline (PixGS) that directly denoises 3D Gaussian attributes at each diffusion timestep in pixel space, enabling splat-level regularization of appearance and geometry. It integrates comprehensive supervision signals, including surface normals, depth, and high-frequency structural information, to enhance quality.
AI.result: Empirical results show PixGS outperforms current state-of-the-art methods and maintains fast inference speed (~1s on a single A100 GPU), validating its efficiency and quality as an alternative to multi-stage generation pipelines.
AI.conclusion: PixGS demonstrates that pixel-space diffusion can effectively drive high-quality 3D Gaussian splat generation in a single stage, reducing artifacts, improving geometric and appearance fidelity, and providing a scalable, efficient solution leveraging 2D priors without latent bottlenecks.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: Proposes a heavy-tailed PoE-based energy-based model framework for merging single-task models into a multi-task model, addressing Gaussian residual assumptions and demonstrating improved empirical performance.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solutions and implicit Gaussian residuals, which poorly capture the observed heavy-tailed residuals between merged and task-specific models, limiting statistical guidance for update directions.
AI.method: Formulates merging as probabilistic inference in a product-of-experts (PoE) framework where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM); shows that several existing methods are special cases under Gaussian residuals; introduces a heavy-tailed PoE design using Cauchy experts to capture heavy-tailed residuals with a provably convergent inference procedure.
AI.result: Empirical experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines; code provided in GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: Heavy-tailed PoE design better matches observed residual behavior, providing a robust, convergent framework for model merging that improves multi-task performance over prior Gaussian-based approaches.

title: The Turning Point of 3D Plant Phenotyping: 3D Foundation Models Enable Minute-to-Second Cross-Crop Reconstruction and Beyond
summary: 3D plant phenotyping is notoriously known to be procedure-complicated and of low throughput due to the extensive multi-view imaging, the fragile 3D reconstruction pipeline, and the additional cost from reconstructed geometry to phenotypic extraction. These limitations are further amplified in low-cost data acquisition, where smartphone videos or sparsely sampled multi-view images provide limited view overlap and self-occlusion. In this work, we show that the conventional 3D plant phenotyping pipeline could be streamlined and significantly accelerated with 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs), and particularly, present one of the first cross-crop 3D phenotyping frameworks powered by 3DFMs. The framework replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, enables few-view reconstruction through iterative view synthesis and refinement, and converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. We further construct a cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition, diverse plant morphologies, and manual annotations for segmentation and phenotypic evaluation. Experiments across 26 plant sequences show that 3D Foundation Models reduce the average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. These results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

AI.tldr: A cross-crop 3D plant phenotyping framework that leverages 3D foundation models to enable fast, low-cost reconstruction and accurate phenotyping across crops.
AI.motivation: Current 3D plant phenotyping suffers from procedure complexity and low throughput due to multi-view imaging, fragile geometry pipelines, and limited view overlap in smartphone data.
AI.method: Replace COLMAP sparse initialization with 3D foundation-model-based feed-forward geometric recovery; apply geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction; enable few-view reconstruction via iterative view synthesis and refinement; perform 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation to extract measurable phenotypes; construct cross-crop smartphone-based dataset.
AI.result: Reconstruction time drops from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while preserving reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy across 26 plant sequences.
AI.conclusion: 3D foundation models enable high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping from low-cost imagery, providing fast reconstruction, scale recovery, and quantitative phenotypic measurements across crops.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Introduces Pre-Flight, an open 300-question aviation benchmark for domain-specific reasoning, evaluated with Inspect; reveals current LLMs lag behind expert aviation reliability, prompting domain-focused evaluation for safe deployment.
AI.motivation: Aviation is high-stakes and regulated; generic benchmarks fail to assess safe, correct reasoning on aviation knowledge, necessitating a domain-specific evaluation framework.
AI.method: Construct 300 MCQs from international standards and ground operations; questions authored/reviewed by aviation practitioners; evaluate diverse models using the Inspect framework with accuracy-based scoring; maintain a rolling leaderboard; release dataset and harness.
AI.result: Strongest model (2026) achieves 82.7% accuracy, rising from ~75% in early 2025; informal expert baseline ~95%; notable performance gap remains, indicating limited current reliable deployment for aviation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is essential for responsible AI deployment in aviation; dataset and leaderboard are released and integrated with inspect_evals to support ongoing benchmarking and improvement.

title: Robust Image Processing Techniques for Construction Environment Monitoring Using Underwater Robots
summary: This paper proposes a robust image processing framework for underwater robot-based construction environment monitoring, targeting complex degradations observed in real marine environments. Unlike conventional approaches that mainly consider absorption and backscattering, real underwater imagery is strongly affected by depth-dependent forward scattering blur and particle-induced degradations such as marine snow. To address this, we introduce a staged processing pipeline that sequentially models background degradation via depth-aware forward scattering and foreground degradation using realistic marine snow patterns extracted from real images. The resulting synthetic data are used to retrain an existing Joint-ID network without modifying its architecture, enabling an isolated evaluation of dataset realism. In addition, a lightweight post-processing scheme is applied to enhance contrast and structural clarity. Experiments on real underwater datasets collected in Korean coastal environments demonstrate consistent improvements in visual quality and UIQM scores. The results indicate that explicitly modeling forward scattering and realistic particle effects effectively reduces the synthetic-to-real gap and improves practical applicability in real-world underwater robotic operations.

AI.tldr: A depth- and particle-aware underwater image processing pipeline that uses staged degradation modeling and synthetic data to retrain a Joint-ID network, yielding improved visual quality and reduced synthetic-to-real gap on Korean coastal underwater datasets.
AI.motivation: Underwater images suffer from depth-dependent forward scattering and marine snow, beyond simple absorption/backscattering. Realistic degradation modeling and dataset realism are needed to enhance restoration and tracking networks.
AI.method: A staged pipeline: model background degradation via depth-aware forward scattering; model foreground degradation via marine snow patterns from real images; synthesize data; retrain existing Joint-ID network without changing its architecture; apply lightweight post-processing to boost contrast; evaluate on real datasets.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in visual quality and UIQM scores on real underwater datasets; reduced synthetic-to-real gap; better practical applicability for underwater robotic operations.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling forward scattering and realistic particle effects improves restoration effectiveness and dataset realism; this approach enhances transferability of models to real-world underwater tasks.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: A beginner-friendly, proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the sampling perspective, linking classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers; layered pedagogy with full proofs of core definitions, error-friendly estimates under simplifying assumptions, and proof-roadmaps for advanced theorems; aimed at early-stage graduate students with probability background.
AI.motivation: Fill a pedagogical gap by offering a rigorous, accessible pathway into diffusion models from sampling, connecting traditional probabilistic sampling theory to contemporary diffusion techniques, with emphasis on error analysis and inference-time control.
AI.method: A three-layered exposition: (1) core definitions and identities with complete proofs, (2) representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and (3) research-level theorems presented with a roadmap to their proofs; traces a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, including error analysis and inference-time control.
AI.result: The notes provide a structured, proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from a sampling viewpoint, offering a coherent learning trajectory for beginners in probability without requiring prior exposure to SDEs or diffusion literature; emphasis on definitions, estimates, and theorem roadmaps rather than empirical results.
AI.conclusion: The work lays a solid foundational framework for diffusion models from a sampling perspective, equipping readers to tackle stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, and diffusion-model inference in future study.

title: ProSAC-CT: Progressive Spectral-Anatomical Co-Guided Multi-Stage Diffusion Model for Low-Dose CT Denoising
summary: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces stronger quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation, which can obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Diffusion models are promising for LDCT denoising by progressively recovering normal-dose CT (NDCT) images from degraded LDCT inputs, but existing methods often suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling. We propose ProSAC-CT, a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for image-domain LDCT denoising. ProSAC-CT integrates an anatomical-prior-guided conditioning (APGC) module, a residual frequency-domain decoupling stage (RFDDS), and a time-step-decoupling denoising decoder (TD3). APGC extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance, RFDDS enhances frequency-aware representations, and TD3 assigns them to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery. Experiments on four LDCT degradation benchmarks show that ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 further indicates that ProSAC-CT retains task-relevant anatomical information, supporting its practical use for low-dose CT denoising.

AI.tldr: ProSAC-CT introduces a three-module, multi-stage diffusion framework for LDCT denoising that jointly leverages anatomical prior guidance, spectral-frequency decoupling, and stage-specific denoising to improve fidelity and preserve boundary-sensitive details, with downstream task-information retention.
AI.motivation: LDCT reduces radiation but suffers from high quantum noise, streak artifacts, and degraded textures that obscure boundaries and low-contrast structures. Existing diffusion-based denoising lacks robust anatomical guidance and frequency-aware recovery, and often uses a uniform reverse diffusion process.
AI.method: A progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model (ProSAC-CT) comprising: (1) APGC: anatomical-prior-guided conditioning to extract LDCT-derived structural guidance; (2) RFDDS: residual frequency-domain decoupling to enhance frequency-aware representations; (3) TD3: time-step-decoupling denoising decoder to assign guidance to different reverse-diffusion stages for stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery.
AI.result: On four LDCT degradation benchmarks, ProSAC-CT yields higher image fidelity, SSIM, perceptual quality, and information preservation compared with representative methods, while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details; downstream Mayo-2020 classification shows retention of task-relevant anatomical information.
AI.conclusion: ProSAC-CT provides improved LDCT denoising with better anatomical fidelity and task-relevant information preservation, supporting practical deployment for LDCT imaging.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: Fault trees are analyzed through Halpern–Pearl actual causality to classify notions of causality in terms of fault-tree structure; minimal cut sets are shown to correspond to actual causes.
AI.motivation: Enhance failure diagnostics by answering 'why did it go wrong?' using formal causality theory applied to fault trees.
AI.method: Represent fault-tree graphs with AND/OR structures and basic events, map to Halpern–Pearl definitions of actual causality, classify each causality notion by graph and logical configurations, and derive how minimal cut sets instantiate actual causes.
AI.result: Provide a complete classification of the different notions of actual causality for fault trees based on their graph and logical structure; establish how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees can be used for principled failure diagnostics by leveraging actual-causality classification; the minimal cut-set framework naturally embeds into Halpern–Pearl causal analysis.

title: NeoMap: Training-free Novel-View Synthesis from Single Images and Videos
comment: ECCV 2026. Jinxi and Tianyi are co-first authors. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/vLAR-group/NeoMap
summary: We study the challenging problem of novel view video synthesis from single images or monocular videos. Existing methods, which operate under the assumption that pre-trained video models lack native novel view synthesis capability and enforce view alignment via camera conditioning, task-specific fine-tuning, or stepwise hard denoising guidance, often suffer from artifacts and compromised global scene consistency. In this paper, we introduce NeoMap, a novel training-free framework designed to locate high-fidelity, view-consistent novel view solutions from general pre-trained video models. The key to our approach is the core insight that promising novel view solutions are inherently encoded within the natural video data manifold learned by pre-trained models, and the core challenge is simply to locate this optimal solution. We solve this via our core mechanism: convergent manifold alternating projection iterations that optimize the initial noise. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoMap significantly outperforms all existing methods across 3 standard novel view synthesis benchmarks, including the challenging Tanks-and-Temples, LLFF and DAVIS datasets, achieving state-of-the-art generation fidelity and top-tier view consistency.

AI.tldr: NeoMap is a training-free framework that locates high-fidelity, view-consistent novel-view video solutions within pre-trained video models using convergent manifold alternating projection to optimize the initial noise.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches rely on task-specific fine-tuning or conditioning to achieve novel-view synthesis, often at the expense of global scene consistency; there is latent novel-view capability within general pre-trained video models that can be retrieved without training.
AI.method: Introduce convergent manifold alternating projection iterations that optimize the initial noise, effectively locating the optimal novel-view solution within the model's learned video data manifold without additional training.
AI.result: NeoMap significantly outperforms prior methods on standard benchmarks (Tanks-and-Temples, LLFF, DAVIS), achieving state-of-the-art generation fidelity and strong view consistency.
AI.conclusion: Promising novel-view solutions are encoded in the natural video data manifolds of pre-trained models and can be efficiently retrieved via training-free manifold projection, enabling robust, training-free novel-view video synthesis.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM introduces an additive frequency-shift mechanism for weight initialization in physics-informed extreme learning machines to alleviate spectral bias, achieving robust high-frequency PDE solutions with a single linear solve. Two variants exist: FS-PIELM-L (independent neuron frequencies) and FS-PIELM-G (grouped frequencies); theoretical analysis shows bounded frequency variance approaching unity, unlike quadratic growth in scaling-based methods. Empirically, the linear variant attains best accuracy in 6 of 7 PDE problems (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) across regular and complex geometries, with 1–5 orders of magnitude improvements over prior PIELM methods. Code will be released publicly.
AI.motivation: Address spectral bias in neural networks when solving PDEs with high-frequency content, which hampers learning of oscillatory solutions; physics-informed learning methods like PIELM suffer from variance amplification when attempting to encode high frequencies. A lightweight, efficient strategy that preserves ELM's single linear solve while enabling high-frequency accuracy is needed.
AI.method:
Replace scaling-based frequency augmentation with an additive shift in the Gaussian weight distribution's mean, keeping variance fixed at 1. This translates the prior distribution to target higher frequencies without variance amplification. Two variants:
- FS-PIELM-L: each neuron gets an independent target frequency magnitude.
- FS-PIELM-G: neurons are grouped to share frequency magnitudes for robustness. Theoretical analysis shows frequency variance remains bounded and tends to unity as target frequency grows, avoiding the quadratic growth of traditional scaling. The framework retains ELM’s efficiency (one linear solve) and extends to multiple PDE types and geometries.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across seven benchmark problems spanning Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein–Gordon, heat, and advection–diffusion equations on regular and complex geometries shows the FS-PIELM linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases. Reported improvements range from 1 to nearly 5 orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants, indicating substantial gains in high-frequency solution accuracy.
AI.conclusion: FS-PIELM effectively mitigates spectral bias in physics-informed ELMs by using an additive frequency-shift initialization that preserves variance and remains computationally efficient (single linear solve). The approach generalizes across PDE types and geometries, with strong empirical performance, particularly for the linear variant. Code and data are slated for public release.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: Closed-loop CLAP framework for domain adapter post-training that converts business data into structured samples, diagnostics, and release records to decide adapter suitability for target chains; shows modest average gains across five anonymized manufacturing batches with some regressions; RAG improves factual extraction but adds latency; advocates an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop over single offline scores.
AI.motivation: Domain agents face noisy data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and release risk. A fully integrated loop is proposed to continuously validate and gate adapters using data-driven, decision-focused evaluation.
AI.method: Convert business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. Apply data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide adapter suitability for the target application chain. Evaluate with five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches using QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT; compare performance with and without RAG under a 3B backbone and 100 replay cases.
AI.result: Modest average gains: overall score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280; hallucination and wrong facts decrease. However only 3 of 5 batches improve; some batches regress; GRPO reveals high KL risks. Application-chain replay shows RAG is necessary for factual extraction; with 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency.
AI.conclusion: Integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop is more effective than relying on training completion or a single offline score for domain-agent post-training.

title: Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift
summary: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

AI.tldr: Deterministic, auditable memory consolidation for long-running agents that updates a separate semantic knowledge layer without altering the agent’s certified identity, enabling provenance-backed knowledge growth.
AI.motivation: Resolve the conflict between memory consolidation and identity-bounded governance (auditability, cryptographic identity) in regulated deployments by decoupling knowledge updates from the identity manifest.
AI.method: Define a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem that produces a separable semantic knowledge layer from episodic memory. The agent’s identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the certified identity. Provide a formal agent representation, prove identity invariance via a lemma on the manifest’s hash-input set, design a deterministic aggregation algorithm that outputs auditable database rows with confidence and provenance, and validate using synthetic experiments showing per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean ~79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts vs a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline across 10 seeds.
AI.result: A formal account of decoupled knowledge updates for autonomic agents; a structural lemma ensuring identity invariance; an auditable deterministic aggregation algorithm; and synthetic evaluation demonstrating field-level correctness, byte-identical identity across consolidation passes, and substantial reductions in wasted planning attempts.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge updates accumulate as queryable facts in a separate semantic layer while the agent’s certified identity remains byte-equal; demonstrates feasibility of a knowledge-update discipline for regulated autonomic agents with an embodied service agent as case study.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: CROF: a composite offline checkpoint score combining Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) with structural regularizers to predict and improve closed-loop performance of a latent world model (RSSM) on LunarLander v3; enables efficient model-based policy learning and zero-shot MPC.
AI.motivation: Validation-time metrics (e.g., validation loss, multi-step RMSE) can continue to improve even after closed-loop performance collapses; hence reliable diagnostics are needed to select checkpoints that won't jeopardize real-world control.
AI.method: Train an RSSM world model; define Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) and three additional structural regularizers; combine them into a single CROF score for offline checkpoint selection. Use per-checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. Evaluate 40 metrics against the oracle. Select by CROF. Train a model-based A2C policy with the CROF-selected model and compare to a model-free A2C baseline; also test zero-shot CEM-MPC.
AI.result: ROF emerges as the strongest single predictor of closed-loop quality among the evaluated diagnostics. The CROF score, combining ROF with the three structural regularizers, yields a practical offline checkpoint selector. A CROF-selected world model enables a model-based A2C policy that outperforms the model-free baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions; the same model also supports a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.conclusion: Structural validation-time diagnostics can reliably predict downstream closed-loop performance and guide offline checkpoint selection for world-model learning; CROF provides an effective, single-number criterion for choosing checkpoints that improve sample efficiency and enable strong episodic control.

title: ProCal: Inference-Time Proposal Calibration for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to localize and classify objects beyond the fixed set of categories seen dur ing training. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods improve localization and classification for unseen categories by leveraging a frozen VLM as a detector backbone. However, VLM classification score lacks recognizing position and scale of the object in an image. We observe that pretrained VLMs en able to classify foreground and background regions. According to this observation, we propose a simple inference-time Pro posal Calibration (ProCal) that improves localization quality of the classification score. ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining two scores: localization-aware foreground score and background-aware suppression score. Localization-aware foreground score captures whether a proposal contains an object area. Background-aware suppression score measures the extent to which the proposal resembles background. We analyze that ProCal suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals. Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr +2.5 on OV-LVIS. The analyses show that proposal-level localization-aware reranking effects to mitigate ranking miscalibration for novel objects.

AI.tldr: ProCal is an inference-time proposal calibration method that improves localization in open-vocabulary object detection by fusing a localization-aware foreground score with a background suppression score to re-rank proposals, boosting novel-object localization (e.g., +AP_r 2.5 on OV-LVIS with CLIPSelf ViT-L/14).
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary DET relies on frozen VLMs that often lack localization cues. While VLMs can distinguish foreground from background, their classification scores do not reflect object position/scale. A simple, inference-time calibration can leverage region-level signals to improve localization and reduce false activations.
AI.method: Compute two proposal-level scores for each region: a localization-aware foreground score (object-area likelihood) and a background-aware suppression score (background-like residual). Combine these into a proposal prior to re-ranking proposals at inference time, thereby improving localization quality of VLM-based detectors. Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14.
AI.result: ProCal yields an improvement of AP_r by +2.5 on OV-LVIS. Analyses show the method suppresses false novel activations on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals, indicating mitigation of ranking miscalibration for novel objects.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time proposal-level calibration effectively improves localization and ranking for open-vocabulary detectors, reducing background miscalibration and boosting detection of unseen categories.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: STEER reveals multilingual safety gaps in LLMs by attacking refusals through code-switching; high attack success across models and transfer to GPT-4o-mini, underscoring need for broader multilingual alignment and OOD abstention.
AI.motivation: Safety training for LLMs is predominantly English-centric, risking poor generalization to low-resource languages and code-mixed inputs. This creates epistemic gaps where models refuse or allow harmful content inconsistently across languages. Assessing cross-lingual robustness and developing multilingual defenses are essential.
AI.method: Introduces STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that pinpoints tokens contributing to refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusals while preserving harmful intent. Evaluated on six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER outperforms random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). Transfered prompts also work on GPT-4o-mini without target-model access.
AI.result: STEER achieves up to 93.0% attack success on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench across six 8B models, surpassing baselines. The attacks transfer to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% success, indicating the weakness is not architecture-specific.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment trained mainly on English cannot be assumed to generalize to multilingual inputs. To improve multilingual safety, expand alignment coverage and implement explicit detection/abstention for out-of-distribution multilingual inputs.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: Finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states using observed source–successor pairs, yielding a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ and an antisymmetric circulation W_Δ^ρ; affine-covariant, stable, and capable of separating deterministic recurrent motion from infinitesimal geometry; linear-Gaussian calibration; experiments show architecture-dependent transport patterns and metric-dependent coherent displacement.
AI.motivation: Representations of dynamical systems are trajectories, yet geometry is often inferred from static snapshots. This work develops a finite-lag transport framework for recurrent hidden states to capture how mass moves across time steps, enabling decomposition into spread and coherent displacement and highlighting deterministic lagged motion not seen by infinitesimal carré-du-champ geometry.
AI.method: Estimate a conditional transport law Q_Δ(dy|x) from data using a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From Q_Δ derive a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ that decomposes into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ that encodes directed lagged flow. Prove affine covariance with metric dependence, establish estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and prove a finite-lag separation result. Provide a linear-Gaussian closed form calibrated in terms of update A_Δ, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Validate via controlled experiments and performance-matched repeat-copy networks.
AI.result: Obtained an exact decomposition of the transport tensor G_Δ into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric circulation W_Δ^ρ summarizing directed lagged flow. Demonstrated affine covariance and estimator stability; established a finite-lag separation indicating detection of deterministic recurrent motion beyond infinitesimal carré-du-champ geometry. Derived a linear-Gaussian closed form for calibration with A_Δ, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Experiments confirm the framework’s predictions about decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability; in networks with matched performances, the framework reveals architecture-dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, with the coherent displacement fraction showing metric and resolution dependence.
AI.conclusion: The finite-lag transport framework provides a principled, metric-consistent tool to analyze recurrent representations, revealing deterministic lagged motion not captured by infinitesimal geometry and exposing architecture-dependent transport patterns. The results offer interpretable summaries (G_Δ and W_Δ^ρ) and stable estimators, with a tractable linear-Gaussian calibration enabling practical application.

title: JointHOI: Jointly Generating Contact Maps Enhances Hand Object Interaction Generation
summary: Text driven hand object interaction (HOI) generation is gaining attention for immersive applications and robotics, yet producing physically plausible interactions remains challenging. Even when individual motions appear natural, small contact errors can cause conspicuous artifacts such as floating and interpenetration. Prior methods mitigate these issues using explicit contact cues or implicit grasp priors, but typically rely on multi stage pipelines and fail to model temporally evolving contact. We present JointHOI, a single stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand object motion and dynamic, distance based contact maps from text. By treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality, joint generation enables the model to learn contact motion coupling during training. At inference, contact guided sampling enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion implied geometry, improving temporal stability and reducing penetration and floating. Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC demonstrate consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.

AI.tldr: JointHOI introduces a single-stage diffusion model that jointly generates 3D hand-object motions and dynamic, distance-based contact maps from text, using contact as an auxiliary modality to improve temporal consistency and physical plausibility, reducing floating and interpenetration.
AI.motivation: Text-driven hand-object interaction (HOI) generation often yields artifacts like floating, interpenetration, and instability due to imperfect contact modeling. Existing methods rely on multi-stage pipelines and struggle to capture temporally evolving contact.
AI.method: A single-stage diffusion framework that jointly learns 3D hand–object motion and dynamic contact maps (distance-based). Contact is treated as an auxiliary modality, enabling motion–contact coupling during training. During inference, contact-guided sampling enforces consistency between contact maps and motion geometry to enhance temporal stability and reduce penetration/floating.
AI.result: On GRAB and ARCTIC datasets, JointHOI shows consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility compared with prior methods.
AI.conclusion: JointHOI demonstrates that jointly modeling motion and contact as auxiliary signals within a diffusion framework yields more plausible, temporally stable HOI generation from text, mitigating common artifacts without requiring multi-stage pipelines.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS introduces a frequency-aware, multi-resolution NAS framework for Camouflaged Object Detection, jointly optimizing cell operations and downsampling paths while employing an RGB frequency dual-stream (learnable wavelet) to boost camouflaged object cues; achieves state-of-the-art on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: COD is challenged by weak edge cues and boundary ambiguity; traditional COD relies on hand-designed architectures and heuristics. A systematic, learnable architecture search tailored to COD, plus frequency-domain integration, could better capture camouflaged cues.
AI.method: A hierarchical NAS search space that optimizes both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths. It uses an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture with a learnable wavelet transform to complement the RGB spatial stream, integrating frequency cues with deep features for COD.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON. Code released at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: NAS is effective for COD when combined with frequency-domain processing; CamoNAS demonstrates that automated search plus frequency-aware design yields robust, high-performance COD models across diverse datasets.

title: Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS). By leveraging distinct interpolation and extrapolation components, MAS provides a flexible and efficient framework for modeling CCIFs. Theoretically, MAS's interpolation provides strong fitting accuracy, while its extrapolation supports robust generalization, reducing the irreducible approximation gaps of MNNs. Extensive experiments show that MAS achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: MAS uses Monotone Alternating Splines to model CCIFs in temporal point processes, addressing limitations of monotone neural nets and achieving better interpolation and extrapolation, with superior results on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: Current CCIF parameterizations rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs) which impose convexity, saturation, and CCIF-constraint limitations, limiting representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics; a flexible, efficient alternative is needed.
AI.method: Introduce Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS) that separate interpolation (for accurate fitting) and extrapolation (for generalization) components to model CCIFs; theoretical analysis on fitting accuracy and generalization; empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world TPP datasets.
AI.result: MAS achieves superior performance compared to baselines (likely MNNs) on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing improved fit and generalization and reduced approximation gaps.
AI.conclusion: MAS provides a flexible, efficient CCIF modeling framework for TPPs that overcomes MNN bottlenecks, with strong theoretical properties and empirical evidence of improved performance.

title: LLM-Empowered Multimodal Fusion Framework for Autonomous Driving: Semantic Enhancement and Channel-Adaptive Design
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by 2026 IEEE 37th International Symposium on Personal, Indoor and Mobile Radio Communications (PIMRC)
summary: Vision-radar fusion is central to robust autonomous driving, combining dense visual semantics with precise range and velocity measurements from radar. However, real-world fusion quality is fundamentally challenged by dynamically varying input quality, stemming from occlusion, adverse weather, and channel noise. To address this, we re-frame the problem from static data fusion to channel-aware semantic reasoning and propose a Large Language Model-centric Semantic-layer Channel-aware Integrated Perception (LM-SCIP) framework. It places a Large Language Model (LLM) as a central reasoning core to fuse a local visual stream with a quality-varying external radar stream used to cover perception-blind spots. Concretely, LM-SCIP couples a hierarchical radar-vision encoder with a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) that maps link indicators into a "Channel Prompt" to dynamically gate external radar features. A parameter-efficient, LoRA-tuned LLM, in conjunction with a heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE), then arbitrates between local visual cues and the channel-conditioned radar context. Finally, a decoupled multi-task decoder outputs localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction. Experiments on nuScenes and VIRAT validate our approach. On nuScenes, under a controlled toggle of radar input, LM-SCIP reduces localization RMSE by 40.0% versus a vision-only baseline. On VIRAT, the model attains a 0.214m localization RMSE and 0.179m minFDE (k=1). These results reveal that the proposed LM-SCIP enables a robust vision-dominant fallback at low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.

AI.tldr: A vision–radar fusion framework (LM-SCIP) uses an LLM-driven, channel-aware gating mechanism to fuse a quality-varying radar stream with a local vision stream, improving localization and trajectory tasks, especially under low radar quality.
AI.motivation: Real-world perception halves rely on varying input quality from occlusion, weather, and noise. A static fusion is brittle; a channel-aware semantic reasoning approach can adaptively integrate radar data when visual cues are weak.
AI.method: A hierarchical radar–vision encoder augmented by a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) that translates radar/link indicators into a Channel Prompt for gating radar features. An LLM (LoRA-tuned) coupled with a heterogeneous MoE arbitrates between local visual cues and channel-conditioned radar context. A decoupled multi-task decoder outputs localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction.
AI.result: On nuScenes, with radar input toggled, LM-SCIP reduces localization RMSE by 40% vs vision-only. On VIRAT, achieves 0.214 m localization RMSE and 0.179 m minFDE (k=1). Demonstrates robust fallback at low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.
AI.conclusion: LLM-centric, channel-aware fusion enables robust, adaptive perception that leverages radar when visual cues degrade, while preserving vision-dominant performance when radar quality is high.

title: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
summary: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

AI.tldr: SkillCoach: a self-evolving rubric framework that derives skill-grounded process rubrics to evaluate and improve agentic skill-use, across skill selection, following, composition, and reflection, while keeping an external verifier separate.
AI.motivation: Overlapping skills in realistic skill repositories cause unreliable agent actions; final success is too coarse for evaluation and training; need process-level signals.
AI.method: Derives rubrics from real rollouts; evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection; keeps external verifier as a separate outcome signal; rubrics evolve and supervise training trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments show evolved rubrics improve evaluation quality, reveal failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.
AI.conclusion: Rubrics enable better evaluation and supervision of agentic skill-use by separating process quality from outcome, guiding training data selection and improving robustness to overlapping skills.

title: Role-Aware Neural Convex Divergence Heads for Asymmetric Representation Learning
summary: Many representation learning problems involve directed relations, such as lexical entailment, sentence entailment, ontology hierarchy, and citation links. Standard Euclidean, cosine, and Mahalanobis heads are symmetric, while generic neural scorers can model directionality but provide limited geometric structure. This paper proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning. The head applies source- and target-role projections before evaluating an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, yielding a nonnegative structured score in the role-projected space. We characterize its projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature. Experiments on lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed graph benchmarks compare symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads, and the proposed role-aware variant. Across ten random seeds on the main semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while preserving zero observed negative divergence rate. The results also identify a boundary case: on large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy. Overall, the proposed head is best understood as a structured and interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter.

AI.tldr: Proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning, enabling directional distances via source/target role projections and an input-convex neural Bregman divergence; improves directional accuracy across lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed-graph benchmarks with zero negative divergence rate, but shows a boundary case in large fixed-feature citation predictions where symmetric/hyperbolic baselines remain strong.
AI.motivation: Directional relationships (e.g., entailment, hierarchies, citations) are common in data but standard similarity measures are symmetric; a structured, interpretable asymmetric distance is desirable for such tasks.
AI.method: Apply source- and target-role projections, then evaluate an input-convex neural Bregman divergence to obtain a nonnegative score in the role-projected space; analyze projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation over lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed graph benchmarks shows role-aware projections improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads across ten random seeds; zero observed negative divergence rate is preserved; a boundary case on large fixed-feature citation prediction shows symmetric or hyperbolic baselines can outperform in ranking metrics.
AI.conclusion: The role-aware projection head serves as a structured, interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks with directional relations, offering improved directional discrimination while preserving nonnegativity; its benefits are context-dependent and may be limited in certain large-feature settings.

title: SpaceEra++: A Unified Framework Towards 3D Spatial Reasoning in Video
summary: Visual-spatial understanding, defined as the ability to infer object relationships and scene layouts from visual inputs, is fundamental to downstream tasks such as robotic navigation and embodied interaction. However, pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) remain constrained by spatial uncertainty stemming from inherently 2D observations and by the scarcity of data for 3D spatial understanding. To address these limitations, we proposed a novel framework, SpaceEra, in the NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight paper. Although it achieved significant performance gains, we further observed that its effectiveness is hindered by insufficient input from scanning videos and weak reasoning constraints. To tackle these newly emerged challenges, we extend the original framework into a comprehensive system, termed SpaceEra++, which spans data construction, model design, training optimization, and prompting inference. Specifically, to alleviate input insufficiency, we introduce ScenePick, a frame sampling strategy that balances spatial coverage with object semantics to produce compact yet comprehensive scene representations. In addition, to enhance spatial reasoning, we develop SpaceAlign, which enforces pairwise object constraints by jointly exploiting absolute coordinates and relative spatial relations, thereby aligning optimization with spatial accuracy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, while ablation studies validate both the individual and joint contributions of each component, and further analyses provide guidance for future research.

AI.tldr: SpaceEra++ extends SpaceEra to tackle input insufficiency and weak spatial reasoning in vision-language models by (1) ScenePick for balanced frame sampling and (2) SpaceAlign for joint absolute and relational spatial constraints, yielding consistent gains across benchmarks and providing ablations and guidance for future work.
AI.motivation: Address spatial uncertainty from 2D observations and limited 3D spatial data in pre-trained VLMs; enable robust spatial understanding for downstream tasks like robotic navigation and embodied interaction.
AI.method: Extend SpaceEra with ScenePick, a frame-sampling strategy that balances spatial coverage with object semantics; SpaceAlign, a constraint mechanism that jointly uses absolute coordinates and relative spatial relations to align optimization with spatial accuracy; end-to-end training, data construction, model design, training optimization, and prompting inference.
AI.result: Experiments show consistent improvements over strong baselines across multiple benchmarks; ablations validate the individual and joint contributions of ScenePick and SpaceAlign; analyses offer insight for future research directions.
AI.conclusion: SpaceEra++ provides a comprehensive framework to improve 3D spatial understanding in vision-language models by addressing input insufficiency and spatial reasoning constraints, demonstrated through significant gains and thorough analyses.

title: Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

AI.tldr: AUF: acceptance-focused loss for block-draft autoregressive models improves mean emitted block length and token accuracy without changing inference; uses a masked block-drafter and truncates CE support to the first failure, yielding consistent gains across backbones (Qwen3-8B variants) and Domino; key findings reveal interactions with decay weighting and prefix conditioning.
AI.motivation: Address misalignment between full-block cross-entropy supervision and inference-time behavior of block drafters, where only the longest accepted prefix is committed and subsequent tokens are discarded after the first rejection.
AI.method: Apply teacher-forced-inspired supervision as a motivation; implement AUF as a single, detached adjustment to cross-entropy support that concentrates loss on the accepted prefix. Use a mask-only block drafter lacking an input-side gold-prefix channel; approximate prefix-sensitive supervision by keeping cross-entropy support only through the first predicted failure. No auxiliary objectives, verifier rollouts, or inference changes. Evaluate on Qwen3-8B backbones (DFlash and Domino two-branch head) across six benchmarks, measuring the average emitted length τ.
AI.result: AUF increases the average emitted length τ: from 2.40 to 2.61 for the DFlash drafter across six benchmarks, and from 2.56 to 2.68 for Domino's two-branch head. Gains are observed on every benchmark. Two findings: (1) decay-only baseline achieves higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse; (2) for DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.
AI.conclusion: AUF provides a minimal, loss-only modification that aligns supervision with accepted-prefix inference in block-draft autoregressive models, yielding consistent gains in emitted-length across multiple backbones without altering inference. It highlights nuanced interactions between prefix-conditioned supervision and position-decay weighting.

title: Denser $\neq$ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training
summary: Continual post-training enables foundation models to acquire new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Recent work suggests that on-policy learning can mitigate forgetting, with on-policy self-distillation emerging as a particularly attractive approach. In this work, we revisit this optimistic view through self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO). Our experiments show that SDPO can accelerate in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well aligned, but it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can even collapse, whereas on-policy reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO adapt more conservatively and better preserve prior capabilities. Further analyses reveal that denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and can amplify high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher--student loop. These findings suggest that on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL.

AI.tldr: Self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO) can speed up in-domain specialization but tends to forget or collapse in continual post-training, especially out-of-distribution; on-policy RL methods like GRPO preserve prior capabilities more reliably. Dense self-distillation increases drift in parameter and response spaces and can amplify formatting artifacts, indicating that on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. SDPO is useful only when teacher signals are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether on-policy self-distillation can mitigate forgetting in continual post-training of foundation models, and understand the conditions under which it helps or harms performance, including robustness to distribution shifts and dynamics of teacher–student interactions.
AI.method: Empirical study comparing SDPO with on-policy reinforcement learning (GRPO) in continual post-training; analyze effects of distillation density on parameter and response space drift; assess generalization to out-of-distribution data and potential collapse; examine the impact of high-frequency formatting artifacts; provide code repository for reproducibility.
AI.result: SDPO accelerates in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and aligned but underperforms on out-of-distribution data; in continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can collapse, while GRPO adapts more conservatively and preserves prior capabilities; denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter and response spaces and amplifies high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher–student loop; on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning; SDPO can be beneficial when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable but should not be treated as a default stabilizer.
AI.conclusion: On-policy data alone is insufficient for robust continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization under stable targets but risks instability and forgetting; a conservative, stability-focused approach (e.g., GRPO-like methods) better preserves prior capabilities. The work cautions against default reliance on dense self-distillation and suggests using it selectively or in combination with mechanisms that constrain drift.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE introduces prompt-layer complexity metrics for LLM-integrated apps, alongside code-layer metrics. It generates 52 metrics from 25 taxonomic dimensions and identifies 10 surviving metrics (7 novel, 3 conventional). The best metrics capture structural breadth (e.g., LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates) in the prompt layer, and maintain significance even when code size is controlled. Two top metrics predict maintenance effort in held-out repositories, demonstrating generalizability beyond training data.
AI.motivation: Existing complexity metrics focus on code and ignore the prompt layer, which is central to LLM-integrated applications. There is a need for metrics that quantify prompt-layer complexity and its impact on maintenance to better understand and manage software evolution.
AI.method: Propose Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that treats each prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Build 25 dimensions from published taxonomies, yielding 52 candidate metrics. Empirically evaluate on 118 components from 18 open-source repos, using version-history maintenance activity as a proxy for complexity. Discard metrics whose significance vanishes after controlling for code size. Compare with conventional metrics (RFC, Halstead).
AI.result: Ten metrics survive the filtering step; seven are novel and measure structural breadth in the prompt layer (e.g., LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates). Among conventional metrics, RFC shows breadth-like behavior, while Halstead N and V are largely artifacts of size. The top-performing metrics outperform the conventional ones. Prompt-layer metrics remain significant when a strong code-level metric is included as a covariate. Validation on 20 components across six held-out repos shows the two best metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, indicating generalizability beyond training data.
AI.conclusion: HECATE demonstrates that prompt-layer complexity is a distinct dimension with robust, generalizable metrics that can predict maintenance effort, complementing code-level metrics and enabling more comprehensive evaluation of LLM-integrated applications.

title: Set Diffusion: Interpolating Token Orderings Between Autoregression and Diffusion for Fast and Flexible Decoding
comment: ICML 2026. We provide the code at https://github.com/kuleshov-group/setdlms
