We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

AI.tldr: A small, difficult, rubric-based clinical benchmark with five clinician-authored tasks across four specialties; evaluates three frontier LLMs using weighted MECE criteria; finds critical criteria are rarely met despite higher overall rubric pass rates; demonstrates a scalable pipeline for future large-scale benchmarking.
AI.motivation: To move beyond saturated multiple-choice benchmarks and assess open-ended clinical reasoning using clinician-authored, weighted, MECE rubrics; to establish a defensible, scalable evaluation pipeline for comparing LLMs on clinically relevant tasks.
AI.method: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios across anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics. Each task is paired with an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25–62 criteria per task; total 184 criteria) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. Evaluate three frontier models (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro). Use mean rubric pass rates and analyze weight-5 (critical) versus weight-1 criteria. Include three LLM autoraters who label met/not-met; assess concordance on a subset of 552 criteria.
AI.result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. Critical criteria (weight-5) pass rates: 32.4–41.7%; low-stakes (weight-1) criteria pass: 80–90%. 56 of 108 critical criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Autoraters reproducibly labeled met/not-met with 92.8–94.7% agreement on 552 graded criteria.
AI.conclusion: The study presents a scalable, defensible pipeline and five-task benchmark as a foundation for future large-scale evaluation of open-ended clinical reasoning in LLMs, highlighting misalignment between high-stakes criteria and overall rubric success.

title: Probabilistic Low-Voltage Peak Load Forecasting with Time Series Foundation Models Evaluated on Application-Oriented Metrics
comment: A poster abstract of this publication will be available at the 15th DACH+ Conference on Energy Informatics (2026 in Linz, Austria)
summary: Low-voltage load forecasting is an important component in current and future energy systems with a high degree of electrification and decentralized generation. However, current forecasting methods require significant manual effort, often lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and they are often not adequately evaluated in terms of grid requirements. In the present study, we provide an extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts of 200 real-world low-voltage feeders with a focus on the rapidly evolving time series foundation models. Our study compares Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to six baseline models and demonstrates superior performance, in particular for Chronos-2. An ablation study, in which weather covariates are omitted, shows that time series foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty, despite the importance of weather information. A novel application-oriented metric links the model's forecasting capabilities in peak prediction to the trade-off in grid asset planning and operation between cost reduction and minimizing the risk of failure.

AI.tldr: Time-series foundation models (Chronos-2, Chronos-Bolt, TabPFN-TS) outperform baselines on short-term net load forecasts for 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, with Chronos-2 most effective; weather covariates improve accuracy, but models still adapt to higher uncertainty when omitted; a new application-oriented metric links forecast quality to grid planning decisions.
AI.motivation: Enhance short-term low-voltage load forecasting by leveraging time-series foundation models, addressing uncertainty estimation, peak prediction, and alignment with grid requirements.
AI.method: Extensive empirical evaluation on 200 real-world low-voltage feeders comparing Chronos-2, Chronos-Bolt, and TabPFN-TS against six baselines; ablation study removing weather covariates; introduction of an application-oriented metric connecting peak forecasts to grid asset planning/operation trade-offs.
AI.result: Chronos-2 delivers superior forecasting performance relative to baselines; time-series foundation models display robustness to omitted weather covariates by adapting to increased uncertainty; Chronos-2 particularly strong in short-term net-load forecasting and peak prediction under evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Time-series foundation models are promising for low-voltage net-load forecasting and can offer actionable insights for grid planning and operation, especially when paired with metrics that capture peak-related costs and risk.

title: Open-Weather Robust 3D Detection via Dual-Critic Diffusion Alignment
summary: Robust 3D object detection under adverse weather remains a critical hurdle for autonomous driving. Despite progress with LiDAR-4D radar fusion, most methods are constrained by a closed-world assumption, implicitly requiring training and test weather to align in both type and severity. This premise fails in practice: the open-ended nature of weather, and even variations within a single type like rain, cause dramatically different LiDAR degradation patterns, leading to significant performance drops in unseen conditions. To address this, we present Dual-Critic Guided Diffusion Alignment (DCDA), a weather-agnostic framework that learns to recover degraded LiDAR features toward a clean manifold. Rather than modeling specific weather types, DCDA employs a 4D radar-conditioned diffusion process to progressively refine features, guided by two complementary critics. (i) A detection-guided critic, anchored by a pre-trained clean-weather model, ensures that the refined features retain object-level discriminability and localization accuracy. (ii) A weather adversarial critic enforces holistic distributional consistency with clean-weather representations. By aligning features through semantic and distributional constraints rather than explicit weather modeling, DCDA generalizes effectively to unseen weather types and severities without requiring paired data or weather labels. We further introduce a structured open-weather benchmark with held-out type-severity combinations and extensive experiments verify DCDA's advantages.

AI.tldr: DCDA introduces a weather-agnostic 3D object detection framework that uses a 4D radar-conditioned diffusion process to refine LiDAR features toward a clean-manifold, guided by two critics (detection-guided and weather adversarial) to achieve robust performance under unseen weather without paired data or weather labels; and provides a structured open-weather benchmark.
AI.motivation: Open-world weather variability causes drastic LiDAR degradation and performance drops in current methods that assume matched weather during training and testing. There is a need for weather-agnostic representations that generalize to unseen weather types and severities without requiring weather annotations or paired data.
AI.method: DCDA employs a 4D radar-conditioned diffusion process to progressively refine degraded LiDAR features toward a clean manifold. It uses two complementary critics: (i) a detection-guided critic anchored by a pre-trained clean-weather model to preserve object-level discriminability and localization, and (ii) a weather adversarial critic to enforce distributional consistency with clean-weather representations. This framework avoids explicit weather modeling and weather labels, enabling open-world generalization. A structured open-weather benchmark with held-out type-severity combinations is proposed for evaluation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments indicate that DCDA achieves robustness to unseen weather conditions, outperforming baselines that rely on weather-specific modeling. The framework effectively aligns degraded features to the clean manifold under diverse, unseen weather patterns, validated on the proposed open-weather benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Feature alignment via semantic (detection) and distributional (weather) constraints, rather than explicit weather modeling, enables generalization to unseen weather without paired data or weather labels. The introduced benchmark supports rigorous evaluation of open-weather robustness.

title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
summary: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

AI.tldr: We present UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that uses token-level log probabilities to quantify uncertainty, applies phase-aware thresholding to trigger retrieval-based verification, and achieves superior performance on SRDD benchmarks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality.
AI.motivation: To mitigate hallucination propagation in autonomous multi-agent software development by treating intermediate agent outputs as potentially uncertain rather than always reliable.
AI.method: Integrates a lightweight token-level uncertainty estimation mechanism; phase-aware threshold calibration; selective retrieval-based verification; phase-aware triggers to involve verification only when uncertainty is high; evaluation on the SRDD benchmark; ablation studies and communication analyses.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over existing single-agent and multi-agent frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics; uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware interactions improve reliability and final software quality by combining uncertainty estimation with selective verification, addressing early-stage error propagation in multi-agent software development.

title: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency
summary: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

AI.tldr: Controlled benchmarking across CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet shows EfficientNet family often provides the best accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, with gains that are selective and hardware-dependent; pretrained vs scratch training significantly affects accuracy.
AI.motivation: Assess whether claimed efficiency gains of lightweight CNNs generalize under a unified evaluation protocol across standard datasets and hardware.
AI.method: Benchmark nine lightweight CNN packages on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet using a shared downstream protocol. Measure top-1, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, and batch-size-1 latency on NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA memory, and construct Pareto frontiers. Include comparisons between pretrained and scratch-trained models and report on latency differences across hardware.
AI.result: EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest top-1 on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%); RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 remains near the best across all three datasets while using ~79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficentNetV2-S. B0 appears on every accuracy/resource Pareto frontier, making it a consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC and is the fastest on both hardware settings; SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters but weaker accuracy. Latency rankings vary strongly between L4 and CPU, indicating GMACs do not directly predict real-world latency. Under random initialization, MobileNetV4-Conv-S leads over MobileNetV4-Conv-S; pretrained networks show substantial early advantages (EfficientNet-B0 is ~3.29–17.54 points behind its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training) despite longer training times.
AI.conclusion: Newer CNN designs yield selective gains rather than universal improvements. Model-choice should be guided by the Pareto frontier across datasets and hardware, with attention to training regime (pretrained vs scratch) and the limited role of GMACs in predicting latency.

title: Understanding Geometric Representations in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers via Subspace Intervention
summary: We introduce a controlled subspace intervention framework to investigate how self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) encode dense geometric information. While linear probing is widely used to assess geometric representations, it treats features as a black box, failing to disentangle the underlying topology. To address this issue, we decompose the weights of converged linear probes to isolate the low-rank subspaces containing explicit geometric signals using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Our perspective yields three key insights: (1) Pre-training objectives determine how features are encoded. DINOv2 aligns spatial features for efficient linear extraction, while Masked Autoencoders (MAE) tend to disperse these signals, requiring a broader spatial context. (2) Explicit geometric representations are highly compressible, suggesting dense predictive heads could potentially be constrained to low-rank subspaces with minimal performance loss. (3) The layer-wise task affinity suggests that geometric precision peaks at intermediate layers before yielding to semantic abstraction in the final layers. By connecting internal encoding mechanics with downstream performance, these findings provide a basis for effective feature selection and lightweight decoder design. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zhou-Weichen/Geosubprobe.

AI.tldr: Subspace analysis of self-supervised ViTs using SVD on linear probes reveals geometry encoding shaped by pretraining, its compressibility, and layer-wise precision trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Linear probes treat features as a black box and do not reveal the topological structure of geometric information. A subspace decomposition exposes explicit low-rank geometric signals, enabling better understanding and more efficient decoding.
AI.method: Decompose converged linear probe weights with Singular Value Decomposition to isolate low-rank subspaces containing explicit geometric signals. Compare pretraining objectives (DINOv2 vs MAE) and analyze layer-wise task affinity, signal compressibility, and implications for feature selection and lightweight decoder design. Provide code.
AI.result: Three insights: (1) Pretraining objectives determine encoding; DINOv2 aligns spatial features for efficient linear extraction, while MAE disperses these signals, requiring broader spatial context. (2) Explicit geometric representations are highly compressible, suggesting dense predictive heads could be constrained to low-rank subspaces with minimal performance loss. (3) Layer-wise task affinity shows geometric precision peaks at intermediate layers before yielding to semantic abstraction in the final layers.
AI.conclusion: The framework connects internal encoding mechanics to downstream performance, informing feature selection and lightweight decoder design. Code is available at the provided GitHub URL.

title: Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks
summary: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

AI.tldr: Guard Rail Validation (GRV): a standardizable runtime framework to intercept/validate AI-driven decisions in autonomous telecom networks (A-Nets L4-5) using multi-dimensional criticality scoring and graduated validation, with cross-agent conflict resolution and regulatory logging.
AI.motivation: No standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual AI inferences before they trigger live network changes, creating risk of erroneous autonomous decisions in autonomous networks; need for safe, compliant operation.
AI.method: Propose GRV architecture and algorithms that evaluate decisions across weighted dimensions (action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, temporal patterns) to compute a criticality level. Apply graduated validation: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. Include cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). Provide architecture, procedures, deployment model (O-RAN), and threat-coverage evaluation against known AI/ML attacks in telecoms.
AI.result: Architectural design, algorithmic procedures, deployment model, and threat-coverage evaluation against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications; demonstrates feasibility and outlines regulatory conformance.
AI.conclusion: GRV provides a standardizable runtime validation framework enabling safe, compliant AI-driven decisions in autonomous networks, reducing risk of erroneous actions and supporting regulatory compliance.

title: Liquid Latent State Dynamics for Interpretable Turbofan Degradation Modeling
summary: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated by point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process. We study liquid neural networks as latent dynamics models for aircraft engine health monitoring on the C-MAPSS benchmark. The proposed model encodes a history window into a latent state, evolves that state with a liquid transition model, and decodes future sensor observations. To separate health evolution from operating-condition variation, the latent state is factorized into degradation and condition components. Remaining useful life, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses supervise the degradation component, while condition prediction and decorrelation losses discourage operating-condition leakage. Across FD001--FD004, the full disentangled model improves overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 for a GRU baseline to 0.2266, with the largest gains on the multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state also forms a clearer temporal degradation axis, reaching an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct remaining-useful-life regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, indicating that the proposed representation is currently more effective as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor. These results suggest that liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling.

AI.tldr: Disentangled liquid latent dynamics improve multi-condition sensor forecasting and yield interpretable degradation axis; RUL regression remains stronger for GRU; potential as a health-state world model.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between predictive maintenance forecasting and interpretable health-state modeling by separating health degradation from operating-condition variation using a liquid latent dynamics model.
AI.method: Encode a history window into a latent state, evolve with a liquid transition model, and decode future sensor observations. Factorize latent state into degradation and condition components. Train with supervision on remaining useful life (RUL), monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses for degradation; condition prediction and decorrelation losses prevent operating-condition leakage. Evaluate on C-MAPSS FD001--FD004.
AI.result: Sensor forecasting RMSE improves from 0.2438 (GRU baseline) to 0.2266; largest gains on multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. Learned degradation state forms a clearer degradation axis with average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct RUL regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, suggesting the proposed representation is better as an interpretable degradation-world model than as a calibrated lifetime regressor.
AI.conclusion: Liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling, offering a coherent degradation axis while maintaining forecasting performance.

title: Training-free Controllable Human Motion Generation under Heterogeneous Constraints
summary: Training-free controllable motion generation has attracted growing interest for enabling flexible constraint enforcement without constraint-specific training. However, existing training-free methods require constraints to be continuous objective-based with differentiable losses, while many real-world requirements are criterion-based and provide only discontinuous, sparse, or even black-box feedback. In this paper, we propose Motion-Inference-as-Control (MIC), the first training-free motion generation framework that handles both continuous objective-based and criterion-based motion constraints under a shared mechanism. The key idea is to cast diffusion-based motion generation as a stochastic control problem. This perspective not only provides principled and practically effective step-wise control laws that support criterion-based constraints without requiring differentiability and naturally accommodate objective-based constraints as a special case, but also motivates a control-oriented constraint coordination mechanism that adaptively balances and reconciles motion constraints during generation. Experiments across diverse constraint settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

AI.tldr: Introduces MIC, a training-free framework for controllable motion generation that unifies continuous objective-based and criterion-based constraints via diffusion-as-stochastic-control, with adaptive constraint coordination.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free methods rely on differentiable, continuous losses, while real-world constraints are often discrete, sparse, or black-box. A unified, training-free approach is needed to handle diverse constraint types.
AI.method: Reformulate diffusion-based motion generation as a stochastic control problem, deriving principled step-wise control laws that work for both constraint types and enabling a control-oriented constraint coordination mechanism to balance constraints during generation.
AI.result: Empirical results across diverse constraint settings demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in enforcing both objective-based and criterion-based constraints without training."
AI.conclusion: MIC provides a unified, training-free paradigm for controllable motion generation, accommodating non-differentiable constraints and enabling adaptive constraint coordination, with potential for broad application and future refinement.

title: Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

AI.tldr: OPSD fails on long-CoT due to reference-driven memorization. A two-step fix isolates transferable, question-conditioned supervision via a reference-only teacher and PMI-based distillation, yielding consistent gains on four long-CoT models across two datasets while preserving epistemic behavior.
AI.motivation: Long-CoT reasoning is hindered by on-policy self-distillation's tendency to memorize reference shortcuts; need a supervision signal that emphasizes transferable, question-conditioned reasoning.
AI.method: Decompose the teacher's signal into a reference-induced component and a question-conditioned component. Build a reference-only teacher (same model with reference, no question) to extract the non-transferable part; subtract this to obtain the residual. Transform the residual into a PMI-based target distribution for direct distillation, filtering out the reference shortcut.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four long-CoT models across two datasets shows consistent improvements over the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the model's epistemic behavior during training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-step approach effectively mitigates reference-induced shortcuts in OPSD, enhancing long-CoT reasoning through PMI-based distillation of the transferable supervision.

title: Fast and Accurate Anomaly Detection in Time Series
summary: Anomaly detection is a critical and evolving field in Machine Learning, with applications targeting different domains such as cybersecurity, finance, healthcare, manufacturing and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. Traditionally, anomaly detection algorithms have been designed using both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. The fundamental challenge in real-world anomaly detection scenarios is related to the inherent class imbalance (anomalies are typically rare) and, for supervised methods, to the scarcity of labelled anomalous data. Indeed, labelling is both expensive and time-consuming. Conversely unsupervised methods do not require labelling, but may suffer from high false positive rates when deployed in safety-critical applications. In this work we introduce a novel unsupervised algorithm for anomaly detection in time series based on the Haar discrete wavelet and a suitably designed $t$-test. We establish the theoretical foundation of the proposed $t$-test and, through extensive experimentation across 343 datasets, demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A novel unsupervised time-series anomaly detector based on Haar discrete wavelet transform combined with a designed t-test; supported by theoretical grounding; evaluated on 343 datasets, and outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised baselines.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection is critical across domains but challenged by extreme class imbalance and lack of labelled anomalies; unsupervised methods avoid labeling yet can yield high false positives. A principled, unsupervised detector for time series is needed.
AI.method: Apply Haar discrete wavelet transform to time-series data and compute a specially designed t-test on the wavelet coefficients to detect anomalies, with theoretical justification for the test. The approach is unsupervised and evaluated against state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.result: Empirical results show the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised anomaly detection methods across 343 datasets.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces a theory-grounded, unsupervised time-series anomaly detector using Haar wavelets and a tailored t-test, achieving broad empirical gains and potential applicability in safety-critical, label-scarce settings.

title: Mirror Illusion Art
comment: CVPR 2026 Highlight, also got an Efficient CVPR award
summary: Mirror Illusion Art is a novel reflection-conditioned 3D illusion where one object yields two target appearances (front and mirror). The task is formulated as inverse design from two target 2D images (front and mirror) to a printable 3D object with geometry and texture. Prior topology-driven and shadow-based approaches demand substantial manual effort, optimize shape only, and often yield non-smooth or incomplete geometry. To address these challenges, we propose AutoMIA, an automated Mirror Illusion Art design pipeline that jointly optimizes shape and color. To stabilize optimization and suppress artifacts, four mechanisms are introduced: (1) projection-alignment component (PAC) selection to reduce surface noise, (2) position-weighted adaptive (PWA) suppression for background noise, (3) internal voxel preservation (IVP) to prevent internal fractures, and (4) shape-color decoupled (SCD) optimization that balance shape and color optimization. AutoMIA generate diverse smooth Mirror Illusion artworks successfully both in the digital and physical world, with only around 76s design time and 2.6 GB memory on average using a single RTX 3090, advancing inverse graphics and computational design. Our code is available at https://github.com/zxp555/AutoMIA.

AI.tldr: AutoMIA automates joint geometry-and-texture optimization for Mirror Illusion Art from two target views (front and mirror) to a printable 3D object, using four stabilization mechanisms to produce smooth results quickly on a RTX 3090.
AI.motivation: Replace manual, topology-driven, and shadow-based approaches that require substantial effort and often yield incomplete or noisy geometry by delivering an automated, end-to-end inverse design pipeline for 3D printing with color.
AI.method: A four-mechanism pipeline: (1) projection-alignment component (PAC) to reduce surface noise, (2) position-weighted adaptive (PWA) suppression to mitigate background noise, (3) internal voxel preservation (IVP) to prevent internal fractures, and (4) shape-color decoupled (SCD) optimization to balance shape and color updates, enabling joint optimization of geometry and texture for two target 2D views (front and mirror). The system yields diverse smooth 3D outputs with a printable geometry+texture specification, validated in both digital and physical fabrication and implemented in an end-to-end pipeline using a single high-end GPU (RTX 3090).
AI.result: AutoMIA successfully generates diverse, smooth Mirror Illusion artworks in both digital renders and physical prints. It achieves design times around 76 seconds and consumes about 2.6 GB memory on average on an RTX 3090, demonstrating practical viability and contributing to inverse graphics and computational design. The codebase is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The work advances automated inverse-design for 3D prints with color by introducing four stabilization mechanisms within a joint shape-and-color optimization framework, enabling rapid production of mirror-illusion artworks and broadening the applicability of inverse graphics in creative design.

title: Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support
summary: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design informed by mental health practitioners. Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. This work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

AI.tldr: Copewell proposes a multi-agent swarm architecture for mental wellness that integrates multi-source assessment, emotion-based routing via Russell's Circumplex Model, and dual-mode interventions, grounded in privacy-first design and ethical oversight, with early practitioner engagement and beta testing.
AI.motivation: Global mental health burden with nearly one billion affected and persistent treatment gaps in LMICs due to workforce shortages, cost, and stigma. Current AI wellness tools rely on single-mode interfaces that are often ineffective and do not adapt to users’ dynamic emotional states.
AI.method: Design of the Copewell architecture featuring (1) a multi-source assessment framework combining self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell’s Circumplex Model to route users to specialized AI agents; (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols; plus a privacy-first architecture, an Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design with mental health practitioners.
AI.result: Conceptual framework with three innovations and initial practitioner feedback; beta deployment planned and early design decisions informed, but no quantitative empirical outcomes reported yet.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception, contributing to responsible AI discourse by embedding privacy, ethics, and stakeholder participation in the design.

title: A Memory Efficient Unified Algorithm for Online Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems
summary: Motivated by the challenge of stabilizing a general unknown linear dynamical system (LDS) from observations, we study the natural prerequisite of online prediction. Our goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics rather than the full hidden -- state dimension. We focus on the practically central regime of systems with low instability complexity -- eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, together with non-semisimple modes-potentially embedded in an otherwise stable real spectrum of much higher dimension; we write $k$ for this count. This regime is the primary setting in which stabilization is plausible: we show that many systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. Thus, prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when the instability complexity is small. Within this regime, we introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of $\widetilde{O}(k)$. Finally, we prove a lower bound showing that $k$ is a valid complexity measure: any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters. Experiments corroborate our theory: on a high-dimensional system, our predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget.

AI.tldr: Sublinear-regret online prediction for unknown linear dynamical systems (LDS) with parameter complexity adapting to intrinsic instability (k), enabling near-optimal memory use; k filters are necessary for any filter-based predictor; lower bound and experiments support efficacy in a regime where instability complexity is small.
AI.motivation: Stabilizing a general unknown LDS from observations requires online prediction with memory that scales with the system's intrinsic instability rather than the full state dimension.
AI.method: Introduce a unified online algorithm that handles all LDS (including non-diagonalizable and complex/exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of ~O~(k). Define instability complexity k as the count of unstable modes outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, including potential embedded non-semisimple modes.
AI.result: Achieves sublinear regret with memory footprint ~O~(k); proves a lower bound showing any filter-based predictor needs at least k filters; experimental results on a high-dimensional system show the proposed predictor outperforms prior methods at the same parameter budget.
AI.conclusion: Instability complexity k is the appropriate measure of problem difficulty for online stabilization; stabilization is feasible (and prediction meaningful) only when k is small; the proposed algorithm attains near-optimal parameter efficiency and has strong empirical support.

title: UnderOneFacade: Worldwide Facade Semantic Segmentation Benchmark Dataset
summary: Globally consistent semantic digital twins require centimeter-accurate and geographically transferable 3D facade segmentation. However, progress in facade parsing is limited by the lack of large-scale, standardized benchmarks for evaluating cross-domain generalization. Existing datasets are geographically narrow, semantically inconsistent, or insufficiently precise. We introduce UnderOneFacade, the largest cross-country and cross-continent 3D facade benchmark to date, comprising centimeter-accurate point clouds with hierarchical, harmonized, and architecturally grounded semantic labels totaling 2.7 billion annotated points. Through a systematic evaluation of representative point-, graph- and transformer-based architectures, we show that current methods struggle to recognize fine-grained architectural elements and degrade significantly across geographic domains, with the best models achieving only up to 33 IoU on the fine-grained LoFG3 benchmark. By combining geometric precision with standardized semantics at unprecedented scale, UnderOneFacade establishes a rigorous benchmark for developing robust and transferable 3D segmentation models. The dataset, evaluation scripts, and pretrained models will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: Introduces UnderOneFacade, the largest cross-country 3D facade benchmark with centimeter-accurate point clouds and 2.7B labeled points; reveals limited cross-domain generalization of current methods and provides data, scripts, and pretrained models.
AI.motivation: Globally consistent semantic digital twins require centimeter-accurate, geographically transferable 3D facade segmentation; existing benchmarks are geographically narrow, inconsistent, or imprecise.
AI.method: Construct UnderOneFacade with centimeter-accurate point clouds, hierarchical, harmonized semantic labels grounded in architectural elements, totaling 2.7B points; systematically evaluate representative point-, graph-, and transformer-based architectures across geographic domains.
AI.result: Current methods struggle to recognize fine-grained architectural elements and degrade across geographic domains; best models achieve up to 33 IoU on the fine-grained LoFG3 benchmark.
AI.conclusion: UnderOneFacade provides a rigorous, scalable benchmark for developing robust and transferable 3D segmentation models; dataset, evaluation scripts, and pretrained models will be released upon publication.

title: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

AI.tldr: Proposes a bounded memory contract for long-horizon LLM agents, isolating the effect of memory layers by not retroactively appending transcripts, and validates it in Slay the Spire 2 with a reproducible testbed.
AI.motivation: Isolate and quantify how explicit memory modules shape long-horizon decision making by avoiding conflation from accumulated cross-decisions and enabling component-wise ablations.
AI.method: Define a per-decision memory contract where each decision is formed from a fresh user message assembled via typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. Implement in Slay the Spire 2 (a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game). Evaluate memory-layer ablations (no-store baseline; add a skill layer). Compare against public baselines and backbones; report results as directional tests. Release a reproducible dataset of 298 trajectories, with condition tags, memory snapshots, prompts, and analysis scripts.
AI.result: In fixed-A0 ablation, enabling the triggered strategic skills increases wins from 3/10 (no-store) to 6/10 (with skill layer). Context suggests the difference is directional but not statistically decisive (Fisher exact p ≈ 0.37) due to small sample size. Cross-backbone probes and public accumulating-context baselines are provided as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable.
AI.conclusion: A bounded memory contract allows isolating the impact of explicit memory layers on long-horizon decision quality. The results indicate memory components can meaningfully affect strategic choices in complex tasks, though larger samples are needed for statistical significance. The study also delivers a reusable methodology and reproducible testbed for studying memory design in LLM agents.

title: Beyond the Performance Illusion: Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization for Spatially Correlated Domains
summary: Performance evaluation in AI systems commonly assumes that random dataset splits produce independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) subsets. We show that this assumption often breaks down in spatiotemporally correlated domains such as aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging, leading to two systematic failures: data leakage, where correlated samples span training and validation splits and inflate performance estimates, and hidden stratification, where errors on minority subpopulations are obscured by aggregate metrics. To address these issues, we propose a unified evaluation and training framework for spatially correlated data. We introduce Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that reduce spatiotemporal leakage while preserving meaningful class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training that stabilizes optimization under these stricter splits. Across multiple benchmarks, this combination yields consistently improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes that remain hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.

AI.tldr: A framework to prevent spatiotemporal leakage and hidden stratification in i.i.d.-assumption-violating domains.
AI.motivation: In spatiotemporally correlated domains (e.g., aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, medical imaging), the common i.i.d. assumption for data splits fails, causing data leakage and hidden stratification that bias performance and masking subpopulation errors.
AI.method: Propose Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP) to create validation splits with reduced spatiotemporal leakage while preserving class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust optimization for stability under these splits.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks, the approach yields improved generalization and reliability (better calibration) and reveals failure modes hidden by conventional random splits.
AI.conclusion: A unified evaluation and training framework for spatially correlated data that mitigates leakage and hidden stratification and provides more trustworthy performance estimates and robustness.

title: Spatio-Temporal and Clinical Conditioning for Fine-Grained Radiology Report Retrieval
summary: Radiology is vital to modern healthcare, but rising imaging demand and persistent workforce shortages strain reporting capacity and clinical workflows. Automated radiology report generation has the potential to support radiologists and help alleviate this burden; however, existing retrieval-based methods remain rigid, lack explicit anatomical grounding, and do not account for longitudinal disease progression or available clinical context. In this work, we introduce STAR3, a multimodal, spatio-temporal, attentive retrieval framework for radiology report generation that aligns region-level anatomical information with clinical indications and longitudinal changes across chest X-ray studies. Our framework employs an object detector to identify anatomically meaningful regions and retrieves semantically relevant report sentences conditioned on both current clinical context and changes observed between prior and current examinations. This design enables anatomically and temporally grounded report generation that better reflects clinical reporting practice. Experiments on the MIMIC-CXR dataset demonstrate that STAR3 outperforms current retrieval-based approaches on retrieval, NLP and clinical metrics, highlighting the value of conditioning retrieval anatomically, temporally and clinically for advancing automated radiology report generation.

AI.tldr: STAR3 is a multimodal, spatio-temporal attentive retrieval framework for radiology report generation that grounds retrieval in region-level anatomy and longitudinal changes across chest X-ray studies, outperforming retrieval-based baselines on MIMIC-CXR.
AI.motivation: Rising imaging demand and persistent radiologist workforce shortages create bottlenecks in reporting; existing retrieval-based methods are rigid and lack explicit anatomical grounding or longitudinal/contextual awareness.
AI.method: STAR3 uses an object detector to identify anatomically meaningful regions and retrieves semantically relevant report sentences conditioned on current clinical context and changes between prior and current examinations, enabling anatomically and temporally grounded report generation.
AI.result: On the MIMIC-CXR dataset, STAR3 outperforms current retrieval-based approaches across retrieval, NLP, and clinical metrics.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning retrieval anatomically, temporally, and clinically improves automated radiology report generation, highlighting the value of integrating region-level anatomy and longitudinal change for radiology reporting.

title: A Hippocampus for Linear Attention: An Exact Memory for What the Recurrent State Forgets
summary: Linear-attention and state-space language models compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, yielding O(1) memory at the cost of a lossy exact memory: when many key--value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, we give linear attention a hippocampal complement. HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) keeps the usual delta-rule state as a compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory: the state models linearly compressible structure, while the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state. The cache writes without a learned eviction module, keeping tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state; a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read then turns these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging. At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), and improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26. It also achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains much more robust than GDN or a matched HOLA+recency cache on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x its training length).

AI.tldr: HOLA adds a bounded exact key-value cache to a linear-attention/state-space LM, creating a semiparametric memory that preserves critical associations while keeping compressive state, yielding better perplexity and retrieval with a modest parameter count.
AI.motivation: Linear attention/state-space models compress the prefix into a fixed-size state, which is memory-efficient but lossy when many key–value associations compete. A selectively exact memory is needed for important tokens to improve recall and long-context performance.
AI.method: Retain the standard delta-rule compressive state and augment it with a bounded exact KV cache. Cache writes occur without a learned eviction policy, prioritizing tokens with large beta * ||e|| (high residuals). Read from the cache using a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma mechanism to convert exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval, forming a semiparametric test-time memory. Trained 340M parameters on 15B SlimPajama tokens; compared to full-attention baselines.
AI.result: Wikitext perplexity improves from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), outperforming a full-attention Transformer++ baseline at 26.88. LAMBADA perplexity improves from 30.95 to 30.26. Achieves best linear in-context retrieval and shows robustness on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall up to 32k tokens (16x training length) compared with GDN or a HOLA+recency cache.
AI.conclusion: HOLA demonstrates that combining a compressive state with a bounded exact KV cache yields a semiparametric memory that delivers meaningful gains in language modeling and retrieval while maintaining the efficiency benefits of linear attention.

title: SA-HGNN: Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network for EEG-Based Depression Recognition
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely used to capture spatial functional connectivity patterns to improve electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression recognition performance. However, the functional connectivity of brain networks in patients with depression exhibits an inherent hierarchical structure, making it difficult to capture accurate connection patterns. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel model named Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN), which aims to accurately extract the authentic hierarchical structure of depression-affected brain networks. Specifically, the proposed model comprises three core modules. First, a Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction module dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies to capture more complex spatial relationships within the brain network. Second, hyperbolic graph convolution is employed to overcome the representation bottlenecks of Euclidean space, leveraging hyperbolic geometry to precisely capture latent hierarchical relationships within the brain network. Finally, an Attention Pooling module adaptively filters out highly redundant noise channels in EEG signals, effectively mitigating the interference of inherent noise on the authentic hierarchical topology. Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method across resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating its robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in brain networks of patients with depression.

AI.tldr: SA-HGNN automatically learns sample-specific brain networks, uses hyperbolic graph convolutions to model hierarchical depressive connectivity, and employs attention pooling to mitigate noise, achieving superior EEG-based depression recognition across resting-state and task paradigms.
AI.motivation: Depression-related brain networks exhibit intrinsic hierarchical organization that is not well captured by Euclidean GNNs or fixed topologies. A model that (1) adapts network topology per sample, (2) leverages hyperbolic geometry to model hierarchy, and (3) suppresses noisy channels could better reveal authentic functional connectivity patterns and improve recognition performance.
AI.method: Three-module architecture: (1) Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction to build personalized brain networks per subject; (2) Hyperbolic Graph Convolution to exploit hierarchical latent structure in hyperbolic space; (3) Attention Pooling to filter out noisy EEG channels and reduce interference with topology.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on public EEG datasets shows SA-HGNN achieves superior performance in both resting-state and task-related EEG paradigms, demonstrates robustness to noise, and effectively captures abnormal functional connectivity patterns in depression.
AI.conclusion: SA-HGNN provides a principled approach to capturing authentic hierarchical brain topology in depression and improves EEG-based depression recognition by combining personalized topologies, hyperbolic representation, and noise-aware pooling.

title: Evaluating Vision-Language Models as a Zero-Shot Learning Alternative to You Only Look Once and Optical Character Recognition for Nigerian License Plate Recognition
summary: License Plate Recognition (LPR) systems are critical tools in traffic monitoring, security enforcement, and urban mobility management. Traditional LPR systems often rely on a multi-stage pipeline involving object detection using You Only Look Once (YOLO) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR), which suffer from limitations such as high resource demands, poor performance in unstructured environments, and the need for large annotated datasets. This study explores the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as a unified, zeroshot learning solution for Nigerian license plate recognition. Using a curated dataset of 88 challenging real-world images collected in Nigeria, we evaluate five selected VLMs: Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp (Google DeepMind), Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (Alibaba), GPT-4o (OpenAI), Claude 4 Sonnet (Anthropic), and Llama 3.2 Vision 90b (Meta). Results based on Character Error Rate (CER) reveal that Gemini and Qwen significantly outperform other models in both accuracy and robustness, on the challenging image scenarios. This work highlights the practical advantages of VLMs over YOLO+OCR, questions the claims by model providers, and compares the performances of the VLMs.

AI.tldr: VLM-based zeroshot Nigerian license plate recognition; Gemini 2.0 and Qwen outperform peers in CER and robustness; VLMs offer practical advantages over YOLO+OCR; evaluation on 88 Nigerian images with five models.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of traditional multi-stage LPR pipelines (high resource use, poor performance in unstructured settings, reliance on large labeled datasets) by evaluating unified Vision-Language Models for zeroshot LPR in Nigeria.
AI.method: Evaluate five VLMs (Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude 4 Sonnet, Llama 3.2 Vision 90b) on a curated set of 88 challenging Nigerian license plate images; use Character Error Rate (CER) as primary metric; compare against YOLO+OCR baseline; analyze scenario robustness and cross-model performance.
AI.result: Gemini 2.0 and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct achieve the best CER and robustness across challenging scenarios; other VLMs lag; results support practical advantages of VLM-based zeroshot LPR over traditional pipelines; raises questions about providers’ claims and warrants direct model comparisons.
AI.conclusion: VLMs show strong potential as zeroshot LPR solutions in constrained, real-world environments and can augment or replace traditional YOLO+OCR pipelines; broader validation on more diverse datasets is recommended.

title: Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics
comment: 39 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop (https://openreview.net/forum?id=R5YXaPgUAx). Includes the pipeline-generated companion physics manuscript as an appendix. Data and scaffolding archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21126996
summary: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors. We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses; pre- and post-pilot stages are fully autonomous, and pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures - operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction. Two paired failure modes - a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation - isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end autonomous-research pipeline converts a large condensed-matter arXiv corpus into a publication-grade manuscript with three physics findings, using multi-phase calibration, first-principles computations, and fault-tolerant grounding to enable autonomous discovery.
AI.motivation: Addresses the fundamental challenge in frontier physical science where external-anchored calibration is essential due to underdocumented toolchains and potential hallucinations from unscaffolded agents, aiming to demonstrate verifiable, autonomous research capable of high-stakes scientific outputs.
AI.method: End-to-end pipeline that ingests 11,083 condensed-matter arXiv papers, autonomously conceives research direction, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, performs novel first-principles computations, and generates a manuscript. Operates across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases with shared on-disk state and 2,162 literature-consultation events; relies on redundancy (fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, adversarial review) for fault tolerance; fully autonomous pre-/post-pilot stages with bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures; two paired failure modes isolating calibration as the grounding mechanism.
AI.result: Produces a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism, grounded in literature across dozens of sessions, along with a demonstrably fault-tolerant autonomous workflow (pre-/post-pilot autonomy, surveillance via adversarial review, and structured calibration).
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a foundational, generalizable framework for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics, emphasizing literature-grounded calibration, robust fault tolerance, and structured evaluation of primitives and failure modes.

title: kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

AI.tldr: kNNGuard is a training-free guardrail that uses hidden activations from a base LLM and a small bank of 50 labeled prompts to perform multi-layer kNN fusion across activation- and embedding-spaces, achieving competitive or better F1 with significantly lower latency than fine-tuned guards, and rapid domain adaptation by updating the bank.
AI.motivation: To reduce the reliance on large-scale fine-tuning for guardrails, improve generalization and latency, and enable fast domain adaptation for detecting unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts in production LLM systems.
AI.method: Extract hidden activations from an off-the-shelf LLM using a small labeled bank of 50 safe/unsafe prompts. Compute kNN-based scores per layer in activation space and in embedding space, then fuse scores across layers and spaces to classify prompts without gradient updates or fine-tuning.
AI.result: In six domains, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to state-of-the-art fine-tuned guardrails, runs about 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and about 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier. Domain adaptation is achieved by updating the labeled bank, which can be done in under 10 seconds.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, activation-space-based guardrail can rival fine-tuned approaches in effectiveness while offering substantial latency and domain-adaptation advantages, with configurable prompts and layer choices for production integration.

title: ComplexMimic: Human-Scene Interaction Imitation in Complex 3D Environments
summary: Physics-based Human-Scene Interaction (HSI) imitation learning is crucial for embodied intelligence as it bridges the gap between kinematic 3D motions and real-world dynamics. However, most existing methods focus on simplified scene settings, leaving complex environments largely unexplored, which limits their applicability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we focus on HSI mimicry in complex environments. Under this complex setting, we observe an inherent trade-off between successfully performing interaction and maintaining natural, physically plausible motions. To address this challenge, we propose ComplexMimic, a framework that reconstructs diverse HSI by interpreting imperfect MoCap data. First, we introduce a Dual Flow Strategy, which learns two complementary experts: an imitation expert for accurate motion tracking and an interaction expert for collision-aware adaptation in complex scenes. Second, naive multi-expert distillation, which treats all experts equally, often under-samples challenging behaviors, limiting effective learning. To mitigate this issue, we propose a difficulty-aware distillation strategy that adaptively weights supervision and prioritizes hard-yet-learnable trajectories guided by failure statistics and learning progress signals. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LuPan23/ComplexMimic.

AI.tldr: Proposes ComplexMimic, a physics-based HSI imitation learning framework for complex environments using a dual-flow dual-expert setup and a difficulty-aware distillation to handle hard trajectories, achieving state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing HSI imitation methods excel in simplified scenes but fail to handle complex environments; there is a trade-off between accurate interaction and natural motion; need to reconstruct diverse HSI from imperfect MoCap data.
AI.method: Dual Flow Strategy with imitation expert and interaction expert; replaces naive multi-expert distillation with a difficulty-aware distillation that weights supervision based on failure statistics and learning progress; validates on three benchmark datasets; code released.
AI.result: Outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on three benchmarks; extensive experiments validate effectiveness; code released.
AI.conclusion: ComplexMimic effectively navigates the interaction-naturalness trade-off in complex HSI by adaptive, difficulty-aware distillation and dual-expert learning; demonstrates strong empirical gains.

title: DRIFTLENS: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models
summary: Personalization changes what a model says to a user; we show that it can also change the reasoning trajectory used to justify the response. Modern LLMs personalize interactions by storing user attributes, preferences, and prior context, then injecting this information into future prompts. We study whether such memory reshapes reasoning on open-ended questions where no single ground-truth answer exists. To quantify this effect, we introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between a question's no-memory trajectory and its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. We first validate that DRIFTLENS distinguishes content-free pragmatic noise from substantive reasoning changes. Across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories, including age, occupation, and disability, user-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. We then evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for reducing drift. Both reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model-and reward-dependent. These results suggest that memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized language models.

AI.tldr: DRIFTLENS is a ground-truth-free framework that quantifies how personalizing memory (user attributes) shifts an LLM's reasoning trajectory, not just its outputs. It shows measurable reasoning drift across models and attributes, and evaluates GRPO/DPO-based post-training methods that partially mitigate drift with model- and reward-dependent effects.
AI.motivation: Personalization reshapes both what an LLM says and how it reasons. Without ground-truth answers for open-ended prompts, it is crucial to quantify whether injected user-attribute memory meaningfully alters reasoning paths and to understand accompanying risks.
AI.method: DRIFTLENS maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and computes divergence between the no-memory trajectory and the trajectory with injected memory. The approach is validated to separate pragmatic noise from substantive changes. Experiments span four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories (e.g., age, occupation, disability). Then GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods are evaluated for their ability to reduce drift across models and reward settings.
AI.result: User-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above the pragmatic-noise floor across models and attributes, even when final answers remain fluent and on-topic. GRPO and DPO post-training reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; impacts on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction-following are model- and reward-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable, partially mitigable failure mode of personalized language models that warrants careful consideration in designing and deploying personalized LMs.

title: Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
summary: We propose an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments instead of full solutions, achieving higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference), while maintaining similar accuracy as demonstrated in previous benchmarks. We show that although FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy remains limited by the resolution of the training data.

AI.tldr: An improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for 2D Rayleigh–Bénard convection predicts time increments rather than full solutions, yielding higher accuracy than a standard FNO with a compact model (314k params, ~1.26 MB) and fast inference (~7 ms). However, accuracy gains saturate with training data resolution, even as FNOs generalize to finer meshes.
AI.motivation: Address efficiency and accuracy limitations of Fourier Neural Operators for simulating 2D Rayleigh–Bénard convection by shifting to time-increment prediction to enable faster surrogate modeling without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: Develop an enhanced FNO architecture trained to predict temporal increments of the solution rather than the full field. The model is compact (≈314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and achieves fast inference (~7 ms). Evaluated against a standard FNO baseline and benchmarks on 2D Rayleigh–Bénard convection data, including mesh refinement scenarios.
AI.result: The proposed method attains higher accuracy than the standard FNO baseline while maintaining a compact size and fast inference. It demonstrates similar accuracy to prior benchmarks. It also shows that FNOs generalize to finer meshes, but their accuracy is ultimately limited by the resolution of the training data.
AI.conclusion: Time-increment prediction with a compact FNO yields efficient surrogates for 2D Rayleigh–Bénard convection, delivering competitive accuracy and fast inference. However, improving accuracy on finer meshes will require higher-resolution or multi-fidelity training data, as performance is capped by the training data resolution.

title: Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics: Protecting Facial Privacy against Customized Diffusion Models
summary: The rise of customized diffusion models has fueled a boom in personalized visual content creation, but it also introduces serious risks of malicious misuse, thereby posing threats to personal privacy. Image aesthetics are strongly correlated with human perception of image quality. Motivated by this observation, we address facial privacy protection from a novel aesthetic perspective by degrading the generation quality of maliciously customized models, thus reducing facial identity leakage. Specifically, we propose a Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics (HAA) framework that exploits aesthetic cues at multiple perceptual levels. HAA consists of two key branches: (1) Global Anti-Aesthetics, which degrades overall aesthetics and generation quality by constructing a global anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and a corresponding loss; and (2) Local Anti-Aesthetics, which disrupts facial identity by using a local anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and loss to guide adversarial perturbations toward facial regions. By integrating both branches, HAA achieves anti-aesthetic degradation from a global to a local level during customized generation. Extensive experiments show that HAA outperforms existing methods in identity removal, providing an effective tool for protecting facial privacy.

AI.tldr: HAA (Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics) degrades generation quality of maliciously customized diffusion models to protect facial privacy by applying global and local anti-aesthetic cues, reducing identity leakage.
AI.motivation: Rising use of personalized diffusion models enables tailored visual content but risks facial privacy via identity leakage; aesthetic cues strongly affect perceived image quality, motivating protection through anti-aesthetic degradation.
