Consequently, it defines a demanding spatio-temporal grounding problem that requires models to identify both when an event occurs and where the referred object appears within extended video sequences. We evaluate existing Video REC approaches, including training-free baselines based on vision-language models combined with Grounded SAM2. Extensive experiments show that even advanced baselines and current state-of-the-art models struggle significantly on LongEgoRefer. These results highlight the intrinsic difficulty of long-form egocentric spatio-temporal grounding and emphasize the need for more robust video understanding models.

AI.tldr: LongEgoRefer is a large, long-form egocentric video benchmark for Video Referring Expression Comprehension (Video REC) with 1,498 expressions over ~45-minute videos, featuring extreme target sparsity and complex narratives, revealing major gaps in current methods.
AI.motivation: Current Video REC benchmarks mainly use short clips where targets are dense; there is a need to evaluate and develop models capable of long-horizon temporal grounding and sparse object localization in untrimmed egocentric data.
AI.method: Construct LongEgoRefer from Ego4D by annotating 1,498 referring expressions over long-form videos; emphasize extreme sparsity and detailed linguistic descriptions; evaluate existing Video REC approaches and vision-language baselines (including Grounded SAM2) on the benchmark.
AI.result: Most existing methods, including strong baselines and state-of-the-art models, perform poorly on LongEgoRefer, indicating the benchmark's intrinsic difficulty and the gap in current video understanding capabilities for long-form, sparse, egocentric grounding.
AI.conclusion: Long-form egocentric spatio-temporal grounding is a hard problem; the benchmark underscores the need for robust models that can handle long temporal horizons, sparse occurrences, and complex human-object interactions, driving future research in video-language grounding.

title: Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
summary: Despite alignment training, LLMs remain prone to generating unsafe outputs at deployment time. Monitoring outputs online and raising an alarm when safety can no longer be assumed is therefore critical. We study a simple real-time monitor that turns a verifier signal from an external model into an alarm decision by thresholding, with the threshold calibrated via risk control. In experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets, we show that this simple design is competitive with more advanced monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.

AI.tldr: A simple real-time safety monitor: it thresholds a verifier signal from an external model to raise an alarm, with the threshold calibrated via risk control; competitive with advanced sequential hypothesis testing monitors.
AI.motivation: LLMs still generate unsafe outputs in deployment despite alignment training; need online monitoring to detect and alarm when safety cannot be guaranteed.
AI.method: Implement a real-time monitor that converts an external verifier signal into an alarm decision via thresholding; calibrate the threshold using risk-control principles; evaluate on mathematical reasoning and red-teaming datasets.
AI.result: The threshold-based monitor performs competitively with more complex monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing across the tested tasks.
AI.conclusion: Simple thresholding-based monitoring can be an effective and practical approach for online safety monitoring of LLM outputs, offering competitive performance with simpler design.

title: Online Resource Allocation with Continuous Random Consumption: Regret under Degeneracy
summary:
We study online resource allocation when both rewards and consumption sizes may be continuously distributed. Requests arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected irrevocably under fixed resource capacities. Each request belongs to one of finitely many observable types; conditional on an observable request type, both the reward and the scalar size are random, and the realized size scales a fixed type-specific resource-consumption vector. The model allows the deterministic fluid relaxation to be degenerate.
  We show that additive regret is governed by the size-weighted mass of requests whose value-to-size ratios lie near the active acceptance cutoffs. We formalize this quantity through an active weighted-mass exponent p. When p > 1, this cutoff mass is thin, and the problem is genuinely hard: every online policy must incur regret of order at least $T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}$, and this holds for every p > 1. A sample-path marginal policy matches this lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors; and when p = 1, so that the mass grows linearly near the cutoff, it attains $O((\log T)^2)$ regret. For example, if the size and the value-to-size ratio are independent and uniformly distributed, then p = 1; if instead the size and the reward are independent and uniformly distributed, then p = 2. Thus the policy achieves $o(\sqrt{T})$ regret throughout this regularity class without any fluid non-degeneracy assumption, allowing both primal degeneracy and dual non-uniqueness.

AI.tldr: Analyzes online resource allocation with stochastic rewards and sizes across finitely many observable types, where both the fluid relaxation can be degenerate. Regret is governed by the size-weighted mass near active acceptance cutoffs, captured by an active weighted-mass exponent p. For p>1 the problem is hard with regret at least T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}, while a sample-path marginal policy matches this up to polylog factors; for p=1 the regret is polylogarithmic (O((log T)^2)). Examples show p=1 and p=2. The policy achieves o(sqrt(T)) regret without non-degeneracy assumptions, handling primal degeneracy and dual non-uniqueness.
AI.motivation: To understand how online allocation performance degrades when the standard fluid relaxation is degenerate and when only observable, type-specific distributions govern rewards and sizes. The goal is to quantify regret in terms of how much mass of near-cutoff requests exists and to identify regimes with dramatically different regret rates.
AI.method: Model extends online allocation with type-conditioned random rewards and sizes; sizes scale a vector per type. Introduces active weighted-mass exponent p to capture near-cutoff mass. Establishes worst-case lower bounds on additive regret for p>1 and matches with a sample-path marginal policy up to polylog factors; analyzes the p=1 boundary to show polylog regret. Provides concrete distributional examples illustrating p values.
AI.result: Regret bounds depend on p: for p>1, at least T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}; for p=1, O((log T)^2); policy achieves o(sqrt(T)) regret across the class; results hold without fluid non-degeneracy and with dual non-uniqueness.
AI.conclusion: Active near-cutoff mass, as captured by p, governs online regret in degenerate-fluid settings. The proposed policy is near-optimal across the regularity class, offering sub-sqrt regret (when p≤1) or near-sqrt regret (when p>1) without relying on non-degenerate fluid relaxations.

title: WBMM: Windowed Batch Matrix Multiplication for Efficient Large Receptive Field Convolution
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures. Accepted as a Spotlight paper at ICML 2026. Code available at http://github.com/wansong-s/WBMM
summary: Large kernel depthwise convolutions achieve strong performance but suffer from significant degradation as kernel size grows due to irregular memory access from gather-based computation; while Large Kernel Acceleration (LKA) helps on small feature maps, it becomes counterproductive on large feature maps, even slower than non-accelerated implementations. We propose Windowed Batch Matrix Multiplication (WBMM), which partitions input into contiguous windows and indexes a compact relative position bias table to construct weight matrices, enabling regular memory access via batched matrix multiplication. This yields a unique property: WBMM's throughput improves with larger windows, opposite to depthwise convolutions that degrade with larger kernels. Operator-level benchmarks show WBMM with 14x14 windows outperforms 5x5 depthwise convolution baselines in speed while providing a 7.8x larger per-layer receptive field. Combined with inter-block cross-window communication and hierarchical window reparameterization, WBMM achieves comparable or higher accuracy on ImageNet-1K, COCO, and ADE20K with 1.31-1.88x training speedup, and demonstrates consistent advantages across GPU, CPU, and edge devices without requiring specialized acceleration kernels. Our code is available at http://github.com/wansong-s/WBMM

AI.tldr: Introducing Windowed Batch Matrix Multiplication (WBMM) for large-kernel operations. It partitions inputs into contiguous windows and builds weight matrices via a relative-position bias table, enabling regular memory access and batched matmul. WBMM's throughput grows with larger windows, outperforming traditional depthwise conv baselines (e.g., 14x14 vs 5x5) and achieving notable receptive-field expansion (7.8x). Combined with inter-block cross-window communication and hierarchical window reparameterization, it delivers 1.31-1.88x training speedups on ImageNet-1K, COCO, ADE20K across GPU/CPU/edge devices, without specialized kernels; code available.
AI.motivation: Large kernel depthwise convolutions degrade with kernel size due to irregular memory access from gather-based computation. LKA helps small feature maps but is counterproductive on large maps. A method that preserves regular memory access while enabling large receptive fields is needed.
AI.method: Partition input into contiguous windows and index a compact relative position bias table to construct weight matrices, enabling regular, batched matrix multiplications. This Windowed Batch Matrix Multiplication (WBMM) is augmented with inter-block cross-window communication and hierarchical window reparameterization to improve accuracy and efficiency.
AI.result: WBMM with 14x14 windows outperforms 5x5 depthwise convolution baselines in speed and provides a 7.8x larger per-layer receptive field. Training speedups of 1.31-1.88x reported on ImageNet-1K, COCO, ADE20K across GPU/CPU/edge devices, with competitive or higher accuracy.
AI.conclusion: WBMM offers an efficient solution for large-kernel processing that benefits from larger windows, avoiding irregular access and enabling regular memory throughput. It achieves practical speedups and accuracy gains across standard benchmarks without specialized kernels, and the authors provide public code.

title: Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control
summary: As AI coding agents become more autonomous, they increasingly ship code iteratively, with the codebase persisting across sessions. This persistence creates a new attack surface: a misaligned or prompt-injected agent can distribute attacks across pull requests (PRs) and time its payload for the PR with the best natural cover. To study the resulting dynamics, we introduce Iterative VibeCoding, a setting for AI control, the study of safely deploying capable but potentially untrusted AI. In Iterative VibeCoding, a coding agent builds software over a sequence of PRs in a persistent codebase while pursuing a covert side task. Our benchmark includes two task families: CLI tools and Flask web services, across 20 total task variations. We use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the attack agent and GPT-4o as the monitor. We compare gradual attacks, which distribute the side task across PRs, against non-gradual attacks concentrated in a single PR. No single monitor is robust to both: which strategy evades best (success while evading the monitor) depends on the monitor type, so a defender cannot close off both gradual and non-gradual attacks with any one monitor. High evasion (>= 65%) generalizes across model attack agent backends (Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.5), confirming this is a property of the persistent-state attack surface rather than a single model's capability. Evasion also remains high across state-of-the-art monitor models and the gap between gradual and non-gradual evasion widens for more capable models. We introduce a stateful link-tracker monitor that tracks suspicious buildup across PRs. On both task families, it detects gradual attacks substantially better than diff monitors that merely see more accumulated history. Combining this stronger monitor with trajectory monitors in a four-monitor ensemble reduces gradual-attack evasion from 93% under the weakest standard diff monitor to 47%.

AI.tldr: A study of persistent-state AI coding agents reveals that attacker strategies can distribute covert tasks over PRs; monitoring must address temporal buildup, and a stateful link-tracker with ensemble monitoring reduces evasion.
AI.motivation: As AI coding agents become capable of persisting code across sessions, risk arises from misaligned or prompt-injected agents executing covert tasks over time. There is a need to understand attack dynamics in iterative, persistent coding environments and to develop defenses that detect gradual, stateful threats.
AI.method: Introduce Iterative VibeCoding, a benchmark where an autonomous coding agent builds software over a sequence of PRs in a persistent codebase while pursuing a covert side task. Two task families (CLI tools and Flask web services) across 20 variations are studied. An attack agent (Claude Sonnet 4.5) and a monitor (GPT-4o) are used to compare gradual vs non-gradual attacks. Attack evasion is measured across multiple model backends (Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.5) and with state-of-the-art monitors.
AI.result: No single monitor robustly defends against both gradual and non-gradual attacks; evasion depends on monitor type. High evasion (≥65%) generalizes across attack backends, indicating vulnerability is tied to the persistent-state surface. Evasion remains high even with advanced monitors, and the gap widens for stronger models. A stateful link-tracker monitor detects gradual attacks much better than traditional diff monitors. A four-monitor ensemble (link-tracker plus trajectory monitors) reduces gradual-attack evasion from 93% to 47%.
AI.conclusion: Persistent-state attack surfaces in iterative AI coding are a general security challenge not solvable by a single monitor. Temporal, trajectory-aware defenses—including stateful monitoring and multi-monitor ensembles—are essential to curb gradual, long-horizon covert actions.

title: Self-explainable Operator Learning for Discovering Spatial Patterns in Functional Data
summary: Operator learning has emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex physical systems in functional spaces. However, their neural network-based architectures make them opaque models, obscuring the reasoning behind their predictions. In this work, we introduce a self-explainable operator learning framework that overcomes this challenge by reformulating operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed through integral equations. Exploiting the additive decomposability of these integral equations, we divide the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals to evaluate the contribution of each region to the final prediction. This decomposition enables direct interpretability where the model explains both inputs and outputs by linking specific input regions to corresponding output patterns, thereby revealing which spatial features drive predictions. We demonstrate the framework on function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in fluid flow problems involving blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics. The results show that the operator most often prioritizes regions with strong feature gradients, providing physically meaningful insight into the model's decision-making process. Comparisons with established post-hoc explainability methods demonstrate qualitative agreement while highlighting the key advantage of the proposed approach: explainability is embedded directly within the operator structure itself and does not require an external tool. Therefore, our framework provides a mathematically transparent and physically interpretable approach to uncover relationships within data, fostering trust in machine learning for scientific applications by enabling more informed data-driven analysis of physical systems.

AI.tldr: A self-explainable operator learning framework decomposes operators into generalized functional linear models via integral equations, enabling local, region-wise interpretability; demonstrated on fluid-flow mappings.
AI.motivation: Address opacity of neural operator models by embedding explainability within the operator, providing transparent, physically meaningful attributions.
AI.method: Represent the operator as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed through integral equations; use additive decomposability to partition the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals that link input regions to outputs; compare with post-hoc methods; apply to function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics.
AI.result: The operator tends to prioritize regions with strong feature gradients; qualitative agreement with established post-hoc explainability methods; explainability is embedded in the operator, not requiring external tools.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a mathematically transparent and physically interpretable approach to operator learning, fostering trust in ML for scientific applications by linking input regions to output patterns without external explainability tools.

title: X-Splat: Gaussian Splatting for 3D CBCT Generation from Single Panoramic Radiograph
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, including appendix. Under review
summary: Generating a 3D dental volume from a single panoramic radiograph (PXR) could provide a low-radiation alternative to Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT), but the problem is highly underdetermined: panoramic acquisition integrates 3D attenuation along curved X-ray paths into a 2D image, leaving depth-resolved anatomy unobserved. Existing implicit and generative approaches often produce oversmoothed geometry or anatomically inconsistent hallucinations, lacking geometry-driven supervision and relying on smooth representations unable to precisely localize sharp anatomical boundaries. We propose X-Splat, the first Gaussian Splatting framework for generating CBCT-like 3D dental volumes from a single PXR. X-Splat uses the known panoramic acquisition geometry as a generation scaffold: learnable anisotropic Gaussian primitives are initialized along the X-ray paths that formed the input image and adjusted in a single feed-forward pass, constrained by Beer-Lambert reprojection and multi-view radiographic training supervision. A lightweight residual refiner adds dataset-level anatomical priors without overriding the geometry already resolved by the Gaussians. We train on synthetic PXR-CBCT pairs, enabling direct volumetric supervision without paired real scans. We further introduce segmentation-based geometry-aware metrics, providing the first evaluation of PXR-based generation over maxillofacial anatomy. X-Splat outperforms NeRF- and GAN-based baselines, recovering individual teeth, cortical boundaries, and alveolar structure, including the mandibular canal which prior methods fail to reconstruct. Code will be available at https://github.com/tomek1911/X-Splat

AI.tldr: X-Splat introduces a Gaussian splatting framework to reconstruct CBCT-like 3D dental volumes from a single panoramic radiograph (PXR) using anisotropic Gaussian primitives aligned to X-ray paths, Beer-Lambert reprojection, and synthetic supervision; it achieves geometry-driven accuracy outperforming NeRF- and GAN-based baselines on maxillofacial anatomy.
AI.motivation: The PXR-to-3D problem is highly underdetermined because a 2D panoramic image integrates 3D attenuation along curved X-ray paths, leading to ambiguous depth and risky anatomically implausible reconstructions. Existing implicit/generative methods tend to oversmooth geometry or hallucinate without geometry-guided supervision.
AI.method: Trainable anisotropic Gaussian primitives are initialized along the X-ray paths that formed the PXR and adjusted in a single forward pass (Gaussian splatting) under Beer-Lambert reprojection constraints and multi-view radiographic supervision. A lightweight residual refiner injects dataset-level anatomical priors without overriding the resolved geometry. Training uses synthetic PXR-CBCT pairs to provide direct volumetric supervision, and segmentation-based geometry-aware metrics assess the reconstructions.
AI.result: X-Splat outperforms NeRF- and GAN-based baselines, recovering fine dental structures (individual teeth, cortical boundaries, alveolar structures) and the mandibular canal that prior methods fail to reconstruct. The approach enables geometry-driven, CBCT-like 3D volumes from a single PXR and demonstrates strong potential for low-radiation dental imaging.
AI.conclusion: This work presents the first Gaussian splatting framework for PXR-to-CBCT-like 3D dental volumes, leveraging acquisition geometry as a scaffold and synthetic supervision, with segmentation-based evaluation and publicly available code forthcoming.

title: HERMES: A Multi-Granularity Labeling Substrate for Pre-training Data Mixtures
summary: Most data-mixing methods assume the corpus has already been partitioned into groups, and the choice of those groups determines what a mixer can express. Existing labels, including provenance, topic or format taxonomies, and flat embedding clusters, commit to one semantic axis at one granularity; changing the resolution rebuilds the labels. We argue the bottleneck is the label system, not the mixer, and provide a hierarchical one. HERMES is a data-derived labeling substrate: a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization annotates each document once into a coarse-to-fine code whose prefix length controls granularity up to approximately 130k cells. At coarse granularity HERMES sits at a plateau with KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics, so the contribution is the substrate, not the clusterer. On 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training, the hierarchy exposes an interaction fixed-granularity pipelines cannot test: at one prefix length, a combined Stage-2 rule contrast, equal-subbucket coverage versus size-proportional within-bucket quality top-30%, lifts a 16-task capability macro-average by +0.0253; at the next finer level, the same rule loses its measurable edge as candidate pools contract approximately 5x. HERMES reframes data mixture design from choosing among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy.

AI.tldr: HERMES proposes a data-derived hierarchical labeling substrate that annotates documents into a coarse-to-fine code (prefix-length control up to ~130k cells) via a Learned Semantic Transform and 3-stage residual vector quantization, shifting data-mixing design from fixed label sets to a reusable granularity hierarchy; the main contribution is the substrate, not the clusterer.
AI.motivation: Current data-mixing approaches assume fixed label sets that encode a single semantic axis at a single granularity; this bottleneck is the labeling system itself. A reusable, hierarchical, data-derived granularity can enable flexible, cross-task data mixtures.
AI.method: Apply a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization to produce a single-pass, coarse-to-fine hierarchical code for each document; up to ~130k cells via prefix-length control; evaluate on a 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-trained model; compare a Stage-2 rule with equal-subbucket coverage vs size-proportional within-bucket quality across prefix lengths; assess macro-average on 16 tasks.
AI.result: At coarse granularity, HERMES sits on a plateau comparable to KMeans-based methods on standard clustering metrics; at one prefix length, a Stage-2 rule improves macro-average by +0.0253; at the next finer level, this edge disappears as candidate pools contract about 5x; overall, the substrate enables exploring how granularity affects mixing performance.
AI.conclusion: Data-mixing should navigate a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy rather than rely on fixed label sets; the HERMES labeling substrate enables this flexible, scalable approach to data partitioning and mixing.

title: AbsoluteDegradation: A Physics-Inspired Synthetic Film-Degradation Pipeline and Archival Film Restoration Benchmark
summary: Restoring archival film remains a fundamentally challenging problem due to the absence of paired training data and the lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks. Pristine versions of deteriorated footage are physically unrecoverable, requiring supervised methods to rely on synthetic data that often fail to capture the complex, temporally coherent nature of real film degradation. At the same time, existing real-world datasets are limited in scale, quality, and accessibility, hindering reliable evaluation and fair comparison across methods. We address both limitations with AbsoluteDegradation, a physics-inspired, modular pipeline for synthesizing realistic film degradations, and a new large-scale archival benchmark. The proposed pipeline models the analog-to-digital process as a structured composition of artifact families, incorporating signal-dependent grain, parametric scratches, and temporally coherent camera motion, enabling controlled generation of diverse degradation regimes. In parallel, we introduce a curated dataset of 81,576 high-resolution frames sourced from real archival footage, designed for consistent evaluation under real-world conditions. Together, these contributions provide a unified framework for training and benchmarking restoration models. Extensive experiments across multiple architectures show that models trained with AbsoluteDegradation generalize better to real-world footage, while the proposed benchmark reveals systematic failure modes of current methods. We hope this work establishes a foundation for reproducible and domain-authentic evaluation in archival film restoration.

AI.tldr: Introduces AbsoluteDegradation: a physics-inspired, modular pipeline to synthesize realistic archival-film degradations, plus a large-scale real archival benchmark (81,576 high-resolution frames) for training and evaluation. Demonstrates that degradation-trained models generalize better to real footage and reveals standard failure modes of current restoration methods.
AI.motivation: Address two core gaps in archival film restoration: (1) lack of paired training data and (2) absence of standardized, large-scale evaluation benchmarks that reflect real-world degradation.
AI.method: Model the analog-to-digital capture as a structured composition of artifact families within a modular pipeline. Simulates signal-dependent grain, parametric scratches, and temporally coherent camera motion to produce realistic degradations. Curate a large real-world archival dataset of 81,576 high-resolution frames for consistent evaluation.
AI.result: Training with AbsoluteDegradation improves generalization to real archival footage; the proposed benchmark exposes systematic failure modes in current restoration methods across architectures.
AI.conclusion: Provides a unified, reproducible framework for training and benchmarking archival film restoration, enabling domain-authentic evaluation and fair comparison across methods.

title: Generalization in offline RL: The structure is more important than the amount of pessimism
summary: While pessimism counteracts overestimation bias in offline reinforcement learning (RL), being overly conservative has been associated with hindering certain forms of generalization. However, in this paper we demonstrate that being overly pessimistic does not inherently prevent optimal generalization in contextual MDPs (CMDPs). Instead, we argue successful generalization depends not on the amount of pessimism, but whether the pessimistic structure respects the underlying symmetries of the optimal solution. We prove that a mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic, symmetric one. In offline RL, the structure of the pessimism is determined by the structure of the dataset coverage. As such, enforcing a symmetric value function can be non-trivial, and might require techniques such as data augmentation (DA). Inspired by our theoretical results, we argue that DA can best be applied through a consistency loss during policy extraction, rather than the common practice of (regular) offline training on an augmented dataset. This is empirically validated using IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.

AI.tldr: Pessimism's effect on generalization in offline RL depends on symmetry with the optimal solution; symmetric pessimism can generalize better than mildly pessimistic non-symmetric approaches; data augmentation can enforce symmetry, but is best applied via a consistency loss during policy extraction rather than standard offline training; validated on a rotationally symmetric reacher using IQL and CQL.
AI.motivation: Identify when and why pessimistic value estimation aids generalization in CMDPs; challenge the idea that more pessimism always improves generalization; examine the role of symmetry and dataset coverage in offline RL.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis comparing mildly pessimistic non-symmetric vs overly pessimistic symmetric value functions; link pessimism structure to dataset coverage in offline RL; propose using data augmentation to enforce symmetry and a consistency loss during policy extraction; empirical validation with IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.
AI.result: Shows that a mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic, symmetric one; the structure of pessimism is dictated by dataset coverage; data augmentation can enforce symmetry, particularly via a consistency loss during policy extraction; empirical validation on rotationally symmetric reacher with IQL and CQL.
AI.conclusion: Generalization in CMDPs hinges on aligning the pessimistic structure with the problem's symmetry; achieving this alignment may require data augmentation, and applying it through a consistency loss during policy extraction is effective for offline RL.

title: AdaCount: Training-Free Similarity-Guided Spatial and Feature Adaptation for Zero-Shot Object Counting
summary: Zero-shot object counting (ZOC) aims to count instances of arbitrary object categories specified only through textual prompts. Recent training-free approaches leverage foundation models such as SAM to reformulate counting as a prompt-driven segmentation task, eliminating the need for costly counting-specific training data with point-level annotations. More recently, SAM3 introduced promptable concept segmentation, enabling the zero-shot segmentation of all instances corresponding to a text-defined concept. However, SAM3 struggles in densely populated scenes containing numerous small objects, where limited image resolution and insufficient attention to target-relevant regions often lead to missed instances and poor instance separation, hindering accurate object counting. To address this limitation, we propose AdaCount, a training-free framework for ZOC based on similarity-guided spatial and feature adaptation. AdaCount first estimates a prototype-driven similarity map that identifies target-relevant regions. This similarity map subsequently guides two complementary adaptations: (i) similarity-guided spatial warping, which reallocates image resolution toward target instances, and (ii) feature modulation, which amplifies target-relevant encoder representations. Together, these adaptations enable SAM3 to devote greater representational capacity to target-relevant regions while preserving global image context, without requiring any model retraining. Extensive experiments across six diverse counting benchmarks establish AdaCount as a new SOTA among training-free ZOC approaches.

AI.tldr: AdaCount is a training-free approach for zero-shot object counting that augments SAM3 with a prototype-driven similarity map and two adaptive modules (similarity-guided spatial warping and feature modulation) to focus representation and resolution on target objects, achieving state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot counting benefits from prompt-driven segmentation, but existing methods like SAM3 struggle in dense scenes due to limited resolution and attention on target regions. There is a need to reallocate computational resources toward target instances without retraining.
AI.method: Compute a prototype-driven similarity map to locate target-relevant regions; use this map to guide (1) similarity-guided spatial warping that reallocates image resolution toward target instances, and (2) feature modulation that enhances target-relevant encoder features. The approach is training-free and leverages SAM3 as the base model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six diverse counting benchmarks show AdaCount sets a new state-of-the-art among training-free ZOC methods, improving counting accuracy in challenging scenarios with densely packed small objects.
AI.conclusion: AdaCount effectively boosts zero-shot counting by injecting a similarity-guided attention mechanism into a prompt-driven segmentation framework, enabling better allocation of representational capacity to target regions without retraining.

title: Optimizing Visual Generative Models via Distribution-wise Rewards
summary: Conventional reinforcement learning strategies for visual generation typically employ sample-wise reward functions, yet this practice frequently results in reward hacking that degrades image diversity and introduces visual anomalies. To address these limitations, we present a novel framework that finetunes generative models using distribution-wise rewards, ensuring better alignment with real-world data distributions. Unlike rewards that evaluate samples individually, distribution-wise reward accounts for the data distribution of the samples, mitigating the mode collapse problem that occurs when all samples optimize towards the same direction independently. To overcome the prohibitive computational cost of estimating these rewards, we introduce a subset-replace strategy that efficiently provides reward signals by updating only a small subset of a generated reference set. Additionally, we apply RL to optimize post-hoc model merging coefficients, potentially mitigating the train-inference inconsistency caused by introducing stochastic differential equation (SDE) in regular RL practices. Extensive experiments show our approach significantly improves FID-50K across various base models, from 8.30 to 5.77 for SiT and from 3.74 to 3.52 for EDM2. Qualitative evaluation also confirms that our method enhances perceptual quality while preserving sample diversity.

AI.tldr: A distribution-wise reward framework with a subset-replace estimator improves generative RL for images, addressing reward hacking and mode collapse while reducing cost; it also optimizes post-hoc model merging to mitigate train-inference mismatch, yielding stronger FID-50K and better perceptual quality with preserved diversity.
AI.motivation: Sample-wise RL rewards in visual generation often cause reward hacking and reduced diversity; aligning rewards with the data distribution can mitigate mode collapse and produce more faithful, diverse images. Computational cost of distribution-wise rewards is prohibitive, necessitating efficient estimation. SDE-based RL can introduce train-inference inconsistencies.
AI.method: 1) Propose distribution-wise rewards that evaluate generated samples against the data distribution rather than individually. 2) Introduce a subset-replace strategy to estimate distribution-level rewards efficiently by updating only a small subset of a reference set. 3) Apply RL to tune post-hoc model merging coefficients to reduce train-inference mismatch caused by SDEs in RL training.
AI.result: Empirical results show significant FID-50K improvements: SiT from 8.30 to 5.77; EDM2 from 3.74 to 3.52. Qualitative analysis reports improved perceptual quality without sacrificing sample diversity across base models.
AI.conclusion: Distribution-wise rewards coupled with subset-replace estimation effectively align optimization with real data distributions, improving image quality and diversity in RL-based visual generation, and the post-hoc merging RL helps stabilize training under SDE-based setups; the approach is validated across multiple backbones.

title: SAMoR: Motion Modelling for Articulated Objects of Any Skeleton and Topology
summary: Modeling motion for articulated objects of arbitrary skeleton topology remains difficult: existing motion generators target a fixed human skeleton, and prior adaptations either fail to share a vocabulary across rigs or discard motion detail through global pooling. Our key observation is that while joint-level motion does not correspond cleanly across species, motion of functional joint groups does: a human arm, a wolf foreleg, and a bird wing share motion structure despite differing joint counts and connectivity, a correspondence that joint names (e.g., "forearm", "wing_L1") partially expose even when topology does not. We introduce SAMoR (Skeleton-Aware Motion Representation for Articulated Objects), a cross-topology motion representation that encodes each motion segment as a small fixed number ($K=8$) of part tokens shared across arbitrary skeletons. A graph-transformer encoder consumes per-joint motion features, kinematic graph structure, and joint-name embeddings, then compresses them into part-level tokens via cross-attention pooling and residual vector quantization, yielding a discrete motion codebook shared across rigs. To keep the part queries from collapsing into redundant global representations, we introduce a topology-agnostic attention supervision loss, with joint-name dropout to reduce over-reliance on text labels. We curate a heterogeneous corpus from HumanML3D, Truebones Zoo, and animated Objaverse-XL assets, and evaluate SAMoR on held-out characters with unseen skeletons. It supports accurate reconstruction and cross-topology transfer, and enables text-conditioned generation and part-wise editing via a MaskGIT token generator. SAMoR reaches $2.75 \times 10^{-2}$ normalized MPJPE on cross-topology reconstruction, $5.8\times$ below the strongest adapted variable-$J$ tokenizer baseline, while remaining competitive with fixed-skeleton specialists on HumanML3D.

AI.tldr: SAMoR introduces a cross-topology motion representation using fixed-size part tokens (K=8) to encode motion across arbitrary skeletons, via a graph-transformer encoder and joint-name embeddings, producing a shared discrete codebook for reconstruction, transfer, and text-conditioned generation.
AI.motivation: Overcome fixed-skeleton motion generation limitations by aligning motion structure at the level of functional joint groups across diverse rigs, enabling cross-topology transfer and reuse of a shared vocabulary.
AI.method: A graph-transformer encoder processes per-joint motion features, kinematic structure, and joint-name embeddings. It compresses information into K=8 part tokens through cross-attention pooling and residual vector quantization to a discrete codebook. A topology-agnostic attention supervision loss and joint-name dropout prevent collapse to global representations. Training uses a heterogeneous corpus from HumanML3D, Truebones Zoo, and Objaverse-XL; MaskGIT enables text-conditioned generation and part-wise editing.
AI.result: On held-out characters with unseen skeletons, SAMoR achieves 2.75e-2 normalized MPJPE for cross-topology reconstruction, outperforms the strongest adapted variable-J tokenizer baseline by 5.8x, and remains competitive with fixed-skeleton specialists on HumanML3D.
AI.conclusion: SAMoR demonstrates effective cross-topology motion representation and generation, achieving accurate cross-skeleton transfer while enabling text-conditioned control and editing, with a shared discrete motion codebook across rigs. It broadens motion synthesis to heterogeneous skeleton topologies.

title: One More Time: Revisiting Neural Quantum States from a Reinforcement Learning Perspective
summary: Neural quantum states (NQS) provide a flexible and scalable framework for approximating quantum many-body wavefunctions. Among NQS parameterizations, autoregressive models are especially attractive because they enable exact, independent sampling from the Born distribution, avoiding the autocorrelation and mixing issues of Markov chain methods. Yet their optimization remains comparatively underexplored: Adam is a scalable method but ignores function space geometry, while stochastic reconfiguration is principled but costly and numerically fragile in large models. To address this gap, we show that variational energy minimization can be viewed as an advantage policy-gradient problem over the Born distribution, motivating trust-region optimization for NQS training. We introduce Proximal Wavefunction Optimization (PWO), a principled trust-region algorithm that clips probability-ratio changes in the amplitude channel and phase increments in the phase channel. PWO avoids explicit matrix inversion, reuses samples across multiple updates, and combines the scalability of first-order optimization with theoretical guarantees. Across Ising and frustrated $J_1$-$J_2$ one- and two-dimensional spin systems, PWO improves stability and wall-clock convergence over Adam, minSR, and SPRING. Finally, we fine-tune a $1.5$B-parameter RWKV-7 model, demonstrating NQS optimization at a scale over three orders of magnitude beyond prior work.

AI.tldr: Proximal Wavefunction Optimization (PWO) is a trust-region method for variational energy minimization of autoregressive neural quantum states that clips probability-ratio changes (amplitude) and phase updates, enabling scalable, stable optimization and proving superior convergence over Adam, minSR, and SPRING, demonstrated on Ising/J1-J2 systems and a 1.5B RWKV-7 model.
AI.motivation: To address instability and inefficiency in optimizing autoregressive neural quantum states (NQS): first-order methods like Adam ignore function-space geometry, while stochastic reconfiguration is principled but costly and brittle at scale. A scalable, theoretically grounded optimizer is needed to train large NQS.
AI.method: Recast variational energy minimization as an advantage-policy gradient over the Born distribution and introduce Proximal Wavefunction Optimization (PWO). PWO is a trust-region algorithm that clips changes in the amplitude-channel probability ratio and constrains phase increments, avoiding explicit matrix inversions, reusing samples across multiple updates, and combining first-order scalability with theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: PWO yields improved stability and faster wall-clock convergence compared with Adam, minSR, and SPRING on Ising and frustrated J1-J2 spin systems in both 1D and 2D. Demonstrated scalability by fine-tuning a 1.5B-parameter RWKV-7 model, performing NQS optimization at a scale three orders of magnitude beyond prior work.
AI.conclusion: PWO provides a principled, scalable optimization framework for neural quantum states that aligns with the geometry of function space, offering stability, efficiency, and theoretical guarantees, enabling training of very large NQS models.

title: Patient-Specific Articulated Digital Twins from a Single Full-Body CT Scan
summary: Patient-specific anatomical models provide individualized context for surgical planning, image-guided intervention, and algorithm development. However, most CT-derived models are static: they preserve the body configuration captured at scan time, but cannot represent how the same anatomy would appear after patient repositioning. This limitation is especially important for radiographic imaging, where appearance depends jointly on imaging geometry and patient pose. We present a proof-of-concept for constructing a patient-specific articulated digital twin from a single full-body CT scan. The method fits a parametric human body model (SMPL) to obtain a patient-aligned kinematic scaffold, binds segmented bones and organs to an anatomy-aware rig, and retargets body-pose changes while preserving skeletal geometry. On three full-body CT subjects, the fitted scaffold achieved 15.8 $\pm$ 4.0 mm chamfer distance and 95.9 $\pm$ 1.8% skeletal enclosure. Recomposition at the acquisition pose preserved major radiographic structure, with overall SSIM of 0.872 $\pm$ 0.016 and PSNR of 18.5 $\pm$ 1.4 dB across paired DRRs. Across unseen target poses, the resulting twins enabled articulation while maintaining high skeletal enclosure (94.4 $\pm$ 0.4%). As a feasibility demonstration, we render the articulated twin as pose-dependent DRRs. These results suggest the feasibility of extending static, view-controllable CT simulation toward pose-controllable anatomical twins for future synthetic imaging and positioning studies.

AI.tldr: Proof-of-concept: build a patient-specific articulated digital twin from a single full-body CT using SMPL, binding segmented anatomy to an anatomy-aware rig to permit pose-controllable radiographic simulation; evaluated with good skeletal enclosure and DRR similarity, suggesting feasibility for synthetic imaging and positioning studies.
AI.motivation: Static CT-derived models preserve pose at scan time and cannot represent postural changes; radiographic appearance depends on imaging geometry and pose, limiting planning, guidance, and algorithm development.
AI.method: Fit SMPL to obtain a patient-aligned kinematic scaffold; bind bones/organs to an anatomy-aware rig; retarget body-pose changes while preserving skeletal geometry; evaluate on three full-body CT subjects by recomposing at acquisition pose and testing unseen poses; render pose-dependent DRRs and compute image similarity metrics.
AI.result: Quantitative: chamfer distance 15.8 ± 4.0 mm; skeletal enclosure 95.9 ± 1.8%. At acquisition pose, SSIM 0.872 ± 0.016; PSNR 18.5 ± 1.4 dB across DRRs. Unseen poses maintain skeletal enclosure 94.4 ± 0.4%. Feasibility demonstration with pose-dependent DRRs.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of pose-controllable anatomical twins derived from static CTs, enabling future synthetic imaging and positioning studies and extending static simulations to dynamic pose scenarios.

title: Self-Gating Attention for Efficient Time Series Forecasting
summary: Transformer architectures have shown strong potential in time series forecasting, where multi-head self-attention is widely used to capture temporal dependencies across historical timestamps. However, standard self-attention has quadratic time and memory complexity with respect to the look-back length. This cost may limit its use in resource-constrained or high-throughput forecasting systems, where fast and memory-efficient inference is important. Through qualitative and quantitative analyses, we observe that self-attention maps in time series forecasting often contain redundant patterns across different timestamps. This phenomenon can be related to the repeated temporal patterns and relatively stable temporal correlations in many real-world time series. Motivated by this observation, we propose Self-Gating Attention (SGA), a plug-and-play attention mechanism that represents the attention score with a shared learnable matrix and an input-dependent residual component. The shared matrix captures common attention patterns, while the residual component captures input-dependent variations. In this way, SGA avoids the query and key projections used in standard attention score computation, leading to linear time and score-matrix memory complexity with respect to the look-back length. We integrate SGA into several forecasting backbones and compare it with standard self-attention and lightweight attention variants on nine publicly available real-world datasets covering electricity, finance, weather, medical monitoring, human activity, and climate records. The results show that SGA improves inference efficiency on public benchmarks while maintaining competitive forecasting performance against state-of-the-art attention mechanisms. These benchmark results provide deployment-oriented evidence.

AI.tldr: Proposes Self-Gating Attention (SGA) for time-series forecasting to reduce attention complexity from quadratic to linear by using a shared learnable matrix and input-dependent residual, while maintaining competitive accuracy across nine real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Quadratic time and memory costs of standard self-attention hinder deployment in resource-constrained or high-throughput forecasting; empirical observation that self-attention maps in time series often contain redundant patterns due to repeated temporal dynamics.
AI.method: SGA factorizes attention score into a shared learnable matrix plus an input-dependent residual, avoiding per-timestamp query/key projections, yielding linear time and memory with respect to look-back length; designed as a plug-and-play module integrated into multiple forecasting backbones and compared against standard self-attention and lightweight variants.
AI.result: Inference efficiency is improved with SGA across nine public real-world datasets from electricity, finance, weather, medical monitoring, human activity, and climate domains, while maintaining competitive forecasting performance relative to state-of-the-art attention mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: SGA offers a practical, scalable attention mechanism for time-series forecasting, achieving substantial efficiency gains without sacrificing accuracy, enabling deployment in resource-limited or high-throughput settings.

title: Efficient PEFT Methods with Adaptive Checkpointing for Vision Models and VLMs on Resource Constrained Consumer-GPUs
summary: Modern pretrained vision models achieve strong accuracy but demand substantial GPU memory for fine-tuning, making edge deployment impractical. This paper compares five parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (Full FT, LoRA, AdaLoRA, QLoRA, BitFit) on Transformers- (ViT-Small, TinyViT) and Mamba-based vision backbones (Vim-Small, MambaVision-T) under an on-device VRAM budget (e.g., 2 GB), together with three gradient-checkpointing strategies (none, static, and a proposed memory-budget-aware adaptive algorithm); and we evaluate three families of foundation-model baselines: zero-shot contrastive vision language models (OpenCLIP, SigLIP), self-supervised vision backbones with lightweight evaluation protocols (DINOv2), and autoregressive VLMs for prompt-based classification (PaliGemma, MobileVLM, SmolVLM). Experiments on CIFAR-100 and DTD report accuracy, training time, energy, and the NetScore family of multi-objective metrics, which we extend with two deployment-aware variants. QLoRA and BitFit cut energy 20-30% at a 1-2% accuracy cost; the adaptive algorithm reduces peak memory 43-79% with 9-30% energy overhead. DINOv2 surpasses fine-tuned models on CIFAR-100 (0.917 vs. 0.897) at a fraction of the energy, while small autoregressive VLMs remain uncompetitive.

AI.tldr: PEFT methods enable on-device fine-tuning within strict VRAM budgets across ViT- and Mamba-based backbones, aided by a memory-budget-aware adaptive checkpointing strategy. QLoRA and BitFit reduce energy by 20–30% with ~1–2% accuracy loss; the adaptive memory strategy cuts peak memory by 43–79% with 9–30% extra energy. DINOv2 surpasses fine-tuned CIFAR-100 baselines in accuracy at lower energy; small autoregressive VLMs remain uncompetitive for on-device tasks.
AI.motivation: To reconcile the strong accuracy of pretrained vision models with the memory constraints of edge devices. The study systematically compares parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, gradient checkpointing strategies, and several foundation-model baselines across diverse backbones under realistic VRAM budgets, and introduces deployment-aware evaluation metrics.
AI.method: Experimental evaluation of five PEFT methods (Full FT, LoRA, AdaLoRA, QLoRA, BitFit) on vision backbones (ViT-Small, TinyViT, Vim-Small, MambaVision-T) under ~2 GB VRAM, with three gradient-checkpointing strategies (none, static, and a memory-budget-aware adaptive algorithm). Baselines span zero-shot vision-language models (OpenCLIP, SigLIP), self-supervised backbones (DINOv2), and autoregressive VLMs (PaliGemma, MobileVLM, SmolVLM). Datasets used include CIFAR-100 and DTD; metrics include accuracy, training time, energy, and NetScore variants (deployment-aware).
AI.result: QLoRA and BitFit reduce energy consumption by 20–30% at a 1–2% accuracy penalty. The adaptive memory-aware checkpointing reduces peak memory by 43–79% but incurs 9–30% additional energy. DINOv2 achieves higher CIFAR-100 accuracy (0.917) than fine-tuned models (0.897) with substantially lower energy; small autoregressive VLMs remain uncompetitive in on-device settings.
AI.conclusion: PEFT with memory-aware checkpointing enables practical on-device fine-tuning under tight VRAM budgets. Energy-efficient PEFT variants (QLoRA, BitFit) offer favorable trade-offs; adaptive checkpointing dramatically reduces peak memory with modest energy overhead. DINOv2 stands out among baselines for CIFAR-100, while small autoregressive VLMs are not competitive for on-device deployment.

title: DecompRL: Solving Harder Problems by Learning Modular Code Generation
summary: How can Large Language Models (LLMs) solve problems they currently cannot? Repeated sampling scales test-time compute but GPU cost grows linearly with attempts, while reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards improves single-attempt accuracy at the expense of sample diversity. Both strategies ultimately fail when the base policy has near-zero probability of producing a correct solution: no amount of sampling or gradient signal can overcome a search space that is simply too large. We take a different approach: rather than sampling harder, we make the task easier by decomposing problems into smaller, independently solvable sub-functions whose implementations can be recombined. Since off-the-shelf models are not trained for this modular generation, we introduce DecompRL, an RL algorithm that explicitly learns to decompose and implement hierarchical code structures. Recombining $k$ implementations of $n$ modules yields up to $k^{n}$ candidate solutions, shifting the bottleneck from GPU inference to cheap CPU evaluation and cutting GPU token cost by $\sim$50$\times$. On LiveCodeBench and CodeContests (Qwen~2.5~7B, Code World Model~32B), DecompRL outperforms standard and diversity-optimized RL baselines beyond $10^5$ tokens per problem, solving problems that standard generation cannot reach.

AI.tldr: DecompRL: decomposes problems into modular sub-functions and recombines implementations to solve complex coding tasks more efficiently, reducing GPU cost and surpassing baselines on LiveCodeBench and CodeContests.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of brute-force sampling and RL with rewards when the base policy has near-zero probability of correct solutions; propose a modular decomposition to simplify tasks.
AI.method: RL algorithm DecompRL learns to decompose problems into n modules and implement hierarchical code structures; combine k implementations per module, yielding k^n candidate solutions; shifts cost to CPU evaluation and reduces GPU usage by ~50x.
AI.result: On LiveCodeBench and CodeContests using Qwen 2.5 (7B) and Code World Model (32B), DecompRL outperforms standard and diversity-focused RL baselines beyond 1e5 tokens per problem, solving problems unreachable by standard generation.
AI.conclusion: Modular decomposition and recombination enable scalable problem solving in LLM-based code generation, offering substantial compute savings and improved performance over traditional generation or flat RL approaches.

title: RadiomicNet: A Hybrid Radiomics-Guided Lightweight Architecture for Interpretable Medical Image Segmentation
comment: Accepted at the IEEE ICIP 2026 LBDL 2 Workshop
summary: Deep learning has achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation, yet it suffers from critical limitations: mathematical intractability, substantial parameter requirements, and lack of clinical interpretability. We propose RadiomicNet, a novel two-stream hybrid architecture that enhances standard deep learning by integrating handcrafted radiomics features directly into the segmentation learning process. The key contribution is the Radiomics Attention Gate (RAG), which leverages Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) and Local Binary Pattern (LBP) features to modulate skip-connection attention in a lightweight MobileNetV2-based encoder-decoder, providing ante-hoc interpretability without post-hoc approximations. A novel Radiomics Consistency Loss further enforces alignment between texture complexity and prediction uncertainty, reducing Expected Calibration Error (ECE) from 0.142 to 0.118. RadiomicNet achieves a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.763 +/- 0.231 on the Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset and 0.854 +/- 0.112 on Kvasir-SEG, outperforming U-KAN by 1.2% and 1.8%, respectively (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), with only 3.27M parameters, 9.5x fewer than standard U-Net and 4.3x fewer than U-KAN. Gradient-based feature importance analysis reveals that GLCM dissimilarity (15.24%), GLCM energy (14.56%), and LBP entropy (11.49%) are the dominant radiomics cues, providing clinically meaningful explanations for segmentation decisions. The proposed approach demonstrates that compact, interpretable models grounded in domain knowledge can deliver state-of-the-art segmentation performance with substantially reduced computational overhead.

AI.tldr: RadiomicNet blends handcrafted radiomics (GLCM, LBP) with a two-stream MobileNetV2 segmentation network via a Radiomics Attention Gate to achieve ante-hoc interpretability, reduced parameters, and improved accuracy; introduces Radiomics Consistency Loss to align texture with uncertainty; achieves DSC ~0.763 (BUSI) and ~0.854 (Kvasir-SEG) with ~3.27M params, outperforming U-KAN; dominant radiomics cues identified; supports interpretable, efficient segmentation.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of DL in medical segmentation: mathematical intractability, high parameter counts, and lack of interpretability; incorporate domain knowledge (radiomics) to improve interpretability and efficiency.
AI.method: Two-stream hybrid architecture; Radiomics Attention Gate leveraging GLCM and LBP features to modulate skip connections in a MobileNetV2 encoder-decoder; Radiomics Consistency Loss to align texture complexity with prediction uncertainty; gradient-based feature importance analysis to identify dominant radiomics cues.
AI.result: DSC: BUSI 0.763±0.231; Kvasir-SEG 0.854±0.112; improvement over U-KAN by 1.2% and 1.8%; p<0.05 (Wilcoxon); params 3.27M; 9.5x fewer than U-Net, 4.3x fewer than U-KAN; ECE reduced 0.142 to 0.118; dominant radiomics cues: GLCM dissimilarity (~15%), GLCM energy (~14.6%), LBP entropy (~11.5%).
AI.conclusion: Supports that compact, domain-informed models can match or exceed state-of-the-art segmentation with lower compute; ante-hoc interpretability through RAG provides clinically meaningful explanations.

title: Neuron-Aware Active Few-Shot Learning for LLMs
summary: Active Few-Shot Learning (AFSL) adapts LLMs to specialized domains by identifying the most valuable unlabeled samples for annotation and use as few-shot demonstrations, effectively reducing human annotation costs while promoting high performance. However, existing methods typically rely on output-level signals for sample identification, such as predictive entropy or semantic similarities with test-time data based on external embeddings, which often overlook models' internal dynamics, which could pinpoint specific knowledge gaps. To bridge this gap, we propose NeuFS, a Neuron-Aware Active Few-Shot Learning framework that shifts the selection paradigm from output-level proxies to models' internal dynamics. NeuFS utilizes neuron activation patterns to represent sample directly, and includes a dual-criteria selection strategy that: (1) ensures few-shot sample diversity with neuron patterns for broader example coverage, while (2) prioritizing on identifying informative and challenging few-shot samples LLMs tend to hallucinate by quantifying neuron consensus. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that NeuFS excels in both reasoning and text classification tasks, outperforming existing AFSL baselines. Ablation studies further highlight that internal neuron activations provide a more principled and effective selection signal than external embeddings, validating the superiority of the proposed NeuFS.

AI.tldr: NeuFS uses neuron-activation patterns for active few-shot sample selection, replacing output-based signals. It employs a dual-criteria strategy—diversity of neuron patterns for broad coverage and neuron-consensus to identify informative, challenging samples prone to hallucinations—leading to improved reasoning and text classification across three datasets, with ablations showing internal activations outperform external embeddings.
AI.motivation: Existing AFSL methods rely on output-level signals (e.g., predictive entropy, external embeddings) that may miss internal model dynamics and knowledge gaps. Leveraging neuron activation patterns could provide a more direct and principled signal for selecting informative unlabeled samples to annotate as few-shot demonstrations.
AI.method: Represent each candidate sample by the model's neuron activation patterns. Apply a dual-criteria selection: (1) ensure diversity across neuron patterns to cover broad example space, (2) prioritize samples where neuron consensus indicates informativeness or error-prone cases the LLM tends to hallucinate. Validate on three datasets for reasoning and text classification, with ablations showing internal activations outperform external embeddings as signals.
AI.result: NeuFS achieves superior performance over existing AFSL baselines on both reasoning and text classification tasks. Ablation studies indicate neuron-activation signals provide a more principled and effective selection signal than external embeddings.
AI.conclusion: Neuron-aware sample selection can improve AFSL by directly leveraging internal model dynamics, yielding better performance with diverse coverage and effective identification of challenging samples; the approach is validated through experiments and ablations, supporting its efficacy over traditional output-level methods.

title: MedSaab-US: A Backpropagation-Free Multi-Scale Wavelet-Saab Framework for Thyroid Nodule Segmentation in Ultrasound Images
comment: Accepted at the IEEE ICIP 2026 LBDL 2 Workshop
summary: Deep learning (DL) methods dominate thyroid nodule segmentation in ultrasound (US) images, achieving high Dice scores but at the cost of millions of parameters, GPU-dependent training via backpropagation, and limited mathematical tractability. These limitations impede deployment in resource-constrained environments. In this paper, we propose MedSaab-US, a backpropagation-free segmentation framework grounded in the Green Learning paradigm. MedSaab-US extracts multi-scale spatial-frequency features by combining multi-level Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) with multi-scale channel-wise Saab (Subspace Approximation with Adjusted Bias) transforms at patch sizes of 5 x 5, 11 x 11, and 21 x 21 pixels. Label-Assisted Greedy (LAG) feature selection retains the most discriminative features, which are fed to an XGBoost classifier for pixel-wise prediction. The Saab transform parameters are determined analytically from data statistics, while XGBoost employs iterative greedy tree construction without requiring backpropagation. Evaluated on the TN3K dataset (2,879 training and 614 test images), MedSaab-US achieves a mean Dice coefficient of 0.4784 +/- 0.2190, precision of 0.5768, and recall of 0.5604, with a model footprint under 500K parameters and CPU-only inference in approximately 0.3 seconds per image. We present this result as an exploratory non-DL baseline for thyroid ultrasound segmentation and analyze the specific challenges posed by isoechoic nodules. An ablation study further quantifies the contribution of each pipeline component, including separate evaluations of LAG feature selection and training-set size.

AI.tldr: Backpropagation-free thyroid US segmentation (MedSaab-US) using Green Learning: multi-scale DWT + Saab transforms, LAG feature selection, and XGBoost; CPU-only, small footprint; exploratory baseline with moderate Dice on TN3K.
AI.motivation: Address deep learning drawbacks (large parameter counts, GPU training, limited interpretability) by offering a mathematically tractable, backpropagation-free segmentation framework suitable for resource-constrained deployment.
AI.method: Extract multi-scale spatial-frequency features via multi-level DWT and multi-scale channel-wise Saab transforms at patch sizes 5x5, 11x11, 21x21. Apply Label-Assisted Greedy (LAG) feature selection to retain discriminative features. Train an XGBoost classifier for pixel-wise prediction. Saab transform parameters derived analytically from data statistics; XGBoost trained with greedy tree construction, no backpropagation. Evaluation on TN3K (2,879 training, 614 test).
AI.result: Mean Dice 0.4784 ± 0.2190; precision 0.5768; recall 0.5604. Model footprint < 500k parameters. Inference on CPU ~0.3 seconds per image. Ablation study quantifies component contributions; performance as exploratory non-DL baseline and analysis of isoechoic nodules.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of a backpropagation-free Green Learning approach for thyroid US segmentation, offering a compact, CPU-friendly alternative and highlighting specific challenges posed by isoechoic nodules; ablation confirms the value of each pipeline component.

title: QFedAgent: Quantum-Enhanced Personalized Federated Learning for Multi-Agent Activity Recognition
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed devices without sharing raw data, making it suitable for privacy-sensitive robotic sensing applications. However, multi-agent systems generate heterogeneous and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) multimodal sensor streams that degrade conventional FL algorithms, while classical fusion modules introduce substantial parameter overhead and communication cost. This paper proposes QFedAgent, a hybrid quantum-classical personalized FL framework for multi-agent activity recognition. The approach integrates a variational quantum circuit fusion module that models accelerometer--gyroscope interactions through quantum state encoding and entanglement, requiring only 72 quantum rotation parameters versus 33K in classical multi-layer perceptron-based fusion, achieving approximately 10x total parameter reduction. Experiments on the OPPORTUNITY dataset under subject-based non-IID partitions demonstrate 97.7% mean test accuracy, confirming that parameter-efficient quantum fusion remains competitive with conventional federated baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes QFedAgent, a quantum-classical personalized FL framework for multi-agent activity recognition, achieving ≈10x parameter reduction with a variational quantum circuit fusion module and 97.7% mean accuracy on OPPORTUNITY under non-IID partitions.
AI.motivation: Address the data heterogeneity and high fusion overhead in federated learning for privacy-sensitive robotic sensing; existing FL struggles with non-IID multimodal streams and bulky fusion modules.
AI.method: Hybrid quantum-classical personalized FL (QFedAgent) using a variational quantum circuit fusion module to capture accelerometer–gyroscope interactions via quantum state encoding and entanglement; substantial reduction in fused model parameters (72 quantum rotation params vs ~33k in a classical MLP) evaluated under subject-based non-IID partitions.
AI.result: On the OPPORTUNITY dataset, achieved 97.7% mean test accuracy with a parameter-efficient quantum fusion, competitive with conventional federated baselines.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-augmented fusion in FL can deliver substantial parameter efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy for multi-agent activity recognition, supporting the viability of quantum components in privacy-preserving sensing systems.

title: DetailAnywhere: Fashion Detail Generation via Cross-Modal Feature Alignment Distillation
summary: Diffusion-based generative AI has achieved remarkable success in e-commerce applications such as virtual try-on, poster generation, and product background synthesis. However, when making online purchasing decisions for apparel, consumers also desire the freedom to examine specific detail regions of interest, such as collars, cuffs, and fabric textures, yet existing methods have not explicitly studied this setting. We therefore formalize a new, non-template task: Fashion Detail Generation with focus conditioning, and release FDBench, the first benchmark comprising 40K+ human-verified reference-detail pairs across 41 different categories. This task poses a unique semantic gap challenge: the model must bridge the correspondence between a focus marker on a product reference image and a photorealistic close-up view of the indicated region, while faithfully preserving the garment's identity, without any precise prompt. To bridge this gap, we propose Cross-modal Feature Alignment Distillation (CFAD), which leverages a fine-tuned DINOv3 teacher to align both branches of a Multimodal Diffusion Transformer in a shared semantic space via dual-branch distillation. To further improve consistency between generated details and reference images, we introduce a consistency reward model that jointly scores image pairs along three quality axes and optimizes generation via reinforcement learning. Experiments show that our model DetailAnywhere significantly outperforms all state-of-the-art opensource methods across all metrics and human evaluations.

AI.tldr: Introduces a new task and dataset for fashion detail generation with focus conditioning (FDBench), and a model (DetailAnywhere) that uses Cross-modal Feature Alignment Distillation (CFAD) with a DINOv3 teacher and a consistency reward model to produce photorealistic detail views aligned with focus regions, outperforming open-source baselines on multiple metrics and human judgments.
AI.motivation: Consumers want to inspect specific garment regions (e.g., collars, cuffs, textures) during online shopping, but existing diffusion-based methods lack explicit focus-conditioned detail generation and robust cross-modal alignment between a focus marker and a close-up region.
AI.method: Formalizes Fashion Detail Generation with focus conditioning and introduces FDBench (40k+ reference-detail pairs across 41 categories). Proposes CFAD: dual-branch distillation to align both branches of a Multimodal Diffusion Transformer in a shared semantic space using a fine-tuned DINOv3 teacher. Introduces a consistency reward model that scores image pairs along three quality axes and optimizes through reinforcement learning. The model, DetailAnywhere, aims to preserve garment identity while accurately rendering indicated regions.
AI.result: DetailAnywhere significantly outperforms all state-of-the-art open-source methods across all evaluation metrics and human studies on the benchmark and tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work advances fashion detail generation with focus conditioning by combining cross-modal alignment distillation and a consistency-based reinforcement objective, supported by a substantial benchmark (FDBench). It establishes a solid foundation for reliable, region-focused garment detail synthesis in e-commerce and related applications.

title: Extreme Adaptive Transformer for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting remains challenging when the underlying data contain rare but critical extreme events. This issue is particularly important in hydrologic forecasting, where streamflow distributions are often highly skewed and extreme peaks can have substantial impacts on flood monitoring, water resource management, and early warning systems. Although Transformer-based forecasting models have achieved strong performance by modeling long-range temporal dependencies, they typically treat all time points uniformly and may therefore underrepresent rare extreme patterns. In this paper, we propose the Extreme-Adaptive Transformer (Exformer), a forecasting framework designed to explicitly model temporal dependencies involving both normal and extreme events. Exformer introduces an extreme-adaptive attention mechanism composed of three sparse components: Local, Stride, and Extreme. The Local and Stride components capture short-term and periodic temporal dependencies, respectively, while the Extreme component selectively models event-aware dependencies between normal and extreme streamflow patterns. Experiments on four real-world hydrologic streamflow datasets show that Exformer achieves superior 3-day forecasting performance compared with state-of-the-art baselines. Our findings demonstrate that explicitly incorporating extreme-aware attention improves the forecasting capacity of Transformer models on imbalanced time series with rare but consequential events.

AI.tldr: Proposes Exformer, a Transformer variant with extreme-adaptive attention (Local, Stride, Extreme) to explicitly model rare extreme events in hydrologic time series, achieving superior 3-day forecasts on four datasets.
AI.motivation: Hydrologic streams are skewed with rare but impactful extreme peaks. Standard Transformers treat all time points equally and may underrepresent these events; there is a need for extreme-aware attention to capture both normal and extreme dynamics.
AI.method: Introduce Extreme-Adaptive Transformer (Exformer) with three sparse attention components: Local (short-term), Stride (periodic), and Extreme (event-aware dependencies between normal and extreme streamflow). The method targets multi-step forecasting (3-day ahead) and evaluates on four real-world hydrologic datasets.
AI.result: Exformer achieves superior 3-day forecasting performance compared with state-of-the-art baselines; ablation suggests the Extreme component improves modeling of imbalanced time series with rare but consequential events.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating extreme-aware attention enhances Transformer-based forecasting for imbalanced time series with rare events, with demonstrated gains in hydrologic flood-related forecasting and potential applicability to other domains with extreme events.

title: Efficient Waste Sorting for Circular Economy: A Confidence-guided comparison between One-Vs-All and One-Vs-Rest Classification Strategies with Human-in-the-Loop for Automated Waste Sorting
summary: The complexity of waste disposal regulations across European countries poses significant challenges for the residents and hinders the transition to a Circular Economy. In Germany, the proper sorting and disposal of household waste remains challenging across municipalities. Consequently, substantially reducing incorrectly disposed waste is vital for improving waste management and advancing the Circular Economy. AI-based waste sorting solutions can support residents through user-friendly tools, such as mobile applications, that guide proper waste disposal. To be effective in supporting the Circular Economy, however, these solutions must be configurable to reflect the specific waste sorting scheme of individual municipalities in Germany. In the scope of this work, an evaluation and analysis are performed of two prominent classification strategies: OvA and OvR. The research uses a dataset constructed in alignment with the waste categories and sorting scheme of the city of Goslar in Germany. Moreover, this work aims to extend beyond the overall performance by examining the behavior of OvA and OvR classification strategies in identifying samples likely to be misclassified. These classification strategies are compared by applying varying confidence thresholds to identify uncertain samples for subsequent human review. This evaluation aims to balance the number of misclassifications against the human effort required for data annotation.

AI.tldr: This study compares OvA and OvR classifiers for AI-based waste sorting in Germany, using a Goslar-aligned dataset, and explores uncertainty estimation via confidence thresholds to balance misclassifications and human review effort, with emphasis on municipal configurability.
AI.motivation: Regulatory complexity in European waste disposal hinders effective waste management and Circular Economy progress; AI-enabled sorting tools must be accurate and configurable to municipal schemes; focus on reducing misclassification and enabling human-in-the-loop for uncertain cases.
AI.method: Construct a dataset aligned with Goslar's waste categories; implement and compare One-vs-All (OvA) and One-vs-Rest (OvR) classifiers; apply varying confidence thresholds to identify uncertain samples; analyze misclassification behavior and quantify trade-offs between accuracy and human annotation workload.
AI.result: Not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; anticipated to discuss the relative performance of OvA vs OvR under different thresholds and the implications for municipality-specific configuration and human-in-the-loop strategies.

title: Understanding the Robustness of Distributed Self-Supervised Learning Frameworks Against Non-IID Data
summary: Recent research has introduced distributed self-supervised learning (D-SSL) approaches to leverage vast amounts of unlabeled decentralized data. However, D-SSL faces the critical challenge of data heterogeneity, and there is limited theoretical understanding of how different D-SSL frameworks respond to this challenge. To fill this gap, we present a rigorous theoretical analysis of the robustness of D-SSL frameworks under non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) settings. Our results show that pre-training with Masked Image Modeling (MIM) is inherently more robust to heterogeneous data than Contrastive Learning (CL), and that the robustness of decentralized SSL increases with average network connectivity, implying that federated learning (FL) is no less robust than decentralized learning (DecL). These findings provide a solid theoretical foundation for guiding the design of future D-SSL algorithms. To further illustrate the practical implications of our theory, we introduce MAR loss, a refinement of the MIM objective with local-to-global alignment regularization. Extensive experiments across model architectures and distributed settings validate our theoretical insights, and additionally confirm the effectiveness of MAR loss as an application of our analysis.

AI.tldr: Masked Image Modeling (MIM) is more robust to non-IID data than Contrastive Learning in distributed SSL; robustness improves with higher network connectivity (federated vs decentralized); MAR loss enhances local-global alignment and matches theoretical predictions across architectures.
